shopping-01.meaning: Asking where a product is in the shop.
shopping-01.order: A question word takes the first position, so the finite verb comes second, then the subject. The second verb (the infinitive) usually closes the verb bracket, after the object.
shopping-01.forms: Kunnen is irregular: ik kan, jij kunt or kan, wij kunnen. Melk is a de-word: de melk.
shopping-01.compare: English also puts "can" before "I", but keeps "find" next to the subject. Dutch sends the infinitive to the end.

mistake.wrong: Waar ik kan de melk vinden?
mistake.right: Waar kan ik de melk vinden?
mistake.why: In a question the finite verb comes before the subject.

shopping-01.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

shopping-02.order: A main clause has the subject first and the finite verb second. Graag comes after the verb and softens the wish; alstublieft ends the request without changing the order.
shopping-02.forms: Willen: ik wil, jij wilt, u wilt. Broodjes is the plural of het broodje (the -je ending makes it a het-word).
shopping-02.compare: English says "I would like"; Dutch uses the plain present ik wil plus graag to be just as polite.

mistake.why: The finite verb stays second; graag follows it.

shopping-02.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

shopping-03.meaning: Asking whether you can pay by card.
shopping-03.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kan), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (betalen) normally occurs toward the end.
shopping-03.forms: Kan ik: ik kan. Kaart is a de-word: de kaart.
shopping-03.compare: English keeps "pay" next to "I"; Dutch puts betalen last, after the manner phrase.

mistake.wrong: Ik kan met de kaart betalen?
mistake.right: Kan ik met de kaart betalen?
mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

shopping-03.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

shopping-04.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoeveel) takes the first position, so the finite verb (kost) comes second and the subject (deze tas) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
shopping-04.forms: Kosten: het kost, ze kosten. Tas is a de-word, so deze (a het-word would take dit).
shopping-04.compare: English needs "does" in the question; Dutch just moves the verb forward.

mistake.why: Tas is a de-word, so use deze, not dit.

shopping-04.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

shopping-05.meaning: Asking whether the shop has a smaller size too.
shopping-05.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heeft), and the subject (u) follows it.
shopping-05.forms: With hebben, u takes either heeft or hebt; both are standard. Other verbs can differ, so do not assume u always copies hij. Kleinere is kleiner plus -e: after een with a de-word (maat) the adjective takes -e.
shopping-05.compare: English uses "do you have"; Dutch simply inverts heeft and u.

mistake.wrong: Heeft u ook een kleiner maat?
mistake.right: Heeft u ook een kleinere maat?
mistake.why: Maat is a de-word, so the adjective takes -e after een.

shopping-05.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

shopping-06.meaning: Telling the cashier you do not need a bag.
shopping-06.order: A main clause: subject, then finite verb. Nodig completes the expression nodig hebben and normally occurs toward the end.
shopping-06.forms: Hebben: ik heb. Geen replaces een in a negative sentence: een zak becomes geen zak.
shopping-06.compare: English says "I do not need a bag"; Dutch uses geen plus the noun, with no "do".

mistake.wrong: Ik heb niet een zak nodig.
mistake.why: Niet een can express contrast or emphasis. To simply negate an indefinite noun phrase in this intended meaning, the ordinary form is geen. The model practises that unmarked negative form.

shopping-06.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

shopping-07.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it.
shopping-07.forms: Mogen: ik mag, jij mag, wij mogen. Bon is a de-word.
shopping-07.compare: English says "May I have the receipt?"; Dutch usually drops the final verb.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

shopping-07.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

shopping-08.meaning: Saying that these apples cost less.
shopping-08.order: A main clause with the subject first and the finite verb second. After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
shopping-08.forms: A plural subject needs zijn, not is. Goedkoper is goedkoop plus -er.
shopping-08.compare: English forms the comparative with -er too ("cheaper").

mistake.why: A plural subject takes zijn.

shopping-08.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

shopping-09.meaning: Saying what gift you are looking for.
shopping-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zoek) second (verb-second order).
shopping-09.forms: Zoeken: ik zoek. Mijn does not change before de- or het-words. Cadeau is a het-word.
shopping-09.compare: English says "I am looking for"; Dutch uses the simple present ik zoek.

mistake.why: Dutch uses the simple present here, not ben plus an infinitive.

shopping-09.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

shopping-10.meaning: Telling the seller which item you will take.
shopping-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (neem) second (verb-second order).
shopping-10.forms: Nemen: ik neem. Deze stands for a de-word or plural you are pointing at; a het-word needs dit.
shopping-10.compare: English says "I'll take this one"; Dutch uses the plain present for an immediate decision.

mistake.why: Tas is a de-word, so use deze.

shopping-10.practiceFocus: This/that and the noun they refer to
shopping-10.practiceGuide: Use dit/dat with a singular het-word and deze/die with a singular de-word or any plural. Dit boek, deze tas, deze boeken. Distance is usually nearby dit/deze versus farther away dat/die; context can also determine it. Standalone dit/dat in Dit is mijn tas is not agreement with tas: it introduces an identification. Do not transfer the attached-noun rule mechanically to every pronoun.

school-01.meaning: Politely asking a teacher to explain something again.
school-01.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunt), and the subject (u) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (uitleggen) normally occurs toward the end.
school-01.forms: Kunnen with u: u kunt (u kan is also used). Uitleggen is a separable verb but stays whole after a modal.
school-01.compare: English says "Can you explain that again?"; the word order is similar but the Dutch infinitive is last.

mistake.wrong: U kunt dat nog eens uitleggen?
mistake.right: Kunt u dat nog eens uitleggen?
mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

school-01.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

school-02.meaning: Saying you do not understand a question.
school-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (begrijp) second (verb-second order).
school-02.forms: Begrijpen: ik begrijp (the prefix be- means no ge- in the participle: begrepen). Vraag is a de-word, so deze.
school-02.compare: English says "I do not understand"; Dutch has no "do", just niet at the end.

mistake.why: Niet normally comes after the object, not before the verb.

school-02.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
school-02.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

school-03.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (betekent) comes second and the subject (dit woord) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
school-03.forms: Betekenen: het betekent. Woord is a het-word, so dit.
school-03.compare: English says "What does this word mean?" with "does"; Dutch has no auxiliary here.

mistake.why: Woord is a het-word, so use dit.

school-03.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

school-04.meaning: Politely asking for a brief opportunity to ask a question.
school-04.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vragen) normally occurs toward the end.
school-04.forms: Mag is the first-person singular of mogen. Iets means something and vragen is the infinitive. Even softens the request and suggests taking a moment; it does not demand that the question be spoken at high speed.
school-04.compare: A natural English equivalent is May I ask a quick question? Dutch keeps vragen as an infinitive after mag and places even iets before it.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

school-04.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

school-05.meaning: Saying you have already done your homework.
school-05.order: In the perfect tense the auxiliary is the finite verb in second position and the participle normally occurs toward the end.
school-05.forms: This perfect uses hebben: ik heb mijn huiswerk gemaakt. Heb is finite and gemaakt is the participle of maken. Al means already. Mijn is possessive my and stays the same before de- and het-words. The perfect does not always use hebben: some verbs and meanings use zijn, as in ik ben vertrokken.
school-05.compare: English says "I have already done"; Dutch also uses an auxiliary plus participle, but the participle is at the end.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb gemaakt mijn huiswerk al.
mistake.right: Ik heb mijn huiswerk al gemaakt.
mistake.why: Keep the object mijn huiswerk and adverb al before the participle gemaakt in this neutral model. Gemaakt closes the verb bracket; a full prepositional phrase can follow that bracket in other sentences.

school-05.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
school-05.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

school-06.meaning: Asking when something must be handed in.
school-06.order: A question word first, then the finite verb, then the subject. The infinitive normally occurs toward the end.
school-06.forms: Moeten: wij moeten. Inleveren is separable (lever ... in), but it stays whole after a modal.
school-06.compare: English says "When do we have to hand this in?"; Dutch uses moeten plus an infinitive at the end.

mistake.why: In a question the finite verb comes before the subject.

school-06.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

school-07.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Mijn pen) comes first and the finite verb (ligt) second (verb-second order).
school-07.forms: Liggen: het ligt. Op tafel has no article, which is normal in this fixed phrase (op de tafel is also possible).
school-07.compare: English just says "is"; Dutch tells how the object is placed: ligt, staat, zit.

mistake.why: Mijn pen is op tafel is grammatical. Ligt more precisely describes a pen lying on the table. A position verb is useful, not compulsory.

school-07.practiceGuide: Zitten/staan/liggen describe a position: ik zit op de stoel. Gaan zitten expresses moving into sitting: ik ga zitten. Its perfect is ik ben gaan zitten, with gaan as an infinitive in the verb cluster. A posture verb can describe an ongoing action with te: ik sta te wachten. These differ from bare is + infinitive, which is not the progressive.

school-08.meaning: Saying where you are going tomorrow.
school-08.order: When a time word is first, the finite verb must still be second, so it comes before the subject (inversion).
school-08.forms: Gaan: ik ga. Naar school has no article.
school-08.compare: English Tomorrow I am going keeps the subject before the verb. In Dutch, morgen is the first constituent, then finite ga comes before subject ik. The verb is second in the whole clause, not the first word.

mistake.why: After a fronted time word, the verb comes before the subject.

school-08.practiceFocus: One fronted constituent, then finite verb
school-08.practiceGuide: The finite verb is second in a Dutch main clause: one constituent comes first, then the finite verb, then the subject if it was not first. A constituent can contain several words (Na het werk). In a perfect/modal clause the auxiliary/modal is finite and the other verb occurs later. Fronting can emphasise an object as well as time or place; it does not create a question by itself.

school-09.order: After omdat the clause is subordinate, so the finite verb usually closes the verb bracket. In the main clause the verb stays second.
school-09.forms: Zijn: ik ben. Vertraging hebben means to be delayed.
school-09.compare: English keeps the verb in the middle of the because-clause; Dutch moves it to the end.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben te laat omdat mijn trein heeft vertraging.
mistake.right: Ik ben te laat omdat mijn trein vertraging heeft.
mistake.why: After omdat the finite verb goes to the end.

school-09.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

school-10.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (oefenen) normally occurs toward the end.
school-10.compare: English says "Can we practise together?"; the order is similar, but Dutch ends with the infinitive.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

school-10.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

transport-01.meaning: Asking which platform a train leaves from.
transport-01.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Van welk spoor) takes the first position, so the finite verb (vertrekt) comes second and the subject (de trein) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-01.forms: Vertrekken is irregular: ik vertrek, hij vertrekt; past vertrok/vertrokken; perfect is vertrokken. Welk modifies singular het spoor; welke modifies a singular de-word or a plural.
transport-01.compare: English allows From which platform does the train depart? and Which platform does the train depart from? The Dutch model keeps the complete phrase van welk spoor first, followed by finite vertrekt and subject de trein.

mistake.wrong: Welk spoor vertrekt de trein van?
mistake.right: Van welk spoor vertrekt de trein?
mistake.why: The model keeps van welk spoor together. Stranding van can occur in informal speech, but this card teaches the neutral complete fronted prepositional phrase.

transport-01.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

transport-02.meaning: Asking if you have to change trains here.
transport-02.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Moet), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (overstappen) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-02.forms: Moeten: ik moet. Here moet is finite, so overstappen stays together as an infinitive. When overstappen itself is finite in a main clause, it splits: ik stap over. Perfect: ik ben overgestapt. Overstappen means transferring from one vehicle or connection to another, not necessarily only trains.
transport-02.compare: English says "Do I have to change here?"; Dutch uses moeten plus infinitive.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

transport-02.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

transport-03.meaning: Asking if this train goes to Bruges.
transport-03.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Gaat), and the subject (deze trein) follows it.
transport-03.forms: Gaan: de trein gaat. Trein is a de-word, so deze.
transport-03.compare: English says "Does this train go to Bruges?" with "does"; Dutch only inverts.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

transport-03.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

transport-04.meaning: Politely asking for a ticket to a city.
transport-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order).
transport-04.forms: Willen: ik wil. Ticket is a het-word (een ticket).
transport-04.compare: English says "I would like"; Dutch uses the present ik wil.

mistake.wrong: Ik wil een ticket in Gent, alstublieft.
mistake.right: Ik wil een ticket naar Gent, alstublieft.
mistake.why: Naar Gent specifies the destination, as required here. In Gent instead identifies a location, so it could fit buying a ticket while in Ghent but does not express the intended destination.

transport-04.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

transport-05.meaning: Asking what time the train arrives.
transport-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe laat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (komt) comes second and the subject (de trein) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (aan) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-05.forms: Aankomen is separable: de trein komt ... aan.
transport-05.compare: English says "arrive" as one word; Dutch splits the verb in a main clause.

mistake.right: Hoe laat komt de trein aan?
mistake.why: A separable verb splits: the verb is second and the particle goes last.

transport-05.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

transport-06.meaning: Asking if a seat is free.
transport-06.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (deze plaats) follows it.
transport-06.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e: vrij. Plaats is a de-word, so deze.
transport-06.compare: English says "Is this seat free?" with the same order.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

transport-06.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

transport-07.meaning: Saying your train is delayed by ten minutes.
transport-07.order: A main clause: subject first, finite verb second. The duration comes before vertraging.
transport-07.forms: Hebben: de trein heeft. Vertraging hebben means to be delayed.
transport-07.compare: English says "is ten minutes late"; Dutch says "has ten minutes of delay".

mistake.wrong: Mijn trein is tien minuten vertraging.
mistake.right: Mijn trein heeft tien minuten vertraging.
mistake.why: Use heeft vertraging, not is vertraging.

transport-07.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

transport-08.meaning: Asking where you can buy a ticket.
transport-08.order: A question word first, then the finite verb, then the subject. The infinitive normally occurs toward the end.
transport-08.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Ticket is a het-word.
transport-08.compare: English places buy before its object my ticket. Dutch puts the object mijn ticket before infinitive kopen, while finite kan follows waar and precedes subject ik.

mistake.wrong: Waar ik kan mijn ticket kopen?
mistake.right: Waar kan ik mijn ticket kopen?
mistake.why: In a question the finite verb comes before the subject.

transport-08.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

transport-09.meaning: Saying where you will get off.
transport-09.order: A main clause: subject, finite verb, then the rest. The particle uit normally occurs toward the end.
transport-09.forms: Uitstappen is separable: ik stap ... uit. Volgende takes -e before the de-word halte.
transport-09.compare: English says "I get off"; Dutch splits stap and uit.

mistake.wrong: Ik uitstap bij de volgende halte.
mistake.right: Ik stap bij de volgende halte uit.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

transport-09.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

transport-10.meaning: Politely asking for help with your luggage.
transport-10.order: Kunt is the finite modal and starts this polite yes/no question, followed by subject u. Mij is the person receiving help. Helpen stays an infinitive after kunt. The full prepositional phrase met mijn bagage naturally follows helpen here; closing the verb bracket does not mean being the last word of the sentence.
transport-10.forms: Kunnen: u kunt or u kan; both are standard. Mij means me, while mijn means my. Helpen met iets means help with something. Kunt u mij met mijn bagage helpen? is another natural order.
transport-10.compare: English says "Can you help me with my luggage?" with the same order.

mistake.wrong: Kunt u helpen mij met mijn bagage?
mistake.right: Kunt u mij helpen met mijn bagage?
mistake.why: Put the object before the infinitive.

transport-10.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

home-01.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (zijn) comes second and the subject (mijn sleutels) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
home-01.forms: Zijn agrees with the plural subject: sleutels zijn. Mijn does not change.
home-01.compare: English says "Where are my keys?" with the same order.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

home-01.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

home-02.meaning: Saying that you are busy cooking right now.
home-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (koken) normally occurs toward the end.
home-02.forms: Zijn: ik ben. After aan het the verb is an infinitive, not conjugated.
home-02.compare: English uses "-ing" (I am cooking); Dutch uses ben aan het koken.

mistake.why: The progressive needs aan het before the infinitive.

home-02.practiceFocus: An action happening now: aan het
home-02.practiceGuide: Use a conjugated form of zijn + aan het + infinitive. The object normally comes before aan het: Hij is de ramen aan het wassen. These models place aan het directly before the infinitive. With separable verbs, both de ramen aan het schoonmaken and de ramen schoon aan het maken are correct. Dutch simple present can also mean an English ongoing action. Aan het werk contains the NOUN werk, whereas aan het werken contains an infinitive; they are not identical constructions.

home-03.meaning: Asking if someone locked the door.
home-03.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heb), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedaan) normally occurs toward the end.
home-03.forms: This perfect uses hebben: heb je ... gedaan? Doen has participle gedaan. Compare statement je hebt and question heb je: subject je follows the auxiliary, so the ordinary added -t is omitted. De deur op slot doen means lock the door. Other perfects may use zijn, depending on verb and meaning.
home-03.compare: English says "Have you locked the door?"; the participle is also late, but Dutch puts it in the final verb bracket.

mistake.wrong: Je hebt de deur op slot gedaan?
mistake.right: Heb je de deur op slot gedaan?
mistake.why: This statement order can ask for confirmation or express surprise with questioning intonation. For the neutral question/request practised here, put the finite verb before the subject. With following subject je, use heb je or kun je, rather than je hebt or je kunt.

home-03.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
home-03.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

home-04.meaning: Saying you have already done the dishes.
home-04.order: In the perfect tense the auxiliary is second and the participle normally occurs toward the end.
home-04.forms: Perfect: ik heb gedaan. De afwas doen means to do the dishes.
home-04.compare: English says "I have already done the dishes"; Dutch puts the participle last.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb gedaan de afwas al.
mistake.right: Ik heb de afwas al gedaan.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

home-04.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
home-04.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

home-05.meaning: Asking someone to open the window.
home-05.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kun), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (openmaken) normally occurs toward the end.
home-05.forms: Kunnen with je: kun je (the -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb). Raam is a het-word.
home-05.compare: English says "Can you open the window?"; the order is similar.

mistake.why: This statement order can ask for confirmation or express surprise with questioning intonation. For the neutral question/request practised here, put the finite verb before the subject. With following subject je, use heb je or kun je, rather than je hebt or je kunt.

home-05.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

home-06.meaning: Telling someone a cup is theirs.
home-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-06.forms: Dit is a standalone demonstrative introducing an identification: dit is jouw kopje. It is not an adjective attached to kopje. Dutch can also say Dit is jouw tas even though tas is a de-word. Before a noun directly, use dit kopje but deze tas. Jouw/je means your; jou is the object form you.
home-06.compare: English says "This is your cup"; the order is the same.

mistake.why: The possessive is jouw (or je), not jou.

home-06.practiceFocus: This/that and the noun they refer to
home-06.practiceGuide: Use dit/dat with a singular het-word and deze/die with a singular de-word or any plural. Dit boek, deze tas, deze boeken. Distance is usually nearby dit/deze versus farther away dat/die; context can also determine it. Standalone dit/dat in Dit is mijn tas is not agreement with tas: it introduces an identification. Do not transfer the attached-noun rule mechanically to every pronoun.

home-07.meaning: Saying you cycle home after work.
home-07.order: Na het werk is one time constituent in first position. Fiets is the finite verb in second position, followed by subject ik. Second position means second constituent, not second word.
home-07.forms: Fietsen: ik fiets. Naar huis means home.
home-07.compare: English keeps "I" before the verb; Dutch must put the verb second.

mistake.wrong: Na het werk ik fiets naar huis.
mistake.right: Na het werk fiets ik naar huis.
mistake.why: After a fronted time phrase, the verb comes before the subject.

home-07.practiceFocus: One fronted constituent, then finite verb
home-07.practiceGuide: The finite verb is second in a Dutch main clause: one constituent comes first, then the finite verb, then the subject if it was not first. A constituent can contain several words (Na het werk). In a perfect/modal clause the auxiliary/modal is finite and the other verb occurs later. Fronting can emphasise an object as well as time or place; it does not create a question by itself.

home-08.meaning: Saying there is milk in the fridge.
home-08.order: Er comes first, the verb second, then the real subject. Dutch uses staat for things standing or placed somewhere.
home-08.forms: Staan: singular er staat, plural er staan. Milk is understood through its container here, such as a standing carton or bottle. Compare Er staan twee pakken melk in de koelkast. Er is melk is also grammatical and simply states availability.
home-08.compare: English says "There is"; Dutch says "There stands".

mistake.wrong: Er is melk in de koelkast.
mistake.right: Er staat melk in de koelkast.
mistake.why: Er is melk in de koelkast is grammatical. Staat can describe a container standing in the fridge. Dutch often chooses a position verb, but is is not forbidden.

home-08.practiceGuide: Existential er introduces something present or available: er is/zijn, er ligt/staat/hangt. The verb agrees with the noun introduced (er is een boek, er zijn boeken). Ligt/staat/hangt is already the finite verb, so do not add another is. Position verbs make the physical arrangement explicit. If a place phrase comes first, normal V2 still applies.

home-09.meaning: Saying you are tidying your room.
home-09.order: A main clause: the verb is second and the separable particle op normally occurs toward the end.
home-09.forms: Opruimen means tidy up or put things away: ik ruim ... op; perfect ik heb opgeruimd. Schoonmaken means clean dirt away: ik maak ... schoon; perfect ik heb schoongemaakt. You can tidy a room without cleaning it, or clean its floor after putting things away.
home-09.compare: English says "I tidy up my room" with "up" next to the verb; Dutch puts op at the end.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

home-09.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

home-10.order: Zullen we plus an infinitive makes a suggestion. The question starts with the finite verb and ends with the infinitive.
home-10.compare: English says "Shall we eat together?"; the order is the same.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

home-10.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

conversation-01.meaning: Saying you speak a little Dutch.
conversation-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (spreek) second (verb-second order).
conversation-01.forms: Spreken: ik spreek, jij/hij spreekt, wij spreken; simple past sprak/spraken; perfect heb/heeft gesproken. Een beetje means a little. The language name has no article in een beetje Nederlands spreken. An article is possible in other constructions, such as het Nederlands van vandaag (the Dutch of today).
conversation-01.compare: English says "a little Dutch"; Dutch says "a bit Dutch".

mistake.wrong: Ik spreek een beetje de Nederlands.
mistake.why: This amount of a language is een beetje Nederlands, without an article. De Nederlands is not the name of the language. The article het can occur in other expressions, such as het Nederlands van vandaag.

conversation-01.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-02.meaning: Asking someone to speak a bit more slowly.
conversation-02.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kun), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (spreken) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-02.forms: Kun je: the -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb. Langzamer is the comparative of langzaam.
conversation-02.compare: English says "Can you speak more slowly?" with the adverb after "speak"; Dutch puts it before the infinitive.

mistake.why: In this neutral request, put the complete adverb phrase wat langzamer before the infinitive spreken. Do not infer that every possible Dutch phrase must precede the last verb: full prepositional phrases, for example, can follow the verb bracket.

conversation-02.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

conversation-03.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe) takes the first position, so the finite verb (gaat) comes second and the subject (het) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-03.forms: Gaan: het gaat. Met je (informal) or met u (polite).
conversation-03.compare: English says "How are you?"; Dutch literally says "How goes it with you?".

mistake.why: Dutch uses gaat het met je for how someone is.

conversation-03.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (woon) second (verb-second order).
conversation-04.forms: Wonen: ik woon, jij woont, wij wonen; past woonde/woonden; perfect heb gewoond. With this city name use in Roeselare. Also in Gent and in België. This is not a claim that every geographical name always takes in.
conversation-04.compare: English says "I live in"; the order is the same.

mistake.why: For residence in the city of Roeselare use in Roeselare. Op Roeselare does not express the intended location in this sentence.

conversation-04.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (kom) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-05.forms: Komen: je komt, but the -t drops when je follows: kom je.
conversation-05.compare: English says "Where are you from?"; Dutch literally says "Where come you from?".

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject and the -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb.

conversation-05.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-06.meaning: Asking if someone has time tomorrow.
conversation-06.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heb), and the subject (je) follows it.
conversation-06.forms: Heb je: the -t of hebt drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb.
conversation-06.compare: English says "Do you have time tomorrow?" with "do".

mistake.why: This statement order can ask for confirmation or express surprise with questioning intonation. For the neutral question/request practised here, put the finite verb before the subject. With following subject je, use heb je or kun je, rather than je hebt or je kunt.

conversation-06.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

conversation-07.order: A main clause: subject then finite verb. Niet comes before the infinitive at the end.
conversation-07.compare: English says "I cannot come today"; Dutch puts niet before komen.

mistake.why: Niet comes before the infinitive at the end.

conversation-07.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

conversation-08.order: A suggestion starts with Zullen we, and the infinitive normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-08.forms: Om drie uur gives a clock time. Afspreken stays whole after zullen.
conversation-08.compare: English says "Shall we meet at three?"; Dutch uses the verb afspreken (arrange to meet).

mistake.wrong: Zullen we om drie uur spreken af?
mistake.right: Zullen we om drie uur afspreken?
mistake.why: After a modal the separable verb stays whole: afspreken.

conversation-08.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

conversation-09.meaning: Saying you are tired but feel good.
conversation-09.order: Maar joins two main clauses, so each keeps its own verb in second position.
conversation-09.forms: Zich voelen: ik voel me. After zijn and voelen the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-09.compare: English says "I feel good"; Dutch needs the reflexive me.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben moe, maar ik voel goed.
mistake.right: Ik ben moe, maar ik voel me goed.
mistake.why: Voelen is reflexive here: ik voel me.

conversation-09.practiceFocus: Reflexive pronouns refer to the subject
conversation-09.practiceGuide: Match the reflexive to the subject: ik/me, jij/je, hij-zij/zich, wij/ons, jullie/je, zij plural/zich. A question can contain two je forms: Voel je je beter? The first is the subject, the second reflexive. The reflexive belongs to the Dutch expression even if natural English does not say myself. In an embedded clause the verb group normally closes the clause.

conversation-10.order: This is a short phrase with no finite verb, so there is no verb-second order to follow: bedankt comes first and voor introduces what you are thanking someone for.
conversation-10.forms: Je means your before a noun (je hulp).
conversation-10.compare: English says "Thanks for your help"; Dutch uses voor too.

mistake.why: Bedankt voor introduces what you are thanking someone for.

conversation-10.practiceFocus: Short expressions and their intended meaning
conversation-10.practiceGuide: Some useful expressions are fragments rather than full subject-plus-verb clauses: Hartelijk dank, Graag gedaan. Do not invent V2 inversion for a phrase with no finite verb. Learn what the expression does in the conversation, and compare related full sentences. A polite formula can have several natural English equivalents.

conversation-11.meaning: Saying someone is worried about losing his keys.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: over het verliezen van zijn sleutels

conversation-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (maakt) second (verb-second order).
conversation-11.forms: Zich zorgen maken over means worry about. Match the reflexive to the person worrying: ik maak me, jij maakt je, hij maakt zich, wij maken ons. Here hij is worried about losing his own keys. Het verliezen names an activity as a noun; van zijn sleutels says what he might lose. Zijn means his before sleutels, not the verb be.
conversation-11.compare: English says "He worries about losing"; Dutch uses zich zorgen maken over.

mistake.wrong: Hij maakt me zorgen over zijn sleutels.
mistake.right: Hij maakt zich zorgen over zijn sleutels.
mistake.why: The intended person worrying is hij, so the reflexive is zich. Me refers to the speaker instead and would not express his own worry. Keep over het verliezen van zijn sleutels for what worries him.

conversation-11.practiceFocus: Reflexive pronouns refer to the subject
conversation-11.practiceGuide: Match the reflexive to the subject: ik/me, jij/je, hij-zij/zich, wij/ons, jullie/je, zij plural/zich. A question can contain two je forms: Voel je je beter? The first is the subject, the second reflexive. The reflexive belongs to the Dutch expression even if natural English does not say myself. In an embedded clause the verb group normally closes the clause.

administration-01.meaning: Asking for the current exchange rate.
administration-01.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de huidige wisselkoers) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
administration-01.forms: Huidige takes -e because it follows the article de. Wisselkoers is a de-word.
administration-01.compare: English has the same order: "What is the current exchange rate?"

mistake.why: After de the adjective takes -e.

administration-01.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

shopping-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (betaal) second (verb-second order).
shopping-11.forms: Betalen is regular: ik betaal, participle betaald. Mijn stays the same before de-words.
shopping-11.compare: English also says "with" (met) for the means of payment.

mistake.why: Use met for the means of payment.

shopping-11.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

weather-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
weather-01.forms: After zijn an adjective takes no -e. Het is a dummy subject for weather.
weather-01.compare: English also uses a dummy subject: "It is very foggy".

mistake.why: An adjective after zijn takes no -e.

weather-01.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

food-01.meaning: Saying you had already baked the bread.
food-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gebakken) normally occurs toward the end.
food-01.forms: Had plus participle is the past perfect: something done before another moment in the past. Bakken: gebakken. Brood is a het-word.
food-01.compare: English also says "I had already baked", with the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts it last.

mistake.wrong: Ik had het brood gebakken al.
mistake.right: Ik had het brood al gebakken.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

food-01.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
food-01.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

work-01.meaning: Saying you are checking the stock.
work-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (controleer) second (verb-second order).
work-01.forms: Controleren: ik controleer; the participle is gecontroleerd. Voorraad is a de-word.
work-01.compare: English says "I am checking" (progressive); Dutch uses the simple present.

mistake.why: Dutch uses the simple present here.

work-01.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

health-01.meaning: Saying that resting is good for you.
health-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Rusten) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
health-01.forms: The verb is singular because the subject is one activity. No -e on goed after is.
health-01.compare: English uses the -ing form (Resting); Dutch uses the infinitive.

mistake.why: Use the infinitive as the subject.

health-01.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
health-01.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

conversation-12.meaning: Asking for someone's opinion on something.
conversation-12.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (uw mening) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-12.forms: Uw is the polite your (with u). Hierover is hier plus over: about this.
conversation-12.compare: English says "about this" as two words; Dutch joins hier and over.

mistake.wrong: Wat is uw mening over hier?
mistake.why: Hier and over join into hierover.

conversation-12.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-13.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (ging) comes second and the subject (zij) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-13.forms: The simple past of gaan is ging (irregular). Waar ... heen asks where to.
conversation-13.compare: English needs "did" in the question; Dutch just uses ging.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-13.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-02.meaning: Saying you will prepare a report.
work-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (opstellen) normally occurs toward the end.
work-02.forms: Zullen: ik zal. Opstellen is a separable verb but stays whole after a modal. Rapport is a het-word.
work-02.compare: English says "I will prepare a report"; Dutch ends with the infinitive.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

work-02.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

home-11.meaning: Saying they were looking for a flat.
home-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (waren) second (verb-second order).
home-11.forms: The past of zijn: ik was, wij waren, ze waren. Op zoek zijn naar means to look for.
home-11.compare: English uses a progressive ("were looking for"); Dutch uses zijn op zoek naar.

mistake.right: Ze waren op zoek naar een flat.
mistake.why: Op zoek zijn naar is an idiom meaning be looking for. Dutch also has the ordinary verb zoeken: Ze zochten een flat. The issue in the first phrase is using a bare infinitive after waren.

home-11.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De vergadering) comes first and the finite verb (eindigde) second (verb-second order).
work-03.forms: Eindigen has stem eindig. Singular simple past adds -de: de vergadering eindigde. Plural adds -den: de vergaderingen eindigden. These are forms of this verb, not a rule that every singular past ends in -de; other regular verbs use -te, and irregular verbs have their own forms.
work-03.compare: English "The meeting ended" works the same way.

mistake.why: This subject is one meeting, so eindigen takes singular past eindigde here. With plural de vergaderingen use eindigden. Do not generalise -de to every singular past verb.

work-03.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

conversation-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gepraat) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-14.forms: This perfect uses hebben: we hebben urenlang gepraat. Hebben is finite and agrees with plural we; gepraat is the participle of praten. The perfect can use zijn with other verbs/meanings, such as we zijn vertrokken. Compare simple past we praatten, with double t, and present we praten. Urenlang means for hours.
conversation-14.compare: English says "We talked" (simple past); Dutch says "We have talked".

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-14.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
conversation-14.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (houd) second (verb-second order).
work-04.forms: Houden: ik houd or ik hou, both are correct. U is the polite you.
work-04.compare: English says "keep you informed"; Dutch says op de hoogte houden.

mistake.right: Ik houd u op de hoogte.
mistake.why: Use the fixed phrase op de hoogte houden.

work-04.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-15.meaning: Telling the time: half past five.
conversation-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-15.forms: Half zes means half an hour before six, which is 5:30.
conversation-15.compare: English says "half past five"; Dutch counts towards the next hour.

mistake.wrong: Het is half vijf (when you mean 5:30).
mistake.why: Half zes is 5:30; half vijf is 4:30.

conversation-15.practiceGuide: Sinds identifies a starting point that continues to the reference time: Ik woon hier sinds vorig jaar. Dutch commonly uses PRESENT tense for a situation still true, where English uses have lived/have worked. A duration is different: Ik heb twee uur gefietst. Fronted time expressions form one constituent and trigger main-clause inversion. Learn clock expressions carefully: half zes is 5:30, not 6:30.

weather-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (hou) second (verb-second order).
weather-02.forms: Houden van: both ik hou and ik houd are correct. Zonnige takes -e before the plural dagen.
weather-02.compare: English has no preposition ("love sunny days"); Dutch needs van.

mistake.why: Houden van means to like or love: the preposition van is required.

weather-02.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-05.meaning: Saying he is done reading the report.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het lezen van het rapport

work-05.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
work-05.forms: Klaar zijn met means to be finished with. Het lezen is an infinitive used as a noun.
work-05.compare: English says "He has finished reading"; Dutch uses is klaar met.

mistake.wrong: Hij is klaar lezen het rapport.
mistake.right: Hij is klaar met het lezen van het rapport.
mistake.why: To be finished with is klaar zijn met in Dutch.

work-05.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-05.practiceGuide: Klaar met means finished with; bezig met means busy with. Both can introduce a noun-like activity: het lezen van het rapport. Compare Hij is klaar met lezen (finished reading) and Hij is bezig met lezen (still occupied with reading). The related examples practise naming activities and this contrast; being busy does not mean being finished.

conversation-16.meaning: Asking if someone will need help.
conversation-16.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Zul), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (hebben) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-16.forms: Zul je and zal je are both standard future questions. Compare je zult with zul je, where subject je follows the finite verb and the added -t is omitted. Hulp nodig hebben means need help: hebben remains an infinitive after zul/zal, with hulp nodig between the finite verb and infinitive.
conversation-16.compare: English "Will you need help?" has the same inversion.

mistake.why: Je zult hulp nodig hebben? can be a confirmation question with questioning intonation. For the neutral question here, use Zul je hulp nodig hebben? or Zal je hulp nodig hebben? The model is not a rule that statement-order confirmation questions are impossible.

conversation-16.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

conversation-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te blijven) closes the sentence.
conversation-17.forms: Zin hebben om te means to feel like doing something. After te the verb is an infinitive.
conversation-17.compare: English uses an -ing form ("feel like staying"); Dutch uses om te plus infinitive.

mistake.right: We hebben zin om te blijven.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

conversation-17.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

shopping-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (kocht) second (verb-second order).
shopping-12.forms: Kopen has an irregular past: kocht, plural kochten. Souvenir is a het-word.
shopping-12.compare: English "He bought" is also an irregular past.

mistake.why: The past of kopen is kocht.

shopping-12.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

weather-03.meaning: Saying you will check the weather.
weather-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (controleren) normally occurs toward the end.
weather-03.forms: Zullen: wij zullen. Weer is a het-word.
weather-03.compare: English "We will check the weather" keeps check next to will; Dutch puts it last.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

weather-03.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

conversation-18.meaning: Saying you have forgotten someone's name.
conversation-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (vergeten) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-18.forms: Ik ben vergeten is a perfect with zijn. Vergeten can also use hebben in appropriate contexts. Je before naam is possessive your, not the subject pronoun you.
conversation-18.compare: English uses have in I have forgotten your name. Dutch commonly uses zijn here: ik ben je naam vergeten. Ben is a perfect auxiliary in this sentence, not a passive meaning that someone has forgotten the speaker.

mistake.why: Both hebben and zijn occur with vergeten, with differences in meaning and regional preference. Zijn is especially common for no longer remembering something; hebben is common for failing to do something. Do not treat heb ... vergeten as automatically ungrammatical.

conversation-18.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
conversation-18.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

transport-11.meaning: Asking if a place can be reached on foot.
transport-11.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it.
transport-11.forms: Te plus infinitive here means can be done: te lopen.
transport-11.compare: English "Can you walk there?" is built differently.

mistake.why: Use te before the infinitive in this phrase.

transport-11.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

food-02.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it.
food-02.forms: Mogen: ik mag. Wat before a noun means some.
food-02.compare: English says "May I have some water?"; Dutch drops have.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

food-02.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-06.meaning: Promising to get back to someone about something.
work-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kom) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (terug) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
work-06.forms: Terugkomen op splits in a main clause: ik kom ... terug. Er plus op becomes erop.
work-06.compare: English "I will get back to it" uses a different verb; Dutch uses terugkomen op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

work-06.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

food-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedronken) normally occurs toward the end.
food-03.forms: Drinken: gedronken. Dutch often uses the perfect where English uses the simple past.
food-03.compare: English says "We drank coffee"; Dutch says "We have drunk coffee".

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

food-03.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
food-03.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

transport-12.meaning: Saying someone left an hour ago.
transport-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (vertrokken) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-12.forms: Vertrekken uses zijn in the perfect: is vertrokken. Do not generalise this to every movement activity: ik heb gefietst describes cycling, whereas ik ben naar huis gefietst describes reaching home. Geleden follows the duration and means ago.
transport-12.compare: English says "He left an hour ago" (simple past); Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.wrong: Hij heeft een uur geleden vertrokken.
mistake.right: Hij is een uur geleden vertrokken.
mistake.why: Vertrekken takes zijn in this departure sense: hij is vertrokken. Learn auxiliary choice with the particular verb; a different verb such as verlaten uses hebben: hij heeft het gebouw verlaten.

transport-12.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
transport-12.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

home-12.meaning: Saying you would rather stay at home.
home-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (blijf) second (verb-second order).
home-12.forms: Blijven: ik blijf, ik bleef, ik ben gebleven. Liever is the comparative of graag and expresses a preference. Ik blijf liever thuis means I would rather stay home; liever does not itself mark a past or conditional tense. In this model it follows finite blijf, but adverb position depends on the rest of the clause.
home-12.compare: English says "would rather"; Dutch just uses liever.

mistake.why: The comparative of graag is liever.

home-12.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-07.order: In the past tense the verb is second and the particle schoon normally occurs toward the end.
work-07.forms: Schoonmaken splits: maakte ... schoon. Bureau is a het-word.
work-07.compare: English "She cleaned the desk" has no separate particle.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

work-07.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

conversation-19.meaning: Saying something sounded a little strange.
conversation-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (klonk) second (verb-second order).
