conversation-19.forms: Klinken: het klinkt; simple past het klonk, plural klonken; perfect het heeft geklonken. Enigszins means somewhat and is fairly formal. Vreemd describes how it sounded: it is a predicate adjective after linking klonk and has no attributive -e. Compare a noun phrase with an adjective: een vreemd geluid, het vreemde geluid.
conversation-19.compare: English "It sounded somewhat strange" is the same.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-19.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

health-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
health-02.compare: English "I need a doctor" is one verb; Dutch splits it around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig goes after the object.

health-02.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

conversation-20.meaning: Asking someone to say if they need anything.
conversation-20.order: The first part is an imperative. After als the clause is subordinate, so the finite verb hebt usually closes the verb bracket.
conversation-20.forms: Laat het me weten means let me know. Hebt is the je-form of hebben when je comes before the verb.
conversation-20.compare: English keeps "need" next to "you"; Dutch moves hebt to the end.

mistake.wrong: Laat het me weten als je hebt iets nodig.
mistake.right: Laat het me weten als je iets nodig hebt.
mistake.why: After als the finite verb goes to the end.

conversation-20.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

leisure-01.meaning: Saying they have seen the film.
leisure-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gezien) normally occurs toward the end.
leisure-01.forms: Zien has an irregular participle: gezien.
leisure-01.compare: English "They have seen the film" is the same idea.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

leisure-01.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
leisure-01.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-08.meaning: Saying you are confirming the details.
work-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (bevestig) second (verb-second order).
work-08.forms: Bevestigen: ik bevestig; the participle is bevestigd (no ge-).
work-08.compare: English says "I am confirming"; Dutch uses the simple present.

mistake.why: With ik the verb loses -en.

work-08.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-09.meaning: Saying she is busy writing an email.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het schrijven van een e-mail

work-09.order: Ze is the subject, meaning she in this situation; is is the finite form of zijn. Druk bezig describes being occupied. Met introduces the noun-like activity het schrijven van een e-mail.
work-09.forms: An infinitive used as an activity noun takes het: het schrijven, not de schrijven. Van een e-mail names what is being written. Compare the verbal progressive Ze is druk een e-mail aan het schrijven: aan het takes the infinitive schrijven, with een e-mail as its object.
work-09.compare: English says "busy writing"; Dutch says bezig met het schrijven.

mistake.wrong: Ze is bezig schrijven een e-mail.
mistake.right: Ze is druk bezig met het schrijven van een e-mail.
mistake.why: This noun-like activity needs met het schrijven van een e-mail. Alternatively use a te-infinitive with its object: Ze is bezig een e-mail te schrijven. A bare schrijven followed by its object does not fit after is bezig.

work-09.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-09.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

conversation-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). Eens normally occurs toward the end of the clause.
conversation-21.forms: Het eens zijn met means agree with. Met becomes mee in a pronominal adverb: daar + mee = daarmee. Ik ben het daarmee eens means I agree with that.
conversation-21.compare: The whole expression het eens zijn met corresponds to English agree with. Daarmee refers to with that; ermee refers to with it. Het remains a fixed part of the Dutch expression. Do not interpret the English word agree as a word-for-word translation of ben or eens alone.

mistake.why: Include het and put eens last.

conversation-21.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

leisure-02.meaning: Saying what you used to do.
leisure-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ging) second (verb-second order).
leisure-02.forms: Gaan has an irregular past: ging.
leisure-02.compare: English says "I used to go"; Dutch uses the simple past with vroeger.

mistake.wrong: Ik gaan vroeger naar de bioscoop.
mistake.right: Ik ging vroeger naar de bioscoop.
mistake.why: Gaan is irregular: the past is ging (singular) and gingen (plural).

leisure-02.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

transport-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (vertrokken) second (verb-second order).
transport-13.forms: Vertrekken has an irregular past: vertrok (singular), vertrokken (plural).
transport-13.compare: English "They left early." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: The past of vertrekken is irregular.

transport-13.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

conversation-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dat) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-22.forms: Idee is a het-word, so after een the adjective takes no -e: een geweldig idee.
conversation-22.compare: English "That is a great idea!" has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: Het-word after een: no -e.

conversation-22.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

conversation-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-23.forms: Waard zijn means to be worth. Het proberen is an infinitive used as a noun.
conversation-23.compare: English says "worth trying"; Dutch says het proberen waard.

mistake.why: Waard goes to the end of this expression: het proberen waard.

conversation-23.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
conversation-23.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-10.meaning: Asking to work together on this.
work-10.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (samenwerken) normally occurs toward the end.
work-10.forms: Hieraan is hier plus aan: on this.
work-10.compare: English says "work together on this"; the order is similar.

mistake.why: Hieraan normally precedes samenwerken in this compact model. Learn this preferred model order rather than assuming all adverbs must always occur in a single fixed position.

work-10.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

leisure-03.meaning: Saying they are practising their drawing skills.
leisure-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (oefenen) second (verb-second order).
leisure-03.forms: Oefenen: ze oefenen (plural). Hun means their before a noun.
leisure-03.compare: English "They are practising" is a progressive; Dutch uses the simple present.

mistake.why: The possessive for they is hun, placed before the noun.

leisure-03.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (belde) second (verb-second order).
conversation-24.forms: Bellen is regular: belde. Jou is the stressed object form of je.
conversation-24.compare: English "She called you." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: Use the object form jou (or je).

conversation-24.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

conversation-25.meaning: Saying you have met new people.
conversation-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (ontmoet) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-25.forms: Ontmoeten has no ge- in the participle (ont- is an inseparable prefix). Nieuwe takes -e before the plural.
conversation-25.compare: English says "I met" (simple past); Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.why: Verbs that start with ont- have no ge-.

conversation-25.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
conversation-25.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

weather-04.meaning: Saying it is about to rain.
weather-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (regenen) normally occurs toward the end. Gaan plus an infinitive says what is about to happen.
weather-04.forms: Gaan: het gaat. There is no te after gaan.
weather-04.compare: English says "It is going to rain"; Dutch is the same idea.

mistake.why: After gaan the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

weather-04.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

home-13.meaning: Saying he is responsible for tidying up.
home-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-13.forms: Verantwoordelijk zijn voor means to be responsible for.
home-13.compare: English "responsible for tidying up" uses -ing; Dutch uses voor het opruimen (an infinitive used as a noun).

mistake.wrong: Hij is verantwoordelijk om het opruimen.
mistake.right: Hij is verantwoordelijk voor het opruimen.
mistake.why: Use voor after verantwoordelijk.

home-13.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
home-13.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

food-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (dronk) second (verb-second order).
food-04.forms: Drinken has an irregular past: dronk, plural dronken.
food-04.compare: English "I drank a lemonade" is an irregular past too; Dutch drinken becomes dronk (singular) and dronken (plural).

mistake.why: The past of drinken is dronk.

food-04.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

conversation-26.meaning: Saying that thinking of someone makes you smile.
conversation-26.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Aan jou denken) comes first and the finite verb (doet) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (glimlachen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-26.forms: Doen plus an infinitive means to make someone do something. There is no te.
conversation-26.compare: English says "makes me smile"; Dutch says doet me glimlachen.

mistake.wrong: Aan jou denken doet me te glimlachen.
mistake.right: Aan jou denken doet me glimlachen.
mistake.why: After doen the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

conversation-26.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
conversation-26.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

home-14.meaning: Saying you need to charge your phone.
home-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (moet) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (opladen) normally occurs toward the end.
home-14.forms: Moeten: ik moet. Opladen stays whole after a modal.
home-14.compare: English says "I need to charge my phone"; Dutch puts opladen last.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

home-14.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

school-11.meaning: Telling someone to keep trying until they understand.
school-11.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Blijf) and leaves out the subject. After totdat the clause is subordinate, so its finite verb (snapt) comes toward the end of its subordinate clause.
school-11.forms: Blijven plus an infinitive means to keep on doing. Snappen: je snapt.
school-11.compare: English says "until you get it"; Dutch moves snapt to the end.

mistake.wrong: Blijf proberen totdat je snapt het.
mistake.right: Blijf proberen totdat je het snapt.
mistake.why: After totdat the verb goes to the end.

school-11.practiceFocus: Proberen: try a thing or try to act
school-11.practiceGuide: Proberen means try. Ik probeer is present; ik probeerde is singular simple past; wij probeerden is plural past; ik heb geprobeerd uses the participle with hebben. The regular participle is ge + probeer + d. A thing can be tried directly; trying to do something uses proberen + te + infinitive. After zal the verb becomes proberen: ik zal proberen te bellen. Trying on clothes usually uses passen; tasting food can use proeven.

work-11.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wanneer) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de deadline) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
work-11.forms: Deadline is a de-word: de deadline, een nieuwe deadline. Wanneer asks for a time or date; finite is comes before subject de deadline in this direct question.
work-11.compare: English "When is the deadline?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

work-11.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-12.order: Laten we is the fixed way to make a suggestion: the verb comes first, then we, and the infinitive normally occurs toward the end. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (plannen) normally occurs toward the end.
work-12.forms: Laten we introduces a suggestion shared by speaker and listener. Plannen remains an infinitive after laten we; een follow-up is its object. Compare present we plannen and simple past we planden.
work-12.compare: English "Let's schedule a follow-up" uses let's plus a bare verb; Dutch uses laten we plus an infinitive at the end.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

work-12.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

transport-14.meaning: Asking if it is a long walk.
transport-14.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (lopen) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-14.forms: Ver lopen asks about distance on foot.
transport-14.compare: English "Is it a long walk?" uses a noun (walk); Dutch uses the infinitive lopen after ver: is het ver lopen?

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

transport-14.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

transport-15.meaning: Saying it is opposite the park.
transport-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
transport-15.compare: English "It is opposite the park." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: Park is a het-word, so the article is het.

transport-15.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-13.meaning: Saying you are used to working long hours.
work-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the te phrase (te werken) closes the sentence.
work-13.forms: Gewend zijn + te-infinitive describes an activity that is familiar: ik ben gewend lange uren te werken. Om is also possible: ik ben gewend om lange uren te werken. Lange has -e before plural uren; te werken remains an infinitive, not a second finite verb.
work-13.compare: English be used to takes an -ing form here: working. Dutch uses a te-infinitive, optionally introduced by om. This is a current familiar activity, not English used to work meaning a former habit.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben gewend werken lange uren.
mistake.right: Ik ben gewend lange uren te werken.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive.

work-13.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

school-12.meaning: Telling someone to explain it to you.
school-12.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Leg) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (uit) normally occurs toward the end while the imperative verb comes first.
school-12.compare: English "Explain it to me" is one verb; Dutch splits uitleggen: leg het me uit, with uit at the end.

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle last.

school-12.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

transport-16.meaning: Asking where someone will be staying.
transport-16.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (zult) comes second and the subject (u) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (verblijven) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-16.compare: English "Where will you be staying?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

transport-16.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-27.meaning: Saying you had already heard a story before.
conversation-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gehoord) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-27.forms: Had plus participle is the past perfect. Horen: gehoord. Verhaal is a het-word, so dat.
conversation-27.compare: English "I had heard that story before" keeps the participle next to had; Dutch puts it last.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gehoord dat verhaal al eens.
mistake.right: Ik had dat verhaal al eens gehoord.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-27.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
conversation-27.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

conversation-28.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (moet) comes second and the subject (ik) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (doen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-28.compare: English "What should I do?" has the same order.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-28.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dat) comes first and the finite verb (klinkt) second (verb-second order).
conversation-29.forms: Klinken: dat klinkt. No -e after klinken.
conversation-29.compare: English "That sounds great!" has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-29.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

food-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (heb) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gegeten) normally occurs toward the end.
food-05.forms: Perfect: heb je gegeten. Eten: gegeten.
food-05.compare: English says "Where did you eat?" (simple past); Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

food-05.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
food-05.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

conversation-30.meaning: Saying you had already made a choice.
conversation-30.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gemaakt) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-30.forms: Hadden plus participle is the past perfect (plural). Een keuze maken means to make a choice.
conversation-30.compare: English "We had already made a choice" keeps the participle next to had.

mistake.wrong: We hadden gemaakt al een keuze.
mistake.right: We hadden al een keuze gemaakt.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-30.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
conversation-30.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

shopping-13.order: This is a noun phrase with no verb: a number, the unit dozijn (which stays singular after a number) and the thing counted.
shopping-13.forms: As a counting unit here, dozijn stays singular after twee. Het ei has irregular plural eieren. The noun after a unit need not always be plural: compare twee dozijn eieren with drie liter melk.
shopping-13.compare: Both languages keep the counting unit singular here: English two dozen eggs, Dutch twee dozijn eieren. English dozens of eggs is a different construction.

mistake.why: Twee dozijn is the ordinary counting-unit form. A plural such as dozijnen can emphasise separate groups or quantities in an appropriate context. Practise the neutral purchase phrase without claiming the plural is impossible everywhere.

shopping-13.practiceFocus: Short expressions and their intended meaning
shopping-13.practiceGuide: The related bank practises short conversational expressions rather than only quantities. The measure examples use number + unit + item: twee kilo appels, drie liter melk. Appels is countable plural; melk is a mass noun. Thank-you examples practise a separate social formula, not a quantity rule.

work-14.meaning: Suggesting that you set a new deadline.
work-14.order: Laten we plus an infinitive makes a suggestion; the infinitive normally occurs toward the end.
work-14.compare: English says "Let's set a new deadline"; Dutch ends with the infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Laten we stellen een nieuwe deadline.
mistake.right: Laten we een nieuwe deadline stellen.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

work-14.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

administration-02.meaning: Asking for something to be sent to you.
administration-02.order: Laat plus object plus infinitive means have it done. The infinitive normally occurs toward the end.
administration-02.forms: Laat is an imperative of laten: ask the listener to arrange the sending, possibly by a third person. Het is the item sent. Naar me gives its destination/recipient. Opsturen stays joined as an infinitive after laat; a direct command to send it yourself is Stuur het naar me op.
administration-02.compare: English says "Have it sent to me"; Dutch uses the infinitive opsturen.

mistake.why: A full destination phrase may follow an infinitive. The model places naar me before opsturen; the other order is possible.

administration-02.practiceGuide: The related examples practise commands, including separable verbs and recipients. The parent is a causative command: Laat het naar me opsturen asks the listener to arrange for it to be sent. This differs from directly instructing the listener Stuur het me op. Both use an imperative, but the person carrying out the sending need not be the same.

food-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te eten) closes the sentence.
food-06.forms: Zin hebben om te means to feel like.
food-06.compare: English "I feel like eating." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Ik heb zin om te eten.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

food-06.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-15.meaning: Saying you talked about the project.
work-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gesproken) normally occurs toward the end.
work-15.forms: Spreken: gesproken. Spreken over means to talk about.
work-15.compare: English says "We talked about"; Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.wrong: We hebben gesproken over het project.
mistake.right: We hebben over het project gesproken.
mistake.why: A prepositional phrase such as over het project may also follow gesproken. Both orders are possible. This card practises the common verb-bracket order, with the topic before the participle.

work-15.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-15.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

transport-17.meaning: Asking if someone knows an area.
transport-17.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kent), and the subject (u) follows it.
transport-17.forms: Kennen: u kent; ik ken; past kende/kenden; perfect heb/heeft gekend. Here kennen means being familiar with a neighbourhood. Weten typically concerns information, as in Weet u waar het station is? Kennen is not limited to people and places: ik ken dit gevoel means I know this feeling.
transport-17.compare: English says "Do you know this neighbourhood?"; Dutch just inverts.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

transport-17.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

conversation-31.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-31.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-31.compare: English "I am so proud." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-31.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

conversation-32.meaning: Asking what someone is doing right now.
conversation-32.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (ben) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (doen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-32.forms: Zijn aan het plus infinitive shows an action in progress.
conversation-32.compare: English "What are you doing?" uses the -ing form.

mistake.wrong: Wat je bent aan het doen?
mistake.right: Wat ben je aan het doen?
mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-32.practiceFocus: An action happening now: aan het
conversation-32.practiceGuide: Use a conjugated form of zijn + aan het + infinitive. The object normally comes before aan het: Hij is de ramen aan het wassen. These models place aan het directly before the infinitive. With separable verbs, both de ramen aan het schoonmaken and de ramen schoon aan het maken are correct. Dutch simple present can also mean an English ongoing action. Aan het werk contains the NOUN werk, whereas aan het werken contains an infinitive; they are not identical constructions.

leisure-04.meaning: Saying you are looking forward to the holiday.
leisure-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (kijken) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (uit) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
leisure-04.forms: Uitkijken naar means look forward to: we kijken uit naar de vakantie. Kijken is finite, uit is its separable particle, and naar introduces what is anticipated. A full naar-phrase may follow uit, so uit need not be the last word. Perfect: we hebben naar de vakantie uitgekeken.
leisure-04.compare: English look forward to and Dutch uitkijken naar are whole expressions with different particles/prepositions. The Dutch finite verb is kijken, followed here by uit and the full phrase naar de vakantie.

mistake.right: We kijken uit naar de vakantie.
mistake.why: In this ordinary main clause, finite kijken follows subject we and the particle uit comes later. Naar de vakantie may follow uit as a full prepositional phrase; the particle need not be the final word.

leisure-04.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

home-15.meaning: Saying you had already turned off the lights.
home-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (uitgedaan) normally occurs toward the end.
home-15.forms: Uitdoen: ik doe ... uit, ik deed ... uit, ik heb uitgedaan. In the participle, ge goes between the separable prefix uit and the stem: uit + ge + daan.
home-15.compare: English can say turned off the lights or turned the lights off. Dutch keeps uit inside the participle uitgedaan after had; it does not separate gedaan uit.

mistake.wrong: Ik had de lichten al gedaan uit.
mistake.right: Ik had de lichten al uitgedaan.
mistake.why: The separable participle is one word: uitgedaan.

home-15.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
home-15.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

transport-18.meaning: Telling someone to walk down a street.
transport-18.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Loop) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (af) normally occurs toward the end while the imperative verb comes first.
transport-18.forms: Aflopen splits in an imperative: loop ... af.
transport-18.compare: English "Walk down this street" has no particle.

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle goes last.

transport-18.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

shopping-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order).
shopping-14.forms: Willen: ik wil. The verb hebben is left out.
shopping-14.compare: English "I would like this" uses would; Dutch uses the present.

mistake.why: The finite verb stays second.

shopping-14.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

transport-19.meaning: Asking if there is free wifi.
transport-19.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (gratis wifi) follows it.
transport-19.forms: Er is introduces something that exists.
transport-19.compare: English "Is there free Wi-Fi?" also starts with the verb and uses there; Dutch uses er in the same place.

mistake.why: Er is gratis wifi? can ask for confirmation with questioning intonation. The neutral yes/no question starts with finite is: Is er gratis wifi?

transport-19.practiceGuide: Existential er introduces something present or available: er is/zijn, er ligt/staat/hangt. The verb agrees with the noun introduced (er is een boek, er zijn boeken). Ligt/staat/hangt is already the finite verb, so do not add another is. Position verbs make the physical arrangement explicit. If a place phrase comes first, normal V2 still applies.

food-07.meaning: Saying you tried a new dish.
food-07.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (probeerde) second (verb-second order).
food-07.forms: Proberen: ik probeer (present), ik probeerde / wij probeerden (simple past), ik heb geprobeerd (perfect). The regular participle is ge + probeer + d. Het gerecht means the dish; het-word + indefinite een gives een nieuw gerecht. Compare de soep → een nieuwe soep, and het definite noun phrase het nieuwe gerecht.
food-07.compare: English "I tried a new dish." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: A het-word after een takes no -e.

food-07.practiceFocus: Proberen: try a thing or try to act
food-07.practiceGuide: Proberen means try. Ik probeer is present; ik probeerde is singular simple past; wij probeerden is plural past; ik heb geprobeerd uses the participle with hebben. The regular participle is ge + probeer + d. A thing can be tried directly; trying to do something uses proberen + te + infinitive. After zal the verb becomes proberen: ik zal proberen te bellen. Trying on clothes usually uses passen; tasting food can use proeven.

food-08.meaning: Politely asking to see the menu.
food-08.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zien) normally occurs toward the end.
food-08.forms: Mogen: ik mag. Menukaart is a de-word.
food-08.compare: English "May I see the menu?" has the same order.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

food-08.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

weather-05.meaning: Saying it is very cold here.
weather-05.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
weather-05.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
weather-05.compare: English "It is very cold here." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

weather-05.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-16.meaning: Saying you had finished the project early.
work-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (afgerond) normally occurs toward the end.
work-16.forms: Afronden: we ronden ... af; we hebben afgerond. The participle contains ge between the separable prefix af and rond: af + ge + rond. Hadden afgerond is past perfect.
work-16.compare: English "We had finished the project early" keeps the participle next to had.

mistake.wrong: We hadden afgerond het project vroeg.
mistake.right: We hadden het project vroeg afgerond.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

work-16.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
work-16.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

conversation-33.meaning: A polite way to say thank you very much.
conversation-33.order: Hartelijk dank is a conventional thank-you formula, without a finite verb or a subject. It is not a sentence requiring V2 order.
conversation-33.forms: The standalone expression uses hartelijk dank. After a possessive, use the inflected adjective: mijn hartelijke dank. This formula is exceptional; it does not establish a general rule for all de-word adjectives.
conversation-33.compare: English says "Thank you very much"; Dutch uses the fixed phrase hartelijk dank, with no verb.

mistake.why: Hartelijk dank is the conventional standalone formula. With a possessive, the adjective is inflected: mijn hartelijke dank. Learn the fixed expression rather than generalising that hartelijk never takes -e.

conversation-33.practiceFocus: Short expressions and their intended meaning
conversation-33.practiceGuide: Some useful expressions are fragments rather than full subject-plus-verb clauses: Hartelijk dank, Graag gedaan. Do not invent V2 inversion for a phrase with no finite verb. Learn what the expression does in the conversation, and compare related full sentences. A polite formula can have several natural English equivalents.

transport-20.meaning: Asking where the train station is.
transport-20.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het treinstation) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-20.compare: English "Where is the train station?" is the same.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

transport-20.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

food-09.meaning: Suggesting to go and have a cup of coffee.
food-09.order: Laten we is the fixed way to make a suggestion: the verb comes first, then we, and the infinitive normally occurs toward the end. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (gaan) normally occurs toward the end; the infinitive (drinken) normally occurs toward the end.
food-09.forms: Gaan plus infinitive means go and do.
food-09.compare: English "Let's go and have a cup of coffee" uses let's plus go and have; Dutch puts both infinitives at the end: laten we ... gaan drinken.

mistake.wrong: Laten we gaan drinken een kop koffie.
mistake.right: Laten we een kop koffie gaan drinken.
mistake.why: The infinitives go to the end.

food-09.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

conversation-34.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (leek) second (verb-second order).
conversation-34.forms: Lijken has irregular past leek (singular) and leken (plural). Here it is a linking verb meaning seem. Blij describes hij and has no attributive -e; heel means very. Compare the noun phrase een blije man.
conversation-34.compare: English He seemed very happy and Dutch Hij leek heel blij both describe an apparent state. Dutch uses past leek and predicate adjective blij; no extra was is needed.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-34.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

weather-06.order: Er takes the first position, so the finite verb (was) is second and the real subject comes after it.
weather-06.compare: English "There was a thunderstorm" is the same.

mistake.why: The verb agrees with the singular noun: was.

weather-06.practiceGuide: Existential er introduces something present or available: er is/zijn, er ligt/staat/hangt. The verb agrees with the noun introduced (er is een boek, er zijn boeken). Ligt/staat/hangt is already the finite verb, so do not add another is. Position verbs make the physical arrangement explicit. If a place phrase comes first, normal V2 still applies.

food-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (betaald) normally occurs toward the end.
food-10.forms: Betalen uses hebben in the perfect: ik heb betaald. The unstressed prefix be- prevents an extra ge-: betaald, not gebetaald. Rekening is a de-word and names the bill here.
food-10.compare: English says "I paid the bill"; Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

food-10.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
food-10.practiceGuide: These examples practise hebben + participle and objects before the participle. Dutch betalen can take what is paid for directly: het eten betalen means pay for the food. In Ik heb de taxi betaald, the intended meaning is paying the taxi fare/driver, not buying a taxi. Auxiliary choice is learned with the verb; this verb uses hebben.

leisure-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe vaak) takes the first position, so the finite verb (train) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
leisure-05.forms: Trainen: je traint, but the -t drops when je follows: train je.
leisure-05.compare: English "How often do you train?" needs do; Dutch just inverts.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject; -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb.

leisure-05.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-17.meaning: Saying you will discuss it then.
work-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (bespreken) normally occurs toward the end.
work-17.forms: We takes plural zullen. Het is the unstressed object it and comes before dan in this model. Bespreken means discuss and takes a direct object without over. After zullen it remains an infinitive without te.
work-17.compare: English "We will discuss it then" keeps discuss next to will.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

work-17.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

leisure-06.meaning: Suggesting to go for a run.
leisure-06.order: Laten we is the fixed way to make a suggestion: the verb comes first, then we, and the infinitive normally occurs toward the end. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (gaan) normally occurs toward the end; the infinitive (hardlopen) normally occurs toward the end.
leisure-06.forms: Gaan plus infinitive means go and do.
leisure-06.compare: English "Let's go running" uses an -ing form; Dutch uses two infinitives: laten we gaan hardlopen.

mistake.why: Gaan comes before the other infinitive.

leisure-06.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

shopping-15.meaning: Saying he is busy closing the shop.
shopping-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the te phrase (te sluiten) closes the sentence.
shopping-15.forms: Bezig zijn + te-infinitive describes an activity in progress: hij is bezig de winkel te sluiten. The object de winkel comes before te sluiten. Compare bezig met het sluiten van de winkel, which names the activity as a noun-like phrase.
shopping-15.compare: English "He is busy closing the shop" is similar.

mistake.wrong: Hij is bezig sluiten de winkel.
mistake.right: Hij is bezig de winkel te sluiten.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive at the end.

shopping-15.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
shopping-15.practiceGuide: The shared examples compare being occupied with an activity and having finished one. Bezig zijn met/te describes work in progress; klaar zijn met describes completion. Hij is klaar met het lezen van het boek does not mean he is still reading. The parent uses bezig + object + te-infinitive rather than met + noun-like activity.

work-18.meaning: Saying you are thinking about opening a shop.
work-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (denken) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om een winkel te openen) closes the sentence.
work-18.forms: Denken over iets means consider something. In we denken erover om een winkel te openen, erover points ahead to the proposed activity. Om introduces that infinitive clause and te stands immediately before openen. This reports consideration, not a settled plan.
work-18.compare: English thinking about opening uses an -ing form. Dutch uses erover plus an om ... te clause here. Denken aan can instead mean think of or remember; do not treat every combination of aan/over as the same expression.

mistake.wrong: We denken erover om een winkel openen.
mistake.right: We denken erover om een winkel te openen.
mistake.why: After om the infinitive needs te.

work-18.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

shopping-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gekocht) normally occurs toward the end.
shopping-16.compare: English "I bought this yesterday" is the simple past.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

shopping-16.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
shopping-16.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

conversation-35.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (afspreken) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-35.forms: Days have no article here. Afspreken stays whole after a modal.
conversation-35.compare: Both languages start with a modal and subject. Dutch places the time dinsdag before final afspreken; English places on Tuesday after meet. Both dinsdag and op dinsdag can name the day.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

conversation-35.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

health-03.meaning: Saying you felt a little tired.
health-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (voelde) second (verb-second order).
health-03.forms: For how you feel, use zich voelen: ik voelde me, zij voelde zich, wij voelden ons. Voelde is singular simple past; een beetje softens moe. Voelen is not always reflexive: ik voelde de stof means I felt the fabric.
health-03.compare: English "I felt a little tired" has no reflexive pronoun; Dutch zich voelen needs one: ik voelde me.

mistake.right: Ik voelde me een beetje moe.
mistake.why: Zich voelen needs the reflexive pronoun.

health-03.practiceFocus: Reflexive pronouns refer to the subject
health-03.practiceGuide: Match the reflexive to the subject: ik/me, jij/je, hij-zij/zich, wij/ons, jullie/je, zij plural/zich. A question can contain two je forms: Voel je je beter? The first is the subject, the second reflexive. The reflexive belongs to the Dutch expression even if natural English does not say myself. In an embedded clause the verb group normally closes the clause.

administration-03.meaning: Saying you had already written the letter.
administration-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (geschreven) normally occurs toward the end.
administration-03.compare: English "I had already written the letter." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (geschreven) in the final verb bracket.

mistake.wrong: Ik had geschreven de brief al.
mistake.right: Ik had de brief al geschreven.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

administration-03.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
administration-03.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

conversation-36.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kan), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (krijgen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-36.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Nummer is a het-word.
conversation-36.compare: English "Can I have your number?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

conversation-36.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

transport-21.meaning: Promising to show someone the way.
transport-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (wijzen) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-21.forms: Zullen: ik zal. De weg wijzen means to show the way.
transport-21.compare: English "I will show you the way." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (wijzen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik zal wijzen je de weg.
mistake.right: Ik zal je de weg wijzen.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

transport-21.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

conversation-37.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (terugbellen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-37.forms: Terugbellen means call back. Here zal is finite and terugbellen stays together as an infinitive. When terugbellen itself is the finite verb in a main clause, it splits: hij belt terug. Perfect: hij heeft teruggebeld.
conversation-37.compare: English "He will call back" has back after the verb; Dutch keeps terugbellen as one word after zal.

mistake.why: After a modal the separable verb stays whole.

conversation-37.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

transport-22.meaning: Politely asking someone to show you the way.
transport-22.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunt), and the subject (u) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (wijzen) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-22.forms: Kunnen with u: u kunt (u kan also occurs). Mij is the object form.
transport-22.compare: English "Can you show me the way?" has the same order.

mistake.wrong: Kunt u wijzen mij de weg?
mistake.right: Kunt u mij de weg wijzen?
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

transport-22.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

weather-07.meaning: Asking if it is cold outside.
weather-07.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it.
weather-07.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
weather-07.compare: English "Is it cold outside?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

weather-07.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

conversation-38.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (verzetten) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-38.forms: Verzetten means reschedule in this appointment context, without specifying whether the new time is earlier or later. Uitstellen means postpone to a later time. Dit stands alone for the arrangement; it is not attached to an omitted noun whose article you must guess.
conversation-38.compare: English "Can we reschedule this?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-38.practiceGuide: The bank practises modal questions with an infinitive. Related examples can change the situation: dit uitstellen and dit later doen explicitly move something later, while verzetten alone only changes the time. Keep that distinction when using a related example for a new situation.

conversation-39.meaning: Saying he hid something from us.
conversation-39.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (verborgen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-39.forms: Verbergen: verbergt, verborg/verborgen, heeft verborgen. The unstressed prefix ver- does not add ge-. Voor ons in iets voor ons verbergen means from us, not for our benefit. Compare voor jou bewaren, where voor does name a beneficiary.
conversation-39.compare: English "He hid it from us." uses the simple past; Dutch often uses the perfect (auxiliary plus participle) for a finished event, with the participle (verborgen) at the end.

mistake.wrong: Hij heeft verborgen het voor ons.
mistake.right: Hij heeft het voor ons verborgen.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-39.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
conversation-39.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

shopping-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (droeg) second (verb-second order).
shopping-17.forms: Dragen has irregular past droeg (singular), droegen (plural), and participle gedragen. Here it means wear clothing, so droeg can naturally be English was wearing. The same Dutch verb can mean carry in another context.
shopping-17.compare: English "She wore a scarf" is the same simple past; the Dutch verb dragen has an irregular past: droeg.

mistake.why: The past of dragen is droeg.

shopping-17.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

conversation-40.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (nam) second (verb-second order).
conversation-40.forms: Nemen: nam (irregular). Een beslissing nemen means to decide.
conversation-40.compare: English "I made a decision" uses make; Dutch uses nemen.

mistake.why: Use nemen with beslissing.

conversation-40.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

home-16.meaning: Saying your phone battery is dead.
home-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Mijn telefoon) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-16.forms: Leeg means empty; Dutch uses it for a dead battery.
home-16.compare: English says "My phone is dead"; Dutch says mijn telefoon is leeg (empty).

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

home-16.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

health-04.meaning: Saying they will sit and wait until the doctor calls.
health-04.order: The main clause has the verb second. After tot the clause is subordinate, so the verb normally occurs toward the end.
health-04.forms: Gaan zitten means sit down or take a seat; plural ze takes gaan. The first ze is subject they. In tot de dokter ze roept, de dokter is the subject and the second ze is object them. Roept is singular because it agrees with de dokter, not with ze.
health-04.compare: English until the doctor calls them puts calls before them. Dutch tot de dokter ze roept puts object ze before final roept. The sitting begins after gaan zitten; the English will sit conveys this next action.

mistake.why: After tot the verb goes to the end.

health-04.practiceGuide: These examples practise posture and movement into a posture. Gaan zitten and gaan staan mean sit down and stand up; zitten and staan alone describe the state. In the example Ze gaan staan tot de bus komt, they get up and remain standing until the bus comes. A tot-clause has its own final finite verb.

conversation-41.meaning: Saying she is happy about the chance.
conversation-41.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-41.forms: Blij zijn met means to be happy about.
conversation-41.compare: English "happy about" uses about; Dutch uses met.

mistake.wrong: Ze blij is met de kans.
mistake.right: Ze is blij met de kans.
mistake.why: The finite verb stays second: ze is blij. Blij zijn met means to be happy about something.

conversation-41.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

food-11.meaning: Asking where the bag of food is.
food-11.order: Waar is the first question constituent, followed by finite is. The complete subject is de zak met eten: met eten describes what the bag contains, so it belongs inside the noun phrase.
food-11.forms: Met links a container to its contents.
food-11.compare: English "Where is the bag of food?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.wrong: Waar de zak met eten is?
mistake.right: Waar is de zak met eten?
mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

food-11.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-42.meaning: Saying it did not work the first time.
conversation-42.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (werkte) second (verb-second order).
conversation-42.forms: Werken has stem werk, so singular simple past is werk + te = werkte, not werken + te. De eerste keer means the first time. Niet negates working successfully in that instance.
conversation-42.compare: English It did not work needs did plus bare work. Dutch puts the past directly in werkte and adds niet. Dutch needs no counterpart of did here.

mistake.wrong: Het niet werkte de eerste keer.
mistake.right: Het werkte de eerste keer niet.
mistake.why: Keep finite werkte second after subject het. The model places niet after de eerste keer for ordinary sentence negation. The displayed alternative wrongly puts niet before the finite verb; it is not evidence that niet must always follow every time phrase.

conversation-42.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
conversation-42.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

conversation-43.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-43.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-43.compare: English "It is very blurry" has the same pattern; Dutch adds no ending to wazig after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-43.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

shopping-18.meaning: Asking if someone bought it for you.
