shopping-18.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heb), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gekocht) normally occurs toward the end.
shopping-18.forms: Heb je: the -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb.
shopping-18.compare: English "Did you buy it for me?" needs "did" to form the question; Dutch just starts with the finite verb (Heb).

mistake.wrong: Je hebt het voor me gekocht?
mistake.right: Heb je het voor me gekocht?
mistake.why: The statement order can ask for confirmation with questioning intonation. For the neutral question/request here, put the finite verb first. When subject je follows it, the ordinary added second-person -t is omitted.

shopping-18.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
shopping-18.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

school-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
school-13.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
school-13.compare: English "This is very easy" has the same pattern; Dutch adds no ending to gemakkelijk after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

school-13.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

transport-23.meaning: Saying they leave for a holiday on Friday.
transport-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (vertrekken) second (verb-second order).
transport-23.forms: Both vrijdag and op vrijdag are possible time expressions. Op vakantie means on holiday. Keep the holiday phrase separate from the day: Ze vertrekken vrijdag op vakantie, or Ze vertrekken op vrijdag op vakantie.
transport-23.compare: English "They are leaving on holiday on Friday" uses a progressive.

mistake.why: Friday may be vrijdag or op vrijdag. The phrase op vakantie must remain intact: inserting vrijdag between op and vakantie wrongly breaks that holiday expression.

transport-23.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

school-14.meaning: Telling someone to read it aloud to you.
school-14.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Lees) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (voor) normally occurs toward the end while the imperative verb comes first.
school-14.forms: Voorlezen splits in an imperative: lees ... voor.
school-14.compare: English "Read it aloud to me." is also a command with no subject; Dutch starts with the verb (Lees).

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle goes last.

school-14.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

transport-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
transport-24.forms: Iets nodig hebben means need something: ik heb een kaart nodig. Heb is a present finite verb, not a perfect auxiliary here. Kaart means a map in this navigation scenario; in another context it can mean a card or ticket.
transport-24.compare: English "I need a map" is one verb; Dutch splits ik heb ... nodig around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig goes after the object.

transport-24.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

leisure-07.meaning: Saying you are here to play.
leisure-07.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (zijn) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te spelen) closes the sentence.
leisure-07.forms: Om te plus infinitive shows purpose.
leisure-07.compare: English "We are here to play." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Wij zijn hier om te spelen.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

leisure-07.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

health-05.meaning: Saying you wash your hands before every meal.
health-05.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (was) second (verb-second order).
health-05.forms: Here was is present of wassen, not past of zijn: ik was mijn handen means I wash my hands. Compare jij/hij wast, wij wassen; past waste/wasten; perfect heb gewassen. Voor elke maaltijd means before every meal. Mijn is possessive my before plural handen.
health-05.compare: English "I wash my hands before every meal." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Ik was handen mijn voor elke maaltijd.
mistake.right: Ik was mijn handen voor elke maaltijd.
mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

health-05.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

transport-25.meaning: Saying you are ready to go.
transport-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te gaan) closes the sentence.
transport-25.forms: Klaar zijn om te + infinitive means be ready to act: ik ben klaar om te gaan. This describes readiness, not completed departure. Compare klaar met eten (finished eating) and klaar om te eten (ready to eat).
transport-25.compare: English "I am ready to go" uses to; Dutch needs om te: klaar om te gaan.

mistake.right: Ik ben klaar om te gaan.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

transport-25.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-19.meaning: Saying he sometimes arrives late because of traffic.
work-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (komt) second (verb-second order).
work-19.forms: Te laat komen means arrive late. Te modifies laat (too/late), not a following infinitive. Soms means sometimes. Door het verkeer gives the cause, with het because verkeer is a het-word.
work-19.compare: English "He sometimes arrives late because of traffic." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Hij komt soms te laat door de verkeer.
mistake.right: Hij komt soms te laat door het verkeer.
mistake.why: Verkeer is a het-word, so het.

work-19.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

home-17.meaning: Saying they wanted to move to a bigger house.
home-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (wilden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (verhuizen) normally occurs toward the end.
home-17.forms: Wilden is plural past of willen. Verhuizen is inseparable: ik verhuis, not ik huis ver. It stays an infinitive without te after wilden. Huis is a singular het-word, so use een groter huis; compare het grotere huis.
home-17.compare: English wanted to move uses to. Dutch wilden takes the bare infinitive verhuizen, with naar een groter huis before it. This describes a wish, not proof that the move happened.

mistake.wrong: Ze wilden naar een grotere huis verhuizen.
mistake.right: Ze wilden naar een groter huis verhuizen.
mistake.why: Huis is a het-word: after een the adjective takes no -e.

home-17.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

transport-26.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het toilet) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-26.compare: English "Where is the toilet?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

transport-26.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

health-06.meaning: Saying she will become a great doctor one day.
health-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (wordt) second (verb-second order).
health-06.forms: Wordt agrees with singular ze. Op een dag points to the future, so present wordt means will become here. The model uses the ordinary inflected adjective een geweldige dokter. Some adjectives before person or profession nouns can also be uninflected when describing that role; do not turn the model into a universal ban on such forms.
health-06.compare: English uses will be for the future prediction. Dutch can use present wordt with future op een dag. Worden emphasises becoming a doctor, while zijn describes being one.

mistake.wrong: Ze wordt op een dag een geweldig dokter.
mistake.right: Ze wordt op een dag een geweldige dokter.
mistake.why: Een geweldige dokter is the ordinary inflected model. An uninflected adjective can also occur before a person or profession noun when assessing the person in that role. The missing -e is therefore not automatically an error in every such phrase.

health-06.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

weather-08.meaning: Saying it was a beautiful sunset.
weather-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (was) second (verb-second order).
weather-08.forms: Zijn: het was. Prachtige takes -e before the de-word zonsondergang.
weather-08.compare: English "It was a beautiful sunset" has the same pattern; the Dutch past of zijn is was (singular) and waren (plural).

mistake.why: After een a de-word takes -e.

weather-08.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-20.meaning: Saying they used the meeting room for the presentation.
work-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gebruikten) second (verb-second order).
work-20.forms: Ze means they here, so the past form is plural gebruikten, from stem gebruik + ten. Singular ze gebruikte would mean she used and is valid in a different situation. Voor de presentatie gives the purpose of using the room.
work-20.compare: English "They used the meeting room for the presentation".

mistake.wrong: Ze gebruikte de vergaderruimte voor de presentatie.
mistake.right: Ze gebruikten de vergaderruimte voor de presentatie.
mistake.why: Ze gebruikte is grammatical for she used. This scenario concerns several people, so subject ze means they and requires plural gebruikten. The difference is the intended person/number, not a universal ban on gebruikte.

work-20.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-21.meaning: Saying you will know the results by Monday.
work-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (weet) second (verb-second order).
work-21.forms: Weten: ik weet. Uiterlijk means at the latest.
work-21.compare: English "I will know the results by Monday at the latest" uses will; Dutch uses the present: ik weet ... uiterlijk maandag.

mistake.wrong: Ik weet de resultaten uiterlijk bij maandag.
mistake.right: Ik weet de resultaten uiterlijk maandag.
mistake.why: No preposition is needed before the day after uiterlijk.

work-21.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

leisure-08.meaning: Saying you will dance with someone at the wedding.
leisure-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (dans) second (verb-second order).
leisure-08.forms: Dansen met means to dance with. The present tense can express a plan, so ik dans can mean I will dance.
leisure-08.compare: English "I will dance with you at the wedding" uses will; Dutch uses the present tense for a plan: ik dans met je.

mistake.wrong: Ik dans je met op de bruiloft.
mistake.right: Ik dans met je op de bruiloft.
mistake.why: The preposition comes before its pronoun: met je.

leisure-08.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-44.meaning: Saying you want to send it to someone.
conversation-44.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (sturen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-44.compare: English "I want to send it to you." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (sturen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-44.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

conversation-45.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (helpen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-45.forms: Wij takes plural zullen, and helpen remains an infinitive. Je is an object meaning you and comes before helpen in this model, not after it. This je is neither the subject nor possessive your.
conversation-45.compare: English "We will help you" uses will; Dutch uses zullen with the infinitive helpen at the end.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-45.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

conversation-46.meaning: Saying they are on their way.
conversation-46.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (komen) second (verb-second order).
conversation-46.forms: Eraan komen means to be on the way.
conversation-46.compare: English "They are coming" is a progressive; Dutch zij komen eraan also means they are on their way.

mistake.why: Zij komen aan means they are arriving. Zij komen eraan means they are on their way/approaching. Both are grammatical, but the intended situation differs.

conversation-46.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-47.meaning: Saying you are only a guest.
conversation-47.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-47.forms: Maar here means only. Zijn: ik ben.
conversation-47.compare: English "I am only a guest" uses only; Dutch uses maar.

mistake.why: The article comes before the noun.

conversation-47.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

leisure-09.meaning: Saying you will come to someone's party.
leisure-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kom) second (verb-second order).
leisure-09.forms: Komen naar a place or event. Feestje is a het-word.
leisure-09.compare: English "I will come to your party" uses will; Dutch uses the present.

mistake.why: Use naar for the event you go to.

leisure-09.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

home-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-18.forms: Vies is a predicate adjective here and takes no agreement -e after is. Before an appropriate noun the spelling changes to vieze, with z: de vieze keuken. Viese is not the correct inflected spelling.
home-18.compare: English "It is very dirty" has the same pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after is.

mistake.why: Use predicate vies after is, without -e. The corresponding adjective before a noun is spelled vieze, as in de vieze keuken; viese is also misspelled.

home-18.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

conversation-48.meaning: Telling someone to give it to you.
conversation-48.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Geef) and leaves out the subject.
conversation-48.forms: Geef is the ordinary imperative stem of geven. Its spelling changes from the infinitive: long ee is written in closed geef, and v becomes f. The irregular past is gaf/gaven and the participle is gegeven. Het is the thing and me the recipient in Geef het me.
conversation-48.compare: English "Give it to me" uses to; Dutch puts the person straight after the object: geef het me.

mistake.why: The imperative uses the stem, not the infinitive.

conversation-48.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

leisure-10.meaning: Saying you danced with your wife at the reception.
leisure-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (danste) second (verb-second order).
leisure-10.forms: Dansen: ik dans; past ik danste / wij dansten; perfect ik heb gedanst. The stem ends in s, so the regular past uses -te and participle -t. Met mijn vrouw means with my wife. Op de receptie names the reception event; aan de receptie commonly means at the reception desk. In describes a physical room or space.
leisure-10.compare: English "I danced with my wife at the reception." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.wrong: Ik dansde met mijn vrouw op de receptie.
mistake.right: Ik danste met mijn vrouw op de receptie.
mistake.why: After a stem ending in s, the past takes -te, not -de.

leisure-10.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

home-19.meaning: Saying you used to stay up late.
home-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (bleven) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-19.forms: Opblijven splits: bleven ... op. Blijven: bleef, bleven.
home-19.compare: English "We used to stay up late" keeps up after the verb; Dutch splits opblijven: wij bleven ... op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

home-19.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

weather-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (wordt) second (verb-second order).
weather-09.forms: Worden plus adjective describes a change; no -e.
weather-09.compare: English "It is getting cold" uses getting; Dutch uses worden: het wordt koud.

mistake.why: After worden the adjective takes no -e ending.

weather-09.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. home-20.meaning: Saying you lived in the city.

home-20.compare: English "We lived in the city." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den.

A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

leisure-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gekocht) normally occurs toward the end.
leisure-11.compare: English "She bought the tickets" uses the simple past.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

leisure-11.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
leisure-11.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

conversation-49.meaning: Saying it is difficult to help.
conversation-49.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te helpen) closes the sentence.
conversation-49.forms: Het is plus adjective plus om te plus infinitive.
conversation-49.compare: English "It is difficult to help." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Het is moeilijk om te helpen.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

conversation-49.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

conversation-50.meaning: Saying you are thinking about the name.
conversation-50.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (denk) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (na) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
conversation-50.forms: Nadenken splits: ik denk na. Over introduces the topic.
conversation-50.compare: English "I am thinking about the name" has no particle; Dutch splits nadenken: ik denk na over de naam.

mistake.right: Ik denk na over de naam.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

conversation-50.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. weather-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (keken) second (verb-second order).
weather-10.forms: Kijken has irregular past keek/keken and participle gekeken. For looking at the sunset use kijken naar de zonsondergang. This is not a claim that every use of kijken requires naar: een film kijken is also possible.
weather-10.compare: English "We watched the sunset." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: Use kijken naar for looking at this sunset. Kijken can take some objects directly in other expressions, such as een film kijken, so naar is not compulsory after every instance of kijken.

Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

administration-04.meaning: Asking if someone will send it to you.
administration-04.order: This yes/no question starts with finite stuur, followed by subject je. Het is the thing sent and me the recipient. The separable particle op comes later; the finite verb is first here, not second.
administration-04.forms: Opsturen separates in this finite question: stuur je ... op. Compare statement je stuurt, where the added -t appears, with question stuur je. The present can make a request about the next action, naturally translated Will you send it to me?
administration-04.compare: English "Will you send it to me?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: The statement order can ask for confirmation with questioning intonation. For the neutral question/request here, put the finite verb first. When subject je follows it, the ordinary added second-person -t is omitted.

administration-04.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

weather-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De maan) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
weather-11.compare: English "The moon is bright" has the same pattern; Dutch adds no ending to helder after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

work-22.meaning: Saying she received an award for her work.
work-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (ontving) second (verb-second order).

work-22.compare: English "She received an award for her work." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: The past of ontvangen is ontving.

Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

food-12.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het ontbijt) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
food-12.compare: English "How is the breakfast?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

food-12.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

conversation-51.meaning: Saying you had already seen the news.
conversation-51.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gezien) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-51.forms: Zien: gezien. Nieuws is a het-word.
conversation-51.compare: English "I had already seen the news." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (gezien) in the final verb bracket.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gezien het nieuws al.
mistake.right: Ik had het nieuws al gezien.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-51.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
conversation-51.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

school-15.meaning: Saying you cannot explain it to someone.
school-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kan) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (uitleggen) normally occurs toward the end.
school-15.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Het je: the thing first, then the person.
school-15.compare: English "I cannot explain it to you." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (uitleggen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik kan niet het je uitleggen.
mistake.right: Ik kan het je niet uitleggen.
mistake.why: Niet comes after the pronouns, before the infinitive.

school-15.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

conversation-52.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-52.forms: Fout is a de-word; mijn does not change.
conversation-52.compare: English "It is my fault" is the same pattern; Dutch fout is a de-word, and mijn stays the same.

mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

conversation-52.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

transport-27.meaning: Saying you were standing waiting at the bus stop.
transport-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (stond) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (te wachten) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-27.forms: Stond is singular past of staan; plural is stonden. Staan te wachten describes waiting while standing. The full location phrase bij de bushalte can follow te wachten, so the infinitive need not be the final word.
transport-27.compare: English "I was waiting"; Dutch says stond te wachten.

mistake.wrong: Ik stond wachten bij de bushalte.
mistake.right: Ik stond te wachten bij de bushalte.
mistake.why: Add te before the infinitive.

With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

food-13.meaning: Saying she did not drink her coffee.
food-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedronken) normally occurs toward the end.
food-13.forms: Drinken has irregular past dronk/dronken and participle gedronken. Ze is she here and takes heeft. Haar koffie is the object; niet before gedronken negates drinking that coffee in the intended situation.
food-13.compare: English "She did not drink her coffee" uses did not.

mistake.wrong: Ze heeft niet haar koffie gedronken.
mistake.right: Ze heeft haar koffie niet gedronken.
mistake.why: Niet haar koffie can contrast her coffee with something else that she drank. To negate drinking her coffee as a whole in this situation, put niet after haar koffie: Ze heeft haar koffie niet gedronken.

home-21.meaning: Asking if someone is sleeping now.

home-21.forms: Slapen: je slaapt, but the -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb.
home-21.compare: English "Are you sleeping now?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

shopping-19.forms: Kopen: kocht. Wat before a noun means some.
shopping-19.compare: English "I bought some fruit." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: The past of kopen is kocht.

work-23.meaning: Saying they are talking about the details.

work-23.compare: English "They are talking about the details" is a progressive; Dutch uses the simple present: ze praten over de details.

mistake.why: Use over before the topic.

conversation-53.meaning: Telling someone to give it back to you.

transport-29.meaning: Saying you fly with the same airline every time.
transport-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (vliegen) second (verb-second order).
transport-29.forms: Dezelfde goes with de-words (luchtvaartmaatschappij); het-words take hetzelfde.
transport-29.compare: English always says "the same"; Dutch has dezelfde (de-words and plurals) and hetzelfde (het-words).

conversation-54.meaning: Saying you cannot tell someone yet.
conversation-54.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kan) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vertellen) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-54.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Nog niet means not yet.
conversation-54.compare: English "I cannot tell you yet." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (vertellen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik kan het je vertellen nog niet.
mistake.right: Ik kan het je nog niet vertellen.
mistake.why: Nog niet comes before the infinitive.

home-22.meaning: Saying they are thinking about moving.
home-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (denken) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te verhuizen) closes the sentence.
home-22.compare: English "They are thinking about moving" uses -ing; Dutch uses erover om te verhuizen.

mistake.right: Ze denken erover om te verhuizen.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive after om.

mistake.why: Daarginds is written as one word.

leisure-12.compare: English "They made plans" is the same simple past; Dutch maken is regular: maakten in the plural.

mistake.wrong: Ze maakte plannen voor het weekend.
mistake.right: Ze maakten plannen voor het weekend.
mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den/-ten.

school-16.meaning: Telling someone they need to listen.
school-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (moet) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (luisteren) normally occurs toward the end.
school-16.compare: English "You need to listen" uses to; Dutch uses je moet plus a bare infinitive, with no te.

mistake.why: After a modal verb the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

school-16.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

leisure-13.meaning: Saying they were watching the match.
leisure-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (keken) second (verb-second order).
leisure-13.compare: English "They were watching the match" is a past progressive; Dutch uses the simple past keken, followed by naar.

mistake.why: Kijken needs naar before what you look at.

leisure-13.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

home-23.meaning: Saying he is busy cleaning the windows.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het schoonmaken van de ramen

home-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-23.forms: Bezig met can introduce a noun (de was = laundry) or an infinitive naming an activity (het wassen = washing). Het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like cleaning phrase. Compare Hij is de ramen aan het schoonmaken, the verbal progressive. De koken is incorrect: a nominalised infinitive takes het.
home-23.compare: English "He is busy cleaning the windows" uses -ing; Dutch uses bezig met het schoonmaken van.

mistake.wrong: Hij is bezig schoonmaken de ramen.
mistake.right: Hij is bezig met het schoonmaken van de ramen.
mistake.why: To be busy with is bezig zijn met in Dutch.

home-23.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
home-23.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

home-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-24.compare: English "It is clean" has the same pattern; in Dutch schoon takes no ending after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

home-24.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

conversation-56.order: Wie is itself the subject in this question, meaning who. Is is the finite verb; daar says where and nu says when. There is no extra subject after is. Contrast Waar is de dokter?, where waar asks about place and de dokter is the subject.
conversation-56.forms: The model uses singular is when asking who is there. Wie does not inherently mean exactly one person: plural agreement is possible in suitable contexts, as in Wie zijn dat? Learn the whole question rather than a rule that wie is always singular.
conversation-56.compare: English "Who is there now?" has the same order; Dutch daar and nu follow the verb.

mistake.why: Wie is the subject. The neutral direct question places finite is immediately after it, before daar nu. No additional subject is inserted.

conversation-56.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

shopping-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
shopping-20.compare: English "This is my bag" is the same pattern; Dutch uses mijn for both de-words and het-words.

mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

shopping-20.practiceFocus: This/that and the noun they refer to
shopping-20.practiceGuide: Use dit/dat with a singular het-word and deze/die with a singular de-word or any plural. Dit boek, deze tas, deze boeken. Distance is usually nearby dit/deze versus farther away dat/die; context can also determine it. Standalone dit/dat in Dit is mijn tas is not agreement with tas: it introduces an identification. Do not transfer the attached-noun rule mechanically to every pronoun.

conversation-57.meaning: Saying they asked us to come early.
conversation-57.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (vroegen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om vroeg te komen) closes the sentence.
conversation-57.compare: English "They asked us to come early." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Ze vroegen ons om vroeg te komen.
mistake.why: After vragen the infinitive needs om ... te around the rest of the clause.

conversation-57.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

transport-31.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (passeerden) second (verb-second order).
transport-31.compare: English "We passed the bank" has the same simple past; Dutch passeerden has the plural ending -den.

mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den.

transport-31.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

leisure-14.meaning: Saying you did not lose the match.
leisure-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (hebt) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (verloren) normally occurs toward the end.
leisure-14.compare: English "You did not lose the match" uses "did not"; Dutch uses the perfect with niet before the participle: hebt ... niet verloren.

mistake.wrong: Je hebt niet de wedstrijd verloren.
mistake.right: Je hebt de wedstrijd niet verloren.
mistake.why: Putting niet before de wedstrijd can create contrast: not the match, but something else. After the object it normally negates losing that match as a whole. The position depends on what you negate.

leisure-14.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
leisure-14.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

shopping-21.meaning: Saying they paid cash for the furniture.
shopping-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (betaalden) second (verb-second order).
shopping-21.compare: English "They paid cash for the furniture." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.wrong: Ze betaalde contant voor de meubels.
mistake.right: Ze betaalden contant voor de meubels.
mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den.

shopping-21.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

home-25.meaning: Saying you hear the birds singing every morning.
home-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (hoor) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zingen) normally occurs toward the end. After horen you can add an object and an infinitive.
home-25.compare: English "I hear the birds singing" uses an -ing form; Dutch uses a bare infinitive after the object: de vogels zingen.

mistake.wrong: Ik hoor elke ochtend de vogels te zingen.
mistake.right: Ik hoor elke ochtend de vogels zingen.
mistake.why: After horen the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

home-25.practiceGuide: Horen/zien can introduce someone doing an action: Ik hoor de vogels zingen. The birds are the object of hoor and the understood subject of zingen. The second verb is an infinitive without te in this construction. Other verb combinations such as helpen/laten and posture + te have different patterns; do not invent one universal two-verb rule.

leisure-15.meaning: Saying you are tired of this music.
leisure-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
leisure-15.forms: Beu zijn means to be fed up with.
leisure-15.compare: English "I am tired of this music" uses of; Dutch uses beu zijn plus the object before beu.

mistake.why: Beu goes after its object.

leisure-15.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

conversation-58.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (vind) second (verb-second order).
conversation-58.forms: Vinden plus adjective gives an opinion.
conversation-58.compare: English "I like his car" uses like; Dutch uses ik vind ... leuk (I find ... nice), with the adjective last.

mistake.why: The adjective goes after the object.

conversation-58.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

leisure-16.meaning: Saying you used to go to the park.
leisure-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ging) second (verb-second order).
leisure-16.forms: Gaan has an irregular past: ging in the singular, gingen in the plural.
leisure-16.compare: English "I used to go to the park" uses used to; Dutch uses the simple past ging with vroeger.

mistake.wrong: Ik gaan vroeger naar het park.
mistake.right: Ik ging vroeger naar het park.
mistake.why: Gaan is irregular: the past is ging (singular) and gingen (plural).

leisure-16.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

school-17.meaning: Saying you learn something new every day.
school-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (leer) second (verb-second order).
school-17.forms: Leren: ik leer, ik leerde, ik heb geleerd. In iets nieuws, iets means something and nieuw is an adjective used with the ending -s. This is something new; the separate noun het nieuws means the news. The -s here is not a plural ending. Compare iets leuks (something nice), niets nieuws (nothing new), and een nieuw boek (a new book, without that -s).
school-17.compare: English "something new" has no ending; Dutch adds -s after iets: iets nieuws.

mistake.wrong: Ik leer elke dag iets nieuw.
mistake.right: Ik leer elke dag iets nieuws.
mistake.why: After iets the adjective takes -s.

school-17.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-59.meaning: Saying she will believe in herself more.
conversation-59.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (geloven) normally occurs toward the end. Gaan plus an infinitive expresses a plan or something about to happen.
conversation-59.forms: Zichzelf is the reflexive pronoun for hij, zij, ze.
conversation-59.compare: English "She is going to believe in herself more".

mistake.wrong: Ze gaat meer geloven in zichzelf.
mistake.right: Ze gaat meer in zichzelf geloven.
mistake.why: A full prepositional phrase can follow the infinitive. Both orders are possible; the model practises the phrase before geloven.

conversation-59.practiceFocus: Reflexive pronouns refer to the subject
conversation-59.practiceGuide: Match the reflexive to the subject: ik/me, jij/je, hij-zij/zich, wij/ons, jullie/je, zij plural/zich. A question can contain two je forms: Voel je je beter? The first is the subject, the second reflexive. The reflexive belongs to the Dutch expression even if natural English does not say myself. In an embedded clause the verb group normally closes the clause.

health-07.meaning: Saying she woke up and felt much better.
health-07.order: Ze is the shared subject of two coordinated actions: werd wakker and voelde zich veel beter. En joins them. The second action leaves out the repeated subject ze; voelde still agrees with that same woman. Werd and voelde are both finite past verbs, not an infinitive pair.
health-07.forms: Wakker worden: werd wakker. Zich voelen: voelde zich.
health-07.compare: English "She woke up and felt much better" has a phrasal verb and no reflexive; Dutch uses wakker worden and zich voelen (voelde zich).

mistake.wrong: Ze werd wakker en voelde veel beter.
mistake.right: Ze werd wakker en voelde zich veel beter.
mistake.why: For how someone feels, use zich voelen: ze voelde zich beter. Here zich refers back to ze. Voelen does not require a reflexive in every sense; for example, ik voel de stof means I feel the fabric.

health-07.practiceFocus: Reflexive pronouns refer to the subject
health-07.practiceGuide: Match the reflexive to the subject: ik/me, jij/je, hij-zij/zich, wij/ons, jullie/je, zij plural/zich. A question can contain two je forms: Voel je je beter? The first is the subject, the second reflexive. The reflexive belongs to the Dutch expression even if natural English does not say myself. In an embedded clause the verb group normally closes the clause.

conversation-60.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-60.compare: English "He is very tall" is the same pattern; Dutch lang means both long and tall.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-60.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

home-26.meaning: Saying he washes his clothes at the laundrette.
home-26.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (wast) second (verb-second order).
home-26.compare: English "He washes his clothes at the laundrette" has the same pattern; Dutch wassen is irregular in the present: hij wast.

mistake.wrong: Hij wast kleren zijn in de wasserette.
mistake.right: Hij wast zijn kleren in de wasserette.
mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

home-26.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

leisure-17.meaning: Saying bowling is a fun social activity.
leisure-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Bowlen) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
leisure-17.forms: Leuke and sociale take -e because activiteit is a de-word.
leisure-17.compare: English "Bowling is ..." uses an -ing noun; Dutch uses the infinitive bowlen as the subject.

mistake.wrong: Bowlen is een leuk sociaal activiteit.
mistake.right: Bowlen is een leuke sociale activiteit.
mistake.why: After een a de-word takes -e.

leisure-17.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
leisure-17.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

conversation-61.meaning: Saying he called you this morning.
conversation-61.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (belde) second (verb-second order).
conversation-61.forms: Bellen: belde. Me is the object form of ik.
conversation-61.compare: English "He called me this morning." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: After a verb the pronoun takes its object form: me, not ik.

conversation-61.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

conversation-62.meaning: Saying you will be back in a moment.
conversation-62.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-62.forms: Zo here means in a moment.
conversation-62.compare: English "I will be right back" uses will; Dutch uses the present: ik ben zo terug.

mistake.why: The adverb zo comes before terug in this expression.

conversation-62.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

transport-32.meaning: Saying he goes to work by bus.
transport-32.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order).
transport-32.forms: Gaan: hij gaat. Met plus a vehicle means by.
transport-32.compare: English "by bus" uses by; Dutch uses met de bus (with the bus).

mistake.wrong: Hij gaat door de bus naar zijn werk.
mistake.right: Hij gaat met de bus naar zijn werk.
mistake.why: To travel by a vehicle Dutch says met: met de bus.

transport-32.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

leisure-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zingen) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
leisure-18.forms: Haar means her before a noun.
leisure-18.compare: English "Singing is her passion" uses an -ing noun; Dutch uses the infinitive zingen as the subject.

mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

leisure-18.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
leisure-18.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

transport-33.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (gaan) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (weg) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-33.compare: English "We are leaving now" uses a progressive and one verb; Dutch splits weggaan: we gaan nu weg.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

transport-33.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

leisure-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zingen) normally occurs toward the end.
leisure-19.forms: Zijn aan het plus infinitive shows an action in progress.
leisure-19.compare: English "She is singing now" uses -ing; Dutch uses is aan het zingen.

mistake.right: Ze is nu aan het zingen.
mistake.why: The progressive is aan het plus an infinitive; het cannot be left out.

leisure-19.practiceFocus: An action happening now: aan het
leisure-19.practiceGuide: Use a conjugated form of zijn + aan het + infinitive. The object normally comes before aan het: Hij is de ramen aan het wassen. These models place aan het directly before the infinitive. With separable verbs, both de ramen aan het schoonmaken and de ramen schoon aan het maken are correct. Dutch simple present can also mean an English ongoing action. Aan het werk contains the NOUN werk, whereas aan het werken contains an infinitive; they are not identical constructions.

leisure-20.meaning: Saying drawing is a creative hobby.
leisure-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Tekenen) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
leisure-20.forms: Hobby is a de-word, so creatieve takes -e.
leisure-20.compare: English "Drawing is a creative hobby" uses an -ing noun; Dutch uses the infinitive tekenen as the subject.

mistake.why: After een a de-word takes -e.

leisure-20.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
leisure-20.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

home-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (meet) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-27.compare: English "I will measure it" uses will and no particle; Dutch uses the present and splits opmeten: ik meet het op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

home-27.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

conversation-63.meaning: Asking if someone will show it to you.
conversation-63.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Laat), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zien) normally occurs toward the end.
conversation-63.forms: Laten zien means show: je laat het me zien, and Laat je het me zien? with question order. Laat is the stem of laten. Its t stays when subject je/jij follows: laat je, never la je. Only an added second-person -t is omitted in inversion; a stem-final t is retained. Zien remains an infinitive after finite laat.
conversation-63.compare: English "Will you show it to me?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

conversation-63.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

food-14.meaning: Saying she likes cooking for her friends.
food-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (kookt) second (verb-second order).
food-14.forms: Graag after a verb means like to.
food-14.compare: English "She likes cooking" uses like plus -ing; Dutch uses the verb plus graag: ze kookt graag.

mistake.wrong: Ze kookt voor haar vrienden graag.
mistake.right: Ze kookt graag voor haar vrienden.
mistake.why: Graag is commonly early in the middle of the clause, but it is not required to follow the finite verb immediately in every context.

food-14.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-64.meaning: Telling someone they are free to go.
conversation-64.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (bent) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te gaan) closes the sentence.
conversation-64.forms: Vrij zijn om te means to be free to.
conversation-64.compare: English "You are free to go" uses to; Dutch needs om te: vrij om te gaan.

mistake.right: Je bent vrij om te gaan.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive after this adjective.

conversation-64.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

food-15.meaning: Saying she waited in the restaurant for an hour.
food-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zitten) normally occurs toward the end; the infinitive (wachten) normally occurs toward the end.
food-15.forms: Zitten te wachten describes waiting while seated. In the perfect, zitten appears as a replacement infinitive before wachten: ze heeft zitten wachten, not ze heeft gezeten wachten. Heeft is finite; zitten and wachten are infinitives. Een uur gives the duration. The literal seated posture is part of this situation, although posture verbs can also emphasise an ongoing activity.
food-15.compare: English "She waited" is one verb; Dutch says heeft ... zitten wachten (has sat waiting).

mistake.wrong: Ze heeft een uur in het restaurant gezeten wachten.
mistake.right: Ze heeft een uur in het restaurant zitten wachten.
mistake.why: Use the infinitive zitten, not a participle.

food-15.practiceGuide: Zitten/staan/liggen describe a position: ik zit op de stoel. Gaan zitten expresses moving into sitting: ik ga zitten. conversation-65.meaning: Saying he gave you good advice.
conversation-65.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (gaf) second (verb-second order).
conversation-65.forms: Geven: gaf. Advies is a het-word, so goed has no -e.
conversation-65.compare: English "He gave me good advice." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: Advies is a het-word: no -e after goed.

conversation-65.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-24.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (werk) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
work-24.forms: The -t drops when subject je/jij follows the finite verb: werk je.
work-24.compare: English "Where do you work?" needs do; Dutch just inverts: waar werk je?

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

work-24.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

home-28.meaning: Saying you will lift it up.
home-28.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (til) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-28.compare: English "I will lift it up" has up after the object; Dutch splits optillen: ik til het op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

home-28.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

conversation-66.meaning: Saying it is better to help.
conversation-66.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te helpen) closes the sentence.
conversation-66.forms: Beter is the comparative of goed.
conversation-66.compare: English "It is better to help." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Het is beter om te helpen.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive after this adjective.

conversation-66.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

weather-12.meaning: Asking what the weather is like.
weather-12.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat voor weer) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
weather-12.forms: Wat voor asks what kind of.
weather-12.compare: English "What is the weather like?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

weather-12.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

food-16.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heeft), and the subject (iemand) follows it.

food-16.compare: English "Does anyone have water?" needs "does" to form the question; Dutch just starts with the finite verb (Heeft).

mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

food-16.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

school-18.meaning: Saying she explained it to you.
school-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (uitgelegd) normally occurs toward the end.
school-18.compare: English "She explained it to me." uses the simple past; Dutch often uses the perfect (auxiliary plus participle) for a finished event, with the participle (uitgelegd) at the end.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

school-18.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
school-18.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. weather-13.meaning: Saying she was looking at the sky.

mistake.why: Kijken needs naar before what you look at.

mistake.wrong: Ik staat elke ochtend bij de bushalte.
mistake.right: Ik sta elke ochtend bij de bushalte.

work-26.meaning: Saying she will find a new job soon.

work-26.compare: English "She is going to find a new job soon".

mistake.wrong: Ze gaat binnenkort vinden een nieuwe baan.
mistake.right: Ze gaat binnenkort een nieuwe baan vinden.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

work-26.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

school-19.meaning: Saying she did not go to school.
school-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gegaan) normally occurs toward the end.

mistake.wrong: Zij heeft niet naar school gegaan.
mistake.right: Zij is niet naar school gegaan.
mistake.why: Gaan is a verb of movement, so its perfect uses zijn.

mistake.wrong: Wij gaan vroeger elke zomer naar het strand.
mistake.right: Wij gingen vroeger elke zomer naar het strand.
mistake.why: With vroeger Dutch uses the simple past: gingen.

conversation-72.compare: English "It is hard to say" has the same shape; Dutch needs te before the infinitive.

mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive after this adjective.

mistake.right: We hadden het huis al schoongemaakt.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-73.meaning: Saying you had already checked the time.

mistake.right: Ik had de tijd al gecontroleerd.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

home-30.meaning: Saying walking the dog is your job.

mistake.wrong: De hond uitlaten is taak mijn.
mistake.right: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak.
mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

home-30.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. parts.text: met de bouw van het nieuwe gebouw

conversation-74.meaning: Saying she heard the news on the radio.
