conversation-74.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hoorde) second (verb-second order).
conversation-74.compare: English "She heard the news" is the same simple past; Dutch nieuws is a het-word and singular.

mistake.wrong: Ze hoorde de nieuws op de radio.
mistake.right: Ze hoorde het nieuws op de radio.
mistake.why: Nieuws is a het-word, so the article is het.

conversation-74.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

shopping-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
shopping-24.compare: English "I need my wallet" is one verb; Dutch splits ik heb ... nodig around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig goes after the object.

shopping-24.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

food-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order).
food-18.compare: English "They did not have any water" needs "did not"; Dutch simply says ze hadden geen water.

mistake.why: Use geen instead of niet before a noun.

food-18.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
food-18.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

home-32.meaning: Saying they will hang up the decorations this afternoon.
home-32.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hangen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-32.compare: English "They will hang up the decorations" keeps up beside the verb; Dutch splits ophangen: ze hangen ... op.

mistake.right: Ze hangen vanmiddag de versieringen op.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

home-32.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

conversation-75.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (probeer) second (verb-second order).
conversation-75.compare: English "I will try again" uses will; Dutch uses the present tense: ik probeer het opnieuw.

mistake.why: The object comes before opnieuw.

conversation-75.practiceFocus: Proberen: try a thing or try to act
conversation-75.practiceGuide: Proberen means try. Ik probeer is present; ik probeerde is singular simple past; wij probeerden is plural past; ik heb geprobeerd uses the participle with hebben. The regular participle is ge + probeer + d. A thing can be tried directly; trying to do something uses proberen + te + infinitive. After zal the verb becomes proberen: ik zal proberen te bellen. Trying on clothes usually uses passen; tasting food can use proeven.

transport-35.meaning: Saying she is going to fly to London next summer.
transport-35.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vliegen) normally occurs toward the end. Gaan plus an infinitive expresses a plan or something about to happen.
transport-35.compare: English "She is going to fly" uses going to; Dutch uses gaan plus an infinitive at the end: ze gaat ... vliegen.

mistake.wrong: Ze gaat vliegen volgende zomer naar Londen.
mistake.right: Ze gaat volgende zomer naar Londen vliegen.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

transport-35.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

school-21.meaning: Saying you knew the answer but forgot it.
school-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wist) second (verb-second order). Maar joins two main clauses, so each keeps its own verb second.
school-21.forms: Weten: ik weet; simple past wist/wisten. Vergeten has participle vergeten and can use hebben or zijn. Here ben ... vergeten describes no longer remembering the answer.
school-21.compare: English "I knew the answer, but I have forgotten it." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (vergeten) in the final verb bracket.

mistake.wrong: Ik wist het antwoord, maar ik heb het vergeten.
mistake.right: Ik wist het antwoord, maar ik ben het vergeten.
mistake.why: Vergeten can use hebben or zijn depending on meaning and usage. The model uses zijn for no longer remembering the answer; the hebben version is not automatically an error.

school-21.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
school-21.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-28.meaning: Saying you write reports every week.
work-28.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (schrijven) second (verb-second order).
work-28.compare: English "We write reports every week" has the same pattern; Dutch puts the time phrase before the object.

mistake.why: With we the verb ends in -en.

work-28.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

transport-36.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wanneer) takes the first position, so the finite verb (komen) comes second and the subject (ze) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (aan) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-36.compare: English "When will they arrive?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

transport-36.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-29.meaning: Saying you are thinking about changing jobs.
work-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (denk) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om van baan te veranderen) closes the sentence.
work-29.forms: Van baan veranderen means to change jobs.
work-29.compare: English "I am thinking about changing jobs" uses -ing; Dutch uses om ... te plus an infinitive: erover om van baan te veranderen.

mistake.wrong: Ik denk erover om van baan veranderen.
mistake.right: Ik denk erover om van baan te veranderen.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive.

work-29.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

conversation-76.meaning: Asking what kind of noise that is.
conversation-76.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (dat) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. Wat is dat voor ... asks what kind of something it is.
conversation-76.compare: English "What is that noise?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: Keep dat after the verb and voor geluid together.

conversation-76.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

transport-37.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (zijn) comes second and the subject (ze) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gegaan) normally occurs toward the end.
transport-37.compare: English "Where did they go?" uses did; Dutch uses the perfect with zijn: waar zijn ze heen gegaan?

mistake.why: Gaan is a verb of movement, so its perfect uses zijn.

transport-37.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
transport-37.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

home-33.meaning: Saying you will tidy your room before you leave.
home-33.order: The main clause uses gaan plus an infinitive. After voordat the verb normally occurs toward the end.
home-33.forms: Weggaan is one word when the verb is at the end.
home-33.compare: English "before you leave" keeps the verb in the middle; Dutch sends it to the end: voordat je weggaat.

mistake.why: A separable verb at the end is one word.

home-33.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

conversation-77.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (leek) second (verb-second order).
conversation-77.compare: English "She seemed confused." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-77.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

home-34.meaning: Saying you grow your own vegetables in the garden.
home-34.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (kweken) second (verb-second order).
home-34.compare: English "our own vegetables" puts own after our; Dutch does the same: onze eigen groenten.

mistake.why: Eigen comes after the possessive.

home-34.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

shopping-25.meaning: Saying you sold your old car last month.
shopping-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (verkocht) normally occurs toward the end.
shopping-25.forms: Verkopen: verkocht. Oude takes -e before the de-word auto.
shopping-25.compare: English "I sold my old car" is a simple past; Dutch uses the perfect: ik heb ... verkocht.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb vorige maand mijn oud auto verkocht.
mistake.right: Ik heb vorige maand mijn oude auto verkocht.
mistake.why: After a possessive a de-word takes -e.

shopping-25.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
shopping-25.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

conversation-78.meaning: Saying you want to know why.
conversation-78.order: Ik is the subject and wil the finite modal. Weten is an infinitive after wil. Waarom stands for the reason you want to know; this omitted embedded question can follow weten. The last word is therefore not always the action verb.
conversation-78.compare: English "I want to know why" has the same order; Dutch waarom closes the clause.

mistake.why: Both orders occur. In the model, waarom represents an omitted embedded reason question after weten. Ik wil waarom weten can stress the reason word itself. Practise the taught sentence without treating every other order as wrong.

conversation-78.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

transport-38.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (kwamen) second (verb-second order).
transport-38.compare: English "They arrived late" is one verb; Dutch says kwamen te laat (came too late).

mistake.why: The past plural of komen is kwamen.

transport-38.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

shopping-26.meaning: Saying you had already done the shopping.
shopping-26.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedaan) normally occurs toward the end.
shopping-26.forms: Boodschappen doen means to do the shopping.
shopping-26.compare: English "I had already done the shopping." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (gedaan) in the final verb bracket.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gedaan de boodschappen al.
mistake.right: Ik had de boodschappen al gedaan.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

shopping-26.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
shopping-26.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

home-35.meaning: Promising to repair it for someone.
home-35.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (repareren) normally occurs toward the end.
home-35.compare: English "I will repair it for you." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (repareren) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik zal repareren het voor je.
mistake.right: Ik zal het voor je repareren.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

home-35.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

weather-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De herfst) comes first and the finite verb (komt) second (verb-second order).
weather-14.compare: English "Autumn is coming" is the same idea; Dutch adds eraan: de herfst komt eraan.

mistake.why: De herfst komt is possible Dutch. Eraan adds the sense that autumn is approaching; it is not required in every sentence with komen.

weather-14.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

shopping-27.meaning: Saying he stands behind the counter in the bakery.
shopping-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (staat) second (verb-second order).
shopping-27.compare: English "He stands behind the counter in the bakery." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: The preposition comes before its noun.

shopping-27.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-30.meaning: Saying you start working at eight in the morning.
work-30.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (begin) second (verb-second order).
work-30.compare: English "I start work at eight in the morning." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Ik begin om acht uur 's ochtends werken.
mistake.right: Ik begin om acht uur 's ochtends met werken.
mistake.why: Beginnen needs met before the activity that starts.

work-30.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

conversation-79.order: A fixed expression with no finite verb: an adverb followed by a participle (short for ik heb het graag gedaan).
conversation-79.forms: Short for ik heb het graag gedaan.
conversation-79.compare: English "You're welcome" is a different phrase; Dutch graag gedaan literally means "gladly done".

mistake.why: Graag gedaan is a fixed phrase with nothing added.

conversation-79.practiceFocus: Short expressions and their intended meaning
conversation-79.practiceGuide: Some useful expressions are fragments rather than full subject-plus-verb clauses: Hartelijk dank, Graag gedaan. Do not invent V2 inversion for a phrase with no finite verb. Learn what the expression does in the conversation, and compare related full sentences. A polite formula can have several natural English equivalents.

home-36.meaning: Saying you make your bed every morning.
home-36.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (maak) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) normally occurs toward the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-36.compare: English "I make my bed" has no particle; Dutch opmaken splits: ik maak ... op.

mistake.wrong: Ik opmaak elke ochtend mijn bed.
mistake.right: Ik maak elke ochtend mijn bed op.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

home-36.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

home-37.meaning: Saying they use the leftover paint for the bedroom.
home-37.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gebruiken) second (verb-second order).
home-37.forms: Overgebleven is a participle used as an adjective.
home-37.compare: English "the leftover paint" uses leftover; Dutch uses the participle overgebleven as an adjective.

mistake.why: The adjective comes between the article and the noun.

home-37.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-31.meaning: Is this your workplace? You show a new colleague a desk and ask whether this is their workplace.
work-31.order: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb is. The subject dit follows it; uw werkplek identifies what dit refers to.
work-31.forms: Dit is used independently here, so it does not have to agree with the de-word werkplek. Uw is the polite possessive; u would refer to the person rather than possession.
work-31.compare: English also puts is before the subject in this question. Workplace is broader than workstation; the desk scenario makes the intended meaning clear.

mistake.why: Use uw before the possessed noun.

work-31.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-32.meaning: I'll prepare the agenda. During meeting planning, you volunteer to prepare the list of discussion items.
work-32.order: Ik is the first constituent; zal occupies the second position. The infinitive voorbereiden closes the verb bracket after the object.
work-32.forms: Zal is the singular form of zullen. In this context it offers a future commitment. Voorbereiden stays together after zal; without the auxiliary: Ik bereid de agenda voor.
work-32.compare: English keeps will prepare together. Dutch allows de agenda between zal and voorbereiden. Agenda here means meeting agenda, not a diary.

mistake.why: Put this infinitive after the object.

work-32.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-33.meaning: What is the goal? Before a team starts a task, you ask what it is meant to achieve.
work-33.order: The question word wat comes first, then is, then the subject het doel. Wat asks for the identity of the goal.
work-33.forms: Doel is a het-word. Is agrees with the singular subject. Wat is a question word here, not the conjunction dat.
work-33.compare: English uses the same visible sequence: what + is + the goal. Dutch uses het with doel.

mistake.why: A direct question uses this question order; wat het doel is can occur inside an embedded question.

work-33.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-34.meaning: We discussed many things. After a meeting, you tell a colleague that the discussion covered many topics.
work-34.order: The subject we comes first and the finite past-tense verb bespraken is second. Veel dingen is what was discussed.
work-34.forms: Bespraken is the plural simple past of bespreken; singular: ik besprak. Bespreken takes its object directly, without an added over.
work-34.compare: English discuss likewise takes a direct object. Dutch simple past is suitable for reporting the meeting; a perfect-tense retelling can also be natural but is a different form.

mistake.why: The plural subject takes bespraken.

work-34.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-35.meaning: It's nice to be here. At the start of a visit, you tell your hosts that you are pleased to be there.
work-35.order: Het fills the subject position, is is second, and the om-clause explains what is nice. Within that clause hier precedes te zijn.
work-35.forms: The infinitive zijn follows te. Om introduces this explanatory infinitive clause; it does not express a purpose such as in order to in this sentence.
work-35.compare: English uses dummy it and a to-infinitive. Dutch has om ... te here, with hier between om and te zijn.

mistake.wrong: Het is fijn om hier zijn.
mistake.right: Het is fijn om hier te zijn.
mistake.why: Keep te with the infinitive.

work-35.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-36.meaning: Let's make their voices heard. At a discussion, you suggest giving absent team members a chance to express their views.
work-36.order: Laten we introduces a shared suggestion. The object hun stemmen appears before the final infinitives laten horen.
work-36.forms: The two occurrences of laten have different jobs: the first forms let's, the second means let or cause something to be heard. Hun is possessive before stemmen, not a subject pronoun.
work-36.compare: English make their voices heard uses a participle; Dutch uses laten horen with an infinitive. Stemmen means voices here, not votes.

mistake.wrong: Laten we hun stemmen laten gehoord.
mistake.right: Laten we hun stemmen laten horen.
mistake.why: Laten takes an infinitive here.

work-36.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-37.meaning: We met each other yesterday morning. You tell a colleague when you and another person first met.
work-37.order: We precedes the finite past verb ontmoetten. Elkaar identifies the reciprocal participants; the time phrase is placed after it.
work-37.forms: Ontmoetten is plural simple past; it has the same spelling as the infinitive but is finite here. Elkaar means each other; it differs from reflexive onszelf.
work-37.compare: English can simply say we met, but each other preserves the explicit Dutch reciprocal meaning. Gisterochtend is yesterday morning, not last night.

mistake.why: Use the plural past form with we.

work-37.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-38.meaning: Let's look over the contract. Before signing, you suggest reading the contract together.
work-38.order: Laten we marks the joint suggestion. Bekijken is the final infinitive and het contract is its object.
work-38.forms: Contract is a het-word. Bekijken means look at or examine, not necessarily approve or revise. The prefix be- remains attached.
work-38.compare: English let's look over is a natural way to express this examination; review is possible but should not imply making revisions.

mistake.why: Bekijken takes a direct object; kijken normally needs naar for this meaning.

work-38.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-39.meaning: We're considering all the options. Your team compares several possible solutions before choosing one.
work-39.order: We is first and the finite present verb overwegen is second. Alle opties is its direct object.
work-39.forms: Overwegen here means consider and is inseparable. Alle goes directly before the plural noun opties in this phrase.
work-39.compare: Dutch simple present can describe what is happening now; English naturally uses we're considering here. It need not become aan het overwegen.

mistake.why: Do not split overwegen in this meaning.

work-39.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-40.meaning: I've completed my training. You tell your manager that your required training is now finished.
work-40.order: Ik is first and the finite verb Heb is second; voltooid, the participle, closes the perfect-tense bracket at the end, after mijn training.
work-40.forms: Voltooien takes hebben in this transitive use. Voltooid ends in d; it is not voltooit, which can be a finite present form. Mijn specifies whose training.
work-40.compare: English I've completed highlights completion now. Dutch perfect can also correspond to English completed in a finished-past context; it is not a rigid one-to-one tense rule.

mistake.why: Use the participle after heb.

work-40.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-40.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-41.meaning: I need his approval. You explain that a manager must approve a purchase before it can proceed.
work-41.order: Heb is second. The thing needed, zijn goedkeuring, stands before nodig in the phrase iets nodig hebben.
work-41.forms: Zijn is possessive here, not the infinitive be. Nodig is an adjective complement, not a second verb. The noun is de goedkeuring, but zijn replaces the article.
work-41.compare: English uses the verb need; Dutch expresses this with hebben ... nodig. Do not translate each word separately as have necessary.

mistake.why: Use hebben ... nodig.

work-41.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-42.meaning: Give him his report. You ask a colleague to hand a manager the report that belongs to him.
work-42.order: The imperative geef starts the sentence and the understood subject you is omitted. Hem names the recipient, followed by what is given.
work-42.forms: Geef is the stem of geven. Hem is an object pronoun; zijn is possessive before rapport. They have different roles despite referring to the same person.
work-42.compare: English give him his report has the same recipient/object order here. An aan-phrase can make the recipient explicit: Geef zijn rapport aan hem.

mistake.why: The recipient needs the object form hem.

work-42.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-43.meaning: She explained the route. You describe how a colleague explained the journey to a visitor.
work-43.order: Legde is the finite past verb in second position. Uitleggen splits in this main clause, with uit after the object.
work-43.forms: Singular zij takes legde; plural zij would take legden. Uitleggen means explain. Uit alone is not a direction such as out of the room here.
work-43.compare: English explained is one word; Dutch distributes the finite verb and particle around de route.

mistake.why: Split the separable verb in this independent main clause.

work-43.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-44.meaning: We bought it for her. You explain that a gift was bought on behalf of a female colleague.
work-44.order: Hebben is the finite second-position verb; gekocht closes the bracket. Het is what was bought and voor haar identifies the beneficiary.
work-44.forms: Kopen has the irregular participle gekocht. Haar follows the preposition voor; it is not possessive before a noun here.
work-44.compare: English bought expresses a finished past action in this context. Dutch hebben gekocht is perfect; for her is not the same as from her.

mistake.wrong: We hebben het voor zij gekocht.
mistake.right: We hebben het voor haar gekocht.
mistake.why: Use the object form after voor.

work-44.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-44.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-45.meaning: Could you explain this further? You politely ask a presenter to give a fuller explanation of an unclear point.
work-45.order: The yes/no request begins with kunt, followed by u. Uitleggen stays together as the final infinitive after the modal.
work-45.forms: Kunt u retains t; the ordinary t-dropping rule before subject je does not apply to u. Kan u is also used in Belgium. Could expresses politeness here, not a Dutch past-tense form.
work-45.compare: English can you is also possible. Could you is a natural polite rendering in this scenario; it must not be mistaken for past ability.

mistake.why: Do not copy kun je onto polite u.

work-45.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-46.meaning: I'll allocate the resources. As project coordinator, you promise to assign the available resources to tasks.
work-46.order: Zal is second and toewijzen is the final infinitive. The object de middelen stands inside the verb bracket.
work-46.forms: Middelen can mean resources or means; this project context selects resources. Toewijzen is separable, but remains joined after zal; Ik wijs de middelen toe uses the finite lexical verb.
work-46.compare: English will allocate stays together, whereas the Dutch object can stand between auxiliary and infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ik zal de middelen toe wijzen.
mistake.why: Write the infinitive as one word.

work-46.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-47.meaning: He worked late yesterday evening. You explain why a colleague is tired after working late the previous evening.
work-47.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Heeft is second and gewerkt ends the perfect bracket. Gisteravond gives the day/evening, and laat narrows it to a late time.
work-47.forms: Werken forms the perfect with hebben. Heeft agrees with hij; gewerkt is the participle. This phrase order is natural, not a universal rule for all time expressions.
work-47.compare: Gisteravond is yesterday evening. Last night can overlap in context, but Dutch vannacht would refer specifically to the night.

mistake.why: Use the participle in this perfect construction.

work-47.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-47.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-48.meaning: You should bring it to me. You remind a colleague, with softened insistence, that they ought to bring you an item.
work-48.order: Zou occupies second position. The object pronouns stand before the final modal-plus-infinitive group moeten brengen.
work-48.forms: Zou moeten gives a recommendation or expectation rather than an unconditional future promise. Moeten is an infinitive after zou; brengen is the lexical infinitive after moeten.
work-48.compare: English should uses one modal for the idea expressed by Dutch zou ... moeten. Translate me as to me here; it is the recipient.

mistake.wrong: Je zou het me moet brengen.
mistake.right: Je zou het me moeten brengen.
mistake.why: The modal after zou is an infinitive.

work-48.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-49.meaning: I'm making a phone call. You signal to a colleague that you are currently speaking on the phone.
work-49.order: Ben is second. Aan het + infinitive describes an action in progress; bellen is the infinitive, not another finite verb.
work-49.forms: Aan het is a fixed ongoing-action construction here. Ik bel can also mean I am calling; aan het explicitly foregrounds the action as ongoing.
work-49.compare: English I'm on the phone is natural in this scene, but I'm making a phone call directly teaches the activity expressed by bellen.

mistake.why: Use the infinitive after aan het.

work-49.practiceFocus: An action happening now: aan het
work-49.practiceGuide: Use a conjugated form of zijn + aan het + infinitive. The object normally comes before aan het: Hij is de ramen aan het wassen. These models place aan het directly before the infinitive. With separable verbs, both de ramen aan het schoonmaken and de ramen schoon aan het maken are correct. Dutch simple present can also mean an English ongoing action. Aan het werk contains the NOUN werk, whereas aan het werken contains an infinitive; they are not identical constructions.

work-50.meaning: I'll explain it later. You postpone explaining a procedure until after the current task.
work-50.order: Leg is second. Uitleggen splits in the main clause, and uit appears after het later.
work-50.forms: Leg is present tense, but later and the promise context give future reference. Het is the object it, not an article before a noun here.
work-50.compare: English naturally uses I'll explain for this promise. The Dutch present is not a past tense merely because the English uses will.

mistake.why: Split the finite separable verb.

work-50.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-51.meaning: Building a future takes work. You encourage someone who is slowly developing a career and long-term plans.
work-51.order: The whole phrase Een toekomst opbouwen is one subject constituent. Vraagt is second by constituent, although it is the fourth written word.
work-51.forms: The infinitive phrase acts as a singular subject, so vraagt has t. Opbouwen remains together inside that subject phrase; werk is an uncountable noun here.
work-51.compare: English uses building for the activity used as subject; Dutch uses the infinitive opbouwen. Vraagt means requires here, not asks a question.

mistake.why: Treat the activity phrase as a singular subject.

work-51.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-51.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-52.meaning: My proposal is ready. You tell your team that the proposal is ready for them to read.
work-52.order: Mijn voorstel is one subject constituent; is is the second constituent. Klaar says something about the subject.
work-52.forms: Klaar is a predicate adjective and receives no attributive -e ending here. Mijn replaces the article of het voorstel.
work-52.compare: English and Dutch both use a linking verb with ready/klaar. The two-word subject still occupies only the first constituent position.

mistake.why: A predicate adjective does not take this -e ending.

work-52.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-53.meaning: Could you take care of this? You politely ask a colleague to process and finish a particular request.
work-53.order: Kunt starts the yes/no request; u follows. Afhandelen remains one final infinitive after the modal.
work-53.forms: Afhandelen means deal with and bring to completion, especially a request or case. Kunt u is neutral polite written Dutch; kan u is also used in Belgian speech.
work-53.compare: Take care of this expresses the practical request. Could is politeness in English here, not a literal Dutch past conditional.

mistake.why: The verb after kunt must be the infinitive.

work-53.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-54.meaning: He's busy fixing the leak. A colleague is repairing a leaking pipe, and you explain why he cannot answer immediately.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het repareren van het lek

work-54.order: Hij is first and is is second. Bezig describes his activity; the met-phrase specifies what keeps him occupied.
work-54.forms: Het repareren nominalizes the infinitive, so van het lek supplies what is repaired. This is not a second finite verb. Het lek uses het because lek is neuter as a noun.
work-54.compare: English uses busy fixing without with. Dutch uses bezig met in this version; bezig het lek te repareren is another natural construction.

mistake.wrong: Hij is bezig met repareren het lek.
mistake.right: Hij is bezig met het repareren van het lek.
mistake.why: In this noun-like version, use van for its object.

work-54.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-54.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

work-55.meaning: May I suggest something? During a discussion, you politely ask permission to put forward an idea.
work-55.order: Mag starts the yes/no permission question. The infinitive voorstellen stays together at the end after iets.
work-55.forms: Mogen expresses permission here, not ability. Voorstellen means suggest in this context; it can mean introduce in a different context, so the object and scene matter.
work-55.compare: May I makes the permission meaning explicit. Can I is also a natural everyday request, but not a claim about ability in this scene.

mistake.why: Use the infinitive after mag.

work-55.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-56.meaning: I'm ill. You phone your workplace to explain that you are ill and cannot come in.
work-56.order: Ik is first and ben is the second constituent. Ziek describes the subject rather than an object.
work-56.forms: Ben is the first-person present of zijn. Ziek is a predicate adjective, so no attributive -e ending is added. Ill describes illness here, not disgust.
work-56.compare: English likewise uses be with ill or sick. Dutch uses ik ben, not ik is.

mistake.why: Predicate adjectives keep their base form here.

work-56.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-57.meaning: The network needs regular maintenance. You explain that the office network needs routine maintenance to keep it reliable.
work-57.order: Het netwerk is one subject constituent and heeft is second. The thing needed comes before nodig in hebben ... nodig.
work-57.forms: Onderhoud is an uncountable het-noun. Regelmatig is an attributive adjective without -e before this indefinite neuter noun. No article is needed with uncountable onderhoud here.
work-57.compare: English uses need as a verb. Dutch expresses the same need through heeft ... nodig; its maintenance is unnecessarily possessive in this context.

mistake.why: Include the finite verb heeft.

work-57.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-58.meaning: I'm selling my old laptop. You show a colleague the old laptop you are offering for sale.
work-58.order: Ik comes first and verkoop is second. Mijn oude laptop is the direct object being sold.
work-58.forms: Verkopen is inseparable; ver- is not a loose final particle. Oude takes -e inside this possessed noun phrase. The present describes a current sale offer.
work-58.compare: Dutch simple present can correspond to English progressive am selling. The source I'll sell it is possible in a promise context, but is not the only meaning of verkoop.

mistake.why: Do not split inseparable verkopen.

work-58.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-59.meaning: Is it clear? After explaining a task, you check whether the instructions are clear to your colleague.
work-59.order: The yes/no question starts with is, followed by its subject het. Duidelijk describes the explanation referred to by het.
work-59.forms: Het is a subject pronoun here, not an article before a noun. Duidelijk has no -e as a predicate adjective.
work-59.compare: English is it clear has the same verb-first question sequence. It is asking about understanding, not physical transparency in this scene.

mistake.why: Use verb-first order for this independent yes/no question.

work-59.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-60.meaning: Show up. You firmly tell a colleague to attend the appointment rather than miss it.
work-60.order: The command begins with kom; the understood subject you is omitted. Opdagen remains joined as the infinitive in komen opdagen.
work-60.forms: Komen opdagen means appear or show up for an expected event. It is not the main-clause split of one verb called komopdagen.
work-60.compare: English show up is an idiomatic two-word verb. Dutch uses komen plus the infinitive opdagen in this command.

mistake.why: The infinitive keeps its final -n.

work-60.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-61.meaning: This investment is very risky. At a planning meeting, you warn that a proposed investment carries a large risk.
work-61.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Deze investering occupies one first constituent. Is is second, and erg modifies the predicate adjective riskant.
work-61.forms: Investering is a de-word, so deze is the singular nearby demonstrative. Predicate riskant receives no -e; erg means very here, not bad.
work-61.compare: English very risky closely matches erg riskant. Dutch demonstratives distinguish de and het nouns while English this does not.

mistake.why: Use deze with singular de investering.

work-61.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-62.meaning: You pay it to her. You clarify that your colleague, rather than you, is the person who pays a particular amount to a woman.
work-62.order: Jij is first and betaalt is second. Het refers to the amount paid; haar is the recipient. With this unstressed object pronoun, het can precede the recipient.
work-62.forms: Jij is the full subject form and can carry contrastive stress. Betaalt retains -t with a preceding jij. Haar is not possessive here because no possessed noun follows it.
work-62.compare: English commonly makes the recipient explicit with to her. A Dutch aan-phrase is also possible: Jij betaalt het aan haar.

mistake.why: A preceding jij requires this present -t form.

work-62.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-63.meaning: I'm half an hour too early for the meeting. You arrive at an empty meeting room and realize the meeting starts in half an hour.
work-63.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ben is second after ik. Een halfuur specifies how much too early; voor de vergadering identifies the event.
work-63.forms: Te intensifies vroeg beyond the appropriate time, unlike gewoon vroeg. Halfuur and half uur are both accepted spellings for this duration; neither is the clock phrase half acht.
work-63.compare: English half an hour too early corresponds to een halfuur te vroeg. Too early differs from merely early.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben een half uur naar vroeg.
mistake.right: Ik ben een halfuur te vroeg.
mistake.why: Te expresses excessive earliness.

work-63.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-64.meaning: He made it for us. A colleague shows you the shelf another man made for your team.
work-64.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Heeft is second and gemaakt closes the perfect bracket. Het is the thing made; voor ons identifies its intended beneficiaries.
work-64.forms: For this making-something-for-someone sense, voor ons is natural. A bare recipient ons is not a general replacement for every for-phrase. Maken forms its perfect with hebben.
work-64.compare: English for us is preserved rather than changing to to us. The sentence says who benefits, not necessarily who receives a transfer.

mistake.right: Hij heeft het voor ons gemaakt.
mistake.why: The model makes the beneficiary explicit with voor ons. Bare indirect objects are possible with some verbs and contexts; they are not a universal substitute for every voor-phrase.

work-64.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-64.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-65.meaning: Give this folder to the manager. You hand a folder to a colleague and ask them to take it to the manager.
work-65.order: Geef begins the command without an expressed subject. The object comes next; the aan-phrase specifies the recipient.
work-65.forms: Map is a de-word, so this folder is deze map. Aan marks the person receiving it; it does not mean on in this context.
work-65.compare: English give ... to corresponds to Dutch geef ... aan. The original independent dit can stand alone, but attributive deze must agree with map.

mistake.wrong: Geef dit map aan de manager.
mistake.right: Geef deze map aan de manager.
mistake.why: Map requires deze.

work-65.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-66.meaning: I'm ready for my presentation. You have finished preparing and tell your colleague that you can give the presentation.
work-66.order: Ben is second. Klaar describes the subject, and voor mijn presentatie specifies what the readiness concerns.
work-66.forms: Klaar voor means ready for. Klaar alone can also mean finished; the added voor-phrase selects readiness here. Mijn is possessive before presentatie.
work-66.compare: English done is not appropriate for being ready to start this presentation, though it can translate isolated ik ben klaar in other contexts.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben klaar van mijn presentatie.
mistake.right: Ik ben klaar voor mijn presentatie.
mistake.why: Use voor for readiness for an event.

work-66.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-67.meaning: Are you writing the report now? You check whether a colleague is currently working on the report.
work-67.order: The yes/no question starts with schrijf, then subject je. Nu marks the current time and het verslag is what is being written.
work-67.forms: Schrijft becomes schrijf before subject je in inversion. This t-dropping concerns je as subject, not a possessive je before a noun.
work-67.compare: English asks with are ... writing. Dutch can use its simple present for the same ongoing action; no aan het construction is required.

mistake.why: Drop ordinary present -t before subject je.

work-67.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-68.meaning: Do you have to tell me that before the meeting? You ask whether information needs to be given to you before the meeting rather than later.
work-68.order: Moet starts the yes/no question. Vertellen is the final infinitive; the pronouns and time phrase fit between them.
work-68.forms: Moeten expresses necessity, not permission. The accent on vóór emphasizes before rather than for. Dat is the object that, not a subordinator introducing a clause.
work-68.compare: Do you have to ... is natural English for a necessity question. Restore that, omitted by the video English; do not replace must with may.

mistake.why: Use the infinitive after moet.

work-68.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-69.meaning: I need one. A colleague offers you blank forms, and you say that you need one of them.
work-69.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Heb is second. Er links the number één to the previously mentioned items, and nodig completes hebben ... nodig.
work-69.forms: Quantitative er does not mean there in this sentence. Één means one, with accents distinguishing it from the indefinite article een.
work-69.compare: English can simply say I need one without a separate equivalent of quantitative er. Dutch makes the reference to a counted set explicit.

mistake.why: Use quantitative er when referring to one of the mentioned forms; daar would introduce a location.

work-69.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-70.meaning: Intervene. A discussion is turning into a quarrel, and you ask the team leader to intervene.
work-70.order: Grijp begins the command; the understood subject you is omitted. In is the separated particle of ingrijpen.
work-70.forms: Ingrijpen means intervene in this scene. In is not a location or an instruction to grab a physical object.
work-70.compare: English step in is an idiomatic alternative. Intervene avoids confusing it with literally taking a step into a room.

mistake.why: The imperative separates the particle.

work-70.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-71.meaning: That sounds like a plan. A colleague suggests a practical approach, and you respond that it sounds workable.
work-71.order: Dat is the first subject constituent and klinkt is second. Als een plan supplies what the idea sounds like.
work-71.forms: Dat is a demonstrative subject, not a conjunction. Als means like in this comparison, not if introducing a subordinate clause.
work-71.compare: English sounds like maps to klinkt als. Neither language is literally describing an audible plan in this idiomatic approval response.

mistake.why: Singular dat requires klinkt with -t.

work-71.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-72.meaning: Could you give examples? You ask a trainer for concrete examples of a rule they have just described.
work-72.order: Kunt begins the polite yes/no request, u follows, and geven stays as the final infinitive after voorbeelden.
work-72.forms: Voorbeelden is the plural of het voorbeeld. An indefinite plural noun does not require een. Kunt u retains -t, unlike ordinary inversion before je.
work-72.compare: English could signals politeness in this request, not past ability. Can you is also possible.

mistake.why: Een cannot mark this indefinite plural.

work-72.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-73.meaning: They're gone. Someone asks where the visitors are, and you explain that they have already left the office.
work-73.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ze is first and the finite present zijn is second. Weg describes their current absence.
work-73.forms: Ze is plural here because zijn is plural; singular she would use is. Weg means gone or away, not the noun de weg meaning road.
work-73.compare: English they're gone also reports the present state after leaving. Dutch zijn weg is not itself a perfect construction with a participle.

mistake.why: Use zijn when ze refers to multiple visitors.

work-73.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-74.meaning: Could you draw up a quotation? You ask a supplier to prepare a written quotation for a repair job.
work-74.order: Kunt begins the request, followed by u. Opstellen is the joined infinitive at the end after een offerte.
work-74.forms: Offerte means a price quotation, not a quotation from a book. Opstellen means draft or draw up; it remains together after the modal.
work-74.compare: English draw up a quotation makes the preparation action explicit. Offer a quote and prepare a quote are related but context-dependent alternatives.

mistake.why: Use the infinitive after kunt.

work-74.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-75.meaning: We offered her our services. Your team has offered professional help to a client, and you tell a colleague what was offered.
work-75.order: Hebben is second and aangeboden closes the perfect bracket. The recipient haar comes before the full object noun phrase onze diensten.
work-75.forms: Aanbieden has participle aangeboden, with ge between aan and boden. Onze agrees with plural diensten. Wij can emphasize our team.
work-75.compare: English offered her our services has the same recipient/full-object sequence here. The original ze did not identify what was offered.

mistake.wrong: Wij hebben haar ons diensten aangeboden.
mistake.right: Wij hebben haar onze diensten aangeboden.
mistake.why: Plural diensten requires onze.

work-75.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-75.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-76.meaning: Use this form. You point out the correct form for a colleague to fill in.
work-76.order: The command begins with gebruik and omits the understood subject you. Dit formulier is the direct object.
work-76.forms: Formulier is a het-word, so the nearby singular demonstrative is dit. Gebruik is the verb stem in this imperative.
work-76.compare: English this does not distinguish noun gender. Dutch distinguishes dit formulier from deze map.

mistake.why: Formulier takes het and therefore attributive dit.

work-76.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-77.meaning: We need a new strategy. The current approach is failing, and you tell your team a new strategy is needed.
work-77.order: Hebben is second. The object noun phrase comes before nodig in the need construction.
work-77.forms: Strategie is a de-word. Its attributive adjective takes -e even after een: een nieuwe strategie. Compare the indefinite het-word pattern een nieuw plan.
work-77.compare: English uses need directly. Dutch hebben ... nodig surrounds the object; new has no ending changes in English.

mistake.wrong: We hebben een nieuw strategie nodig.
mistake.right: We hebben een nieuwe strategie nodig.
mistake.why: Strategie is a de-word.

work-77.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-78.meaning: Can we use their meeting room? Your team needs a room, and you ask whether another team's meeting room is available for you.
work-78.order: Kunnen begins the yes/no question, followed by we. Gebruiken is the final infinitive after the object.
work-78.forms: Kunnen agrees with plural we. Hun is possessive before vergaderruimte, not the subject of the sentence. The question can ask about practical possibility or permission in context.
work-78.compare: English can also covers possibility or permission here. Meeting room is the natural general sense of vergaderruimte.

mistake.why: Use plural kunnen with we.

work-78.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-79.meaning: This is our legacy. At a company anniversary, you point to projects built by earlier colleagues as the legacy they left you.
work-79.order: Dit is an independent demonstrative subject and is comes second. Onze erfenis identifies what this refers to.
work-79.forms: Erfenis is a de-word, so the possessive is onze. Independent dit does not need to agree with the identifying noun; attributive deze erfenis would be different.
work-79.compare: English legacy suits the figurative inherited contribution here. Erfenis can also mean a legal inheritance in a different situation.

mistake.why: Use onze with singular de erfenis.

work-79.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-80.meaning: Have you finished your task? You ask a colleague whether the assigned task is complete.
work-80.order: Heb begins the yes/no question. The first je is the subject; the second belongs to the object noun phrase. Afgemaakt closes the perfect bracket.
work-80.forms: The first je is the subject, so question-form hebt becomes heb: Heb je ...? The second je is possessive your before taak. Afmaken: maak ... af; perfect afgemaakt. For object it, use Heb je het al afgemaakt? Unstressed het normally comes early in the middle of the clause, before al and the participle.
work-80.compare: English distinguishes you and your; Dutch uses je for both functions. Have you finished focuses on completion at the time of asking.

mistake.why: Use the inverted second-person form heb je.

work-80.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-80.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-81.meaning: I'll check her calendar. You volunteer to check a colleague's appointment diary before arranging a visit.
work-81.order: Ik is the first constituent; zal is finite and second. Haar agenda stands between zal and the final infinitive controleren.
work-81.forms: Haar is possessive before agenda. Agenda means appointment diary/calendar here, unlike the meeting-item sense used earlier. Controleren is an inseparable verb and stays whole.
work-81.compare: English keeps will check together; Dutch puts the calendar between zal and controleren. The chosen calendar sense depends on the appointment context.

mistake.why: After zal use an infinitive, not a second finite verb.

work-81.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-82.meaning: Let's finalize our proposal. Your team has revised a proposal and you suggest finishing its last details together.
work-82.order: Laten we introduces a joint suggestion. The object ons voorstel comes before final infinitive afronden.
work-82.forms: Voorstel is singular and takes het, so our proposal is ons voorstel. Afronden remains joined after laten; as a finite lexical verb it splits: We ronden het voorstel af.
work-82.compare: English let's finalize uses one following verb. Dutch has laten plus final infinitive afronden; ons means our before the noun, not us here.

mistake.why: Use ons before singular het voorstel.

work-82.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-83.meaning: I'd already called the office. You explain that you had phoned the office before someone later asked you to call.
work-83.order: Had is finite and second; gebeld closes the past-perfect bracket. Al and naar kantoor occupy the middle of the clause.
work-83.forms: Had gebeld places the call before another past reference point. Al means already here. Naar kantoor bellen means phone the office, not physically travel there.
work-83.compare: English I'd expands to I had here, not I would. Dutch had plus participle likewise marks the earlier completed call.

mistake.wrong: Ik had al naar kantoor bellen.
mistake.right: Ik had al naar kantoor gebeld.
mistake.why: This past-perfect construction needs the participle gebeld.

work-83.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
work-83.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came).
