Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

work-84.meaning: Our project is challenging. You discuss a demanding project that requires your team to learn new skills.
work-84.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ons project is one first constituent; is is second. Uitdagend is the predicate description of the project.
work-84.forms: Project is a het-word, so singular our project uses ons. Predicate uitdagend has no attributive -e. It means challenging in this context, not deliberately provocative.
work-84.compare: English our has no gender-based variation. Dutch ons/onze depends on the following noun; challenging is a description rather than a verb about someone issuing a challenge.

mistake.why: Singular het project requires ons.

work-84.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-85.meaning: He's busy loading the truck. At a warehouse, a colleague is putting boxes into a truck and cannot join the discussion yet.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het laden van de vrachtwagen

work-85.order: Hij comes first and is is second. The met-phrase identifies the ongoing activity described by bezig.
work-85.forms: Het laden is a noun-like infinitive. Van de vrachtwagen supplies what is being loaded in this version. Laden here means load goods, not charge a battery.
work-85.compare: English busy loading omits a preposition; Dutch uses bezig met plus the noun-like activity here. The infinitive laden is not a second finite verb.

mistake.wrong: Hij is bezig met het laadt van de vrachtwagen.
mistake.right: Hij is bezig met het laden van de vrachtwagen.
mistake.why: Use the infinitive in this nominalized activity phrase.

work-85.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-85.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

work-86.meaning: Can you tell me the access code? You ask a colleague for the access code to an office door, without displaying any actual code.
work-86.order: Kun begins the question, followed by subject je. Recipient me comes before the full object noun phrase, and vertellen is the final infinitive.
work-86.forms: Kun je is the inverted second-person form of kunnen; kan je is also valid. Vertellen means tell, not talk intransitively. Toegangscode is a de-word.
work-86.compare: English tell me the access code has the same recipient/full-object sequence. Dutch places vertellen at the end after the modal.

mistake.wrong: Kun je me de toegangscode vertelt?
mistake.right: Kun je me de toegangscode vertellen?
mistake.why: Use an infinitive after kun.

work-86.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-87.meaning: Find the missing documents. A set of documents is missing from a folder and you ask a colleague to locate it.
work-87.order: Vind begins the command without an expressed subject. The full noun phrase names what should be found.
work-87.forms: Vind is the stem of vinden; it has no extra -t in this imperative. Ontbrekende is an attributive participial adjective before definite plural documenten.
work-87.compare: English find the missing documents has the same command-plus-object sequence. Dutch find is vind, distinct from infinitive vinden.

mistake.why: Do not add an ordinary present -t to this imperative.

work-87.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-88.meaning: Can you explain the new safety rules to me? Before starting a new job, you ask a colleague to explain the workplace's safety rules.
work-88.order: Kun starts the question. Recipient me precedes the full object phrase; uitleggen remains a joined final infinitive after the modal.
work-88.forms: Nieuwe takes -e before the definite plural veiligheidsregels. Uitleggen is separable when finite, but joined after kun. This requests an explanation, not permission to ignore rules.
work-88.compare: English keeps explain early after can; Dutch puts uitleggen after the recipient and object. To me is the recipient of the explanation.

mistake.wrong: Kun je me de nieuwe veiligheidsregels uitleg?
mistake.right: Kun je me de nieuwe veiligheidsregels uitleggen?
mistake.why: The verb after kun must be an infinitive.

work-88.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-89.meaning: She's good at explaining things. You praise a female trainer who makes difficult processes understandable to new colleagues.
work-89.order: Ze precedes finite is. Goed describes her ability, and the in-phrase names the activity she does well.
work-89.forms: Goed in is the fixed combination for being skilled at something. Dingen uitleggen functions as an activity phrase after in; uitleggen is an infinitive and stays together.
work-89.compare: English uses good at, whereas Dutch uses goed in. English explaining corresponds to the Dutch activity infinitive uitleggen.

mistake.wrong: Ze is goed op dingen uitleggen.
mistake.right: Ze is goed in dingen uitleggen.
mistake.why: Use in for this skill construction.

work-89.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-90.meaning: Please talk with me about it. After a disagreement, you ask a colleague to discuss the issue with you instead of staying silent.
work-90.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Praat begins the command. Er and over refer to the topic, but are separated by alsjeblieft met me. Met me identifies the conversation partner.
work-90.forms: Er ... over together mean about it; er is not a location here. When adjacent, the pair is written erover. Alsjeblieft matches informal je-based conversation.
work-90.compare: English keeps about it together. Dutch can separate er from its preposition without losing their link; met is rendered as with in this collaborative conversation.

mistake.wrong: Praat het alsjeblieft met me over.
mistake.right: Praat er alsjeblieft met me over.
mistake.why: The about-it reference uses er with over, not object het in this position.

work-90.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-91.meaning: I'm sorry to have to ask this. You apologize before asking a colleague an uncomfortable but necessary question.
work-91.order: Het supplies the subject and spijt is finite and second. The infinitive clause dit te moeten vragen identifies the regretted necessity.
work-91.forms: Me is the object-form experiencer in het spijt me. Te belongs with moeten; vragen remains a bare infinitive after that modal. Dit is the thing asked.
work-91.compare: English I am sorry has I as subject; Dutch het spijt me uses dummy het and object me. Have to translates the added necessity explicitly.

mistake.wrong: Het spijt ik dit te moeten vragen.
mistake.right: Het spijt me dit te moeten vragen.
mistake.why: Use object me as the experiencer, not subject ik.

work-91.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-92.meaning: She gave me my badge back. A colleague returns the identification badge you lent or left with her.
work-92.order: Heeft is second and teruggegeven closes the perfect bracket. Recipient me comes before the full object noun phrase mijn badge.
work-92.forms: Teruggeven has the irregular participle teruggegeven, with ge inside the separable compound. Mijn is possessive before badge; me is recipient, not possessive.
work-92.compare: English gave ... back is natural for returning a borrowed item. Dutch uses perfect heeft teruggegeven; the English past does not require changing it to simple-past gaf.

mistake.wrong: Zij heeft mijn mijn badge teruggegeven.
mistake.right: Zij heeft me mijn badge teruggegeven.
mistake.why: Use recipient me, keeping possessive mijn before badge.

work-92.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-92.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-93.meaning: Take this package to reception. You ask a colleague to take a parcel to the reception desk elsewhere in the building.
work-93.order: Breng starts the command and omits the understood subject. The object is followed by its destination phrase.
work-93.forms: Pakket is a het-word, so this package is dit pakket. Naar introduces the destination reception; it is not the person receiving something expressed with aan.
work-93.compare: English take is natural when movement is away from the current location. Dutch brengen can cover bring/take depending on the speaker's perspective.

mistake.wrong: Breng deze pakket naar de receptie.
mistake.right: Breng dit pakket naar de receptie.
mistake.why: Use dit with singular het pakket.

work-93.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-94.meaning: What is the agenda for this afternoon? Before an afternoon workshop, you ask which programme has been planned.
work-94.order: Wat is the first question constituent, followed by finite is and the subject noun phrase. Voor vanmiddag specifies which agenda is meant.
work-94.forms: Agenda means the planned meeting programme here, not an appointment diary. Vanmiddag is this afternoon; morgenmiddag would mean tomorrow afternoon.
work-94.compare: English uses the same visible what-is-the-agenda order. For this afternoon matches voor vanmiddag and does not mean since this afternoon.

mistake.wrong: Wat is het agenda voor vanmiddag?
mistake.right: Wat is de agenda voor vanmiddag?
mistake.why: Agenda takes de.

work-94.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-95.meaning: The product needs an update. You explain that an existing software product needs an updated version.
work-95.order: Het product is one subject constituent and heeft is second. The required thing stands before nodig in heeft ... nodig.
work-95.forms: Product is a het-word; update is a borrowed de-noun. Heeft agrees with the singular product. Nodig is an adjective complement, not an extra verb.
work-95.compare: English uses needs as a verb. Dutch has heeft ... nodig with een update in between; this does not mean the product already has the update.

mistake.wrong: Het product hebben een update nodig.
mistake.right: Het product heeft een update nodig.
mistake.why: Singular het product takes heeft.

work-95.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-96.meaning: I'll take care of it. A colleague needs a meeting room booked, and you volunteer to arrange it.
work-96.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and finite regel is second. Het refers to the arrangement already mentioned.
work-96.forms: Regelen means arrange or take care of here. The present tense can express a near-future commitment in this context; it is not a claim that every Dutch present translates as will.
work-96.compare: English naturally uses I'll for volunteering. Do not translate regelen literally as rule, or het as an article without a following noun.

mistake.why: Use the finite first-person regel after ik.

work-96.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-97.meaning: Could you provide a solution to this network problem? You ask a supplier to propose a way to restore a failing office network.
work-97.order: Kunt begins the polite request, then u. The complete solution noun phrase comes before final infinitive bieden.
work-97.forms: Voor dit netwerkprobleem modifies oplossing. Netwerkprobleem is a het-word and takes dit. Bieden is an infinitive after kunt; could expresses polite English, not Dutch past ability.
work-97.compare: English solution to a problem corresponds naturally to Dutch oplossing voor een probleem. Do not mechanically copy English to into every Dutch preposition.

mistake.wrong: Kunt u een oplossing voor deze netwerkprobleem bieden?
mistake.right: Kunt u een oplossing voor dit netwerkprobleem bieden?
mistake.why: Use dit with singular het netwerkprobleem.

work-97.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-98.meaning: Your input is crucial. You politely tell an experienced stakeholder that their contribution is essential to the team's decision.
work-98.order: Uw input forms the subject constituent and is is second. Cruciaal describes the importance of that contribution.
work-98.forms: Uw is the polite possessive. Input is a borrowed noun meaning contribution or information here, not a keyboard action. Predicate cruciaal has no attributive -e.
work-98.compare: English uses the same possessive-subject and linking-verb sequence. Crucial is stronger than merely helpful; retain that importance.

mistake.why: Use possessive uw before input.

work-98.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-99.meaning: I want to go to the trade fair next week. You tell your colleague that you want to attend next week's trade fair.
work-99.order: Wil is finite and second; gaan closes the modal bracket. The time and destination phrases stand between the modal and infinitive.
work-99.forms: Willen expresses desire, not certainty that the trip will happen. Beurs means trade fair in this scene, not stock exchange or scholarship. Naar marks the destination.
work-99.compare: English keeps want to go together. Dutch sends gaan after the time and destination; English has to after want, but Dutch willen takes a bare infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ik wil volgende week naar de beurs te gaan.
mistake.right: Ik wil volgende week naar de beurs gaan.
mistake.why: Do not add te after willen here.

work-99.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-100.meaning: I'm weighing the package. At a dispatch desk, you place a parcel on a scale before choosing its postage.
work-100.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik occupies the first position and finite weeg the second. Het pakket is the thing whose weight is being measured.
work-100.forms: Wegen means physically weigh in this scene, not mentally consider. The finite form is weeg, with doubled ee; the infinitive is wegen.
work-100.compare: Dutch simple present can describe the ongoing weighing; English progressive is natural here. The English present progressive describes a current action, not a future promise.

mistake.why: Keep the long vowel in finite weeg.

work-100.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-101.meaning: Can you hear me? At the start of a video call, you check whether your colleague can hear your voice.
work-101.order: The neutral yes/no question starts with hoor, then subject je. Me is the person being heard.
work-101.forms: Hoort becomes hoor before subject je in ordinary inversion. Horen is hearing, not deliberately listening as luisteren. Me is an object pronoun.
work-101.compare: English naturally asks can you hear me, although Dutch does not need a modal here. This adds no obligation or permission meaning.

mistake.why: Drop ordinary present -t before subject je.

work-101.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-102.meaning: His team is very busy. You explain that another manager's team has many tasks and little spare time.
work-102.order: Zijn team is one subject constituent and heeft is second. Het erg druk belongs to the fixed expression het druk hebben.
work-102.forms: Team is singular here, so heeft is used. Zijn means his before team, not the verb be. Het in het druk hebben is part of the idiom, not an article before druk.
work-102.compare: English is busy corresponds to Dutch heeft het druk. Do not translate each word as has it crowded; erg means very in this expression.

mistake.wrong: Zijn team hebben het erg druk.
mistake.right: Zijn team heeft het erg druk.
mistake.why: Use singular heeft with team.

work-102.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-103.meaning: I'm looking forward to it. You have just been invited to a team event and express happy anticipation of it.
work-103.order: Ik is first and kijk is second. Ernaar refers to the anticipated event, while uit is the separated particle of uitkijken.
work-103.forms: Adjacent er and naar join as ernaar. Uit remains separate because it belongs to uitkijken, not the pronoun/preposition pair. This is anticipation, not physically looking outside.
work-103.compare: English forward to it corresponds to the whole Dutch idiom. Do not translate er simply as there or combine ernaar and uit into one word.

mistake.why: Join er with naar, but keep the verb particle uit separate.

work-103.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-104.meaning: I don't mind. A colleague asks whether opening the window will bother you, and you say you do not object.
work-104.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Vind is second. Het refers to the proposed action; niet erg states that you do not judge it troublesome.
work-104.forms: Vinden means consider or judge here, not locate a lost object. Erg means bad or bothersome in this expression; it is not the degree adverb very used before druk.
work-104.compare: English uses the idiom don't mind. A literal I don't find it bad is possible as analysis but is not the natural learner translation for this permission response.

mistake.why: Negate the adjective erg with niet, not noun-negating geen.

work-104.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
work-104.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

work-105.meaning: Their ideas are innovative. You praise another team's new ideas for improving a product.
work-105.order: Hun ideeën is one subject constituent, followed by finite zijn. Innovatief describes the ideas.
work-105.forms: Hun is possessive before the plural noun, not an independent subject. Plural ideeën takes zijn. The diaeresis separates the vowel sounds in ideeën; predicate innovatief has no -e.
work-105.compare: English their ideas are follows the same visible structure. Dutch hun as possessive is correct even though hun as a subject would not be standard.

mistake.why: A plural subject requires zijn.

work-105.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-106.meaning: I'll get started on it right away. A colleague hands you a new assignment and you immediately open the materials to begin.
work-106.order: Ik comes first and begin is second. Er and mee refer back to the assignment; meteen can stand between them.
work-106.forms: Beginnen met means to start on something. When the object of met is replaced by er, met becomes mee: ermee. Er is not a place word here. Begin is the ik form; the present can express an immediate commitment.
work-106.compare: English uses on it after get started. Dutch replaces met + the previously mentioned thing with er ... mee.

mistake.why: In this pronominal combination met changes to mee.

work-106.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-107.meaning: His efforts were recognized. A supervisor acknowledges a colleague’s months of work during a small recognition ceremony.
work-107.order: The plural subject comes first, werden is second, and erkend closes the passive verb bracket.
work-107.forms: Zijn is possessive here. Inspanningen is plural, so the past passive auxiliary is werden, not werd. Erkennen has the participle erkend without ge- because it starts with the inseparable prefix er-. This is a past passive, not a perfect tense.
work-107.compare: English were recognized and Dutch werden erkend both focus on the efforts receiving recognition; the person recognizing them can remain unnamed.

mistake.why: A plural subject requires werden.

work-107.practiceGuide: In a passive clause the subject receives the action: het formulier wordt ingevuld. Worden forms an ongoing/event passive; zijn plus a participle can describe the completed passive or resulting state. In the simple past use werd/werden. Do not classify every is + participle as an active movement perfect; identify whether the subject performed the action.

work-108.meaning: We need more time. Your team shows an unfinished model to a client and requests extra time to complete it.
work-108.order: We comes first and hebben is second; the required thing meer tijd precedes nodig.
work-108.forms: Iets nodig hebben means to need something. Tijd is an uncountable quantity here, so meer tijd needs no indefinite article. Meer expresses a greater amount, not another separate appointment.
work-108.compare: English need is a single verb; Dutch expresses the need with hebben and nodig around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig is an adjective in this construction, not an infinitive.

work-108.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-109.meaning: They're talking about the price. Two colleagues compare the quoted cost of a piece of equipment while looking at it together.
work-109.order: Ze is the subject, praten is second, and over de prijs gives the topic.
work-109.forms: Praten over introduces the subject of a conversation. The plural verb praten makes ze mean they here. Prijs means the amount charged in this scenario, not an award. De prijs uses de.
work-109.compare: English about and Dutch over introduce the topic. English progressive are talking can correspond to a Dutch present without a separate progressive construction.

mistake.why: For they, the finite verb must be plural.

work-109.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-110.meaning: Well done. You praise a colleague who has just finished a carefully assembled display.
work-110.order: This conventional praise expression has no finite verb. It is a natural short utterance; a full clause would be Dat heb je goed gedaan.
work-110.forms: Gedaan is the irregular participle of doen. Goed tells how the task was done. The omitted subject and auxiliary are understood from the completed action; the fragment is a complete praise speech act.
work-110.compare: English Well done is also a conventional short expression, so neither version needs an explicit subject in this use.

mistake.why: The participle of doen is gedaan.

work-110.practiceFocus: Short expressions and their intended meaning
work-110.practiceGuide: Some useful expressions are fragments rather than full subject-plus-verb clauses: Hartelijk dank, Graag gedaan. Do not invent V2 inversion for a phrase with no finite verb. Learn what the expression does in the conversation, and compare related full sentences. A polite formula can have several natural English equivalents.

work-111.meaning: She sent the photos to us. A colleague sends photographs of a site visit to your team from her laptop.
work-111.order: Zij comes first and stuurde is second; the photos precede the recipient naar ons.
work-111.forms: Stuurde is the singular simple past of sturen. Naar marks the destination/recipient after sturen. Ons is an object pronoun after a preposition. Foto has the plural foto’s with an apostrophe to preserve the vowel sound.
work-111.compare: English sent and Dutch stuurde are simple past forms. Both can put the sent object before to us / naar ons.

mistake.wrong: Zij stuurde de foto’s naar wij.
mistake.right: Zij stuurde de foto’s naar ons.
mistake.why: After naar use the object pronoun ons, not the subject pronoun wij.

work-111.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-112.meaning: I'm not sure yet. You hesitate between two travel options and tell a colleague you have not decided with certainty.
work-112.order: Ik comes first and weet is second; het is followed by nog niet and zeker.
work-112.forms: Weten has the ik form weet. Het refers to the answer or decision. Nog niet means not yet, indicating that certainty may come later. Zeker expresses certainty; the whole expression is idiomatic.
work-112.compare: English says I am not sure; Dutch can use weten with het and zeker. Translate the whole expression rather than replacing weet with am.

mistake.wrong: Ik weet het nog geen zeker.
mistake.right: Ik weet het nog niet zeker.
mistake.why: Negate certainty with niet, not geen.

work-112.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
work-112.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

work-113.meaning: What's the catch? An unusually attractive offer makes you ask about a hidden drawback before agreeing.
work-113.order: Wat asks for the hidden drawback, is is second, and the subject follows it.
work-113.forms: Een addertje onder het gras is an idiom for a concealed problem. Addertje is a diminutive and takes het. In this expression gras is used with het. The phrase is not a warning about a literal animal in this scenario.
work-113.compare: English uses catch for a hidden disadvantage; Dutch uses the full idiom addertje onder het gras.

mistake.wrong: Wat is de addertje onder het gras?
mistake.right: Wat is het addertje onder het gras?
mistake.why: Dutch diminutive nouns use het in the singular.

work-113.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-114.meaning: He spoke with the manager. A colleague reports a completed conversation with the manager after leaving the manager’s office.
work-114.order: Hij comes first and sprak is second; met de manager names the conversation partner.
work-114.forms: Sprak is the irregular singular simple past of spreken; the plural is spraken. Met introduces the person spoken with, while over introduces a topic. Manager is a de-word.
work-114.compare: English spoke and Dutch sprak are irregular simple past forms. With / met makes the partner explicit.

mistake.why: The singular past of spreken is sprak.

work-114.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-115.meaning: Let's delegate tasks. A team leader proposes dividing a pile of tasks among colleagues with different skills.
work-115.order: The shared suggestion begins with Laten we; taken stands before the final infinitive delegeren.
work-115.forms: Laten we + infinitive proposes a joint action. Taken is the plural of de taak; the long vowel is spelled with one a in the open syllable of taken. An indefinite plural does not use een.
work-115.compare: English Let’s and Dutch Laten we both propose action together. Dutch places tasks before the final infinitive.

mistake.why: The proposal requires the infinitive delegeren.

work-115.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-116.meaning: He completed his task. A colleague finishes fitting the last part of a work assignment and puts his tools away.
work-116.order: Hij comes first and voltooide is second; zijn taak is the object.
work-116.forms: Voltooide is the singular simple past of voltooien. Zijn is possessive before de taak. This is a simple past clause, unlike Hij heeft zijn taak voltooid, which uses a perfect auxiliary and participle.
work-116.compare: English completed and Dutch voltooide each use one finite past verb; no auxiliary is required.

mistake.why: The singular past has no plural n.

work-116.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-117.meaning: Who's in charge? You arrive at a coordinated work site and ask which person is supervising the team.
work-117.order: Wie itself is the subject. Heeft follows it; there is no extra subject pronoun after the verb.
work-117.forms: De leiding hebben means to be in charge. Heeft is the usual singular verb form in this question. Leiding refers to leadership here rather than a physical pipe.
work-117.compare: English uses be in charge; Dutch uses have the leadership. A subject question does not need an additional he/she or auxiliary do.

mistake.why: Wie already fills the subject role.

work-117.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-118.meaning: Send the signed contract to him. A colleague asks you to send a completed signed contract to its recipient.
work-118.order: The instruction begins with the imperative Stuur, followed by the object and naar hem.
work-118.forms: An ordinary imperative uses the stem stuur. Contract is a het-word; after definite het the attributive participle receives -e: ondertekende. Ondertekenen is inseparable, with participle ondertekend. Hem is the object form after naar.
work-118.compare: English and Dutch both start an instruction with the verb and can put the sent item before its recipient.

mistake.wrong: Stuur het ondertekende contract naar hij.
mistake.right: Stuur het ondertekende contract naar hem.
mistake.why: A preposition requires the object pronoun hem.

work-118.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-119.meaning: I have to find a solution to this leak. You examine a leaking pipe and explain that you need to find a way to fix the problem.
work-119.order: Ik comes first and moet is second. The whole object phrase stands before the final infinitive vinden.
work-119.forms: Moeten expresses necessity; the main action is the infinitive vinden, without te. Oplossing is a de-word but uses een when indefinite. Voor introduces the problem requiring a solution. Deze agrees with de lekkage.
work-119.compare: English to find follows have to; Dutch moeten takes an infinitive without te and places it after the object.

mistake.wrong: Ik moet een oplossing voor deze lekkage te vinden.
mistake.right: Ik moet een oplossing voor deze lekkage vinden.
mistake.why: After moet the infinitive has no te.

work-119.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-120.meaning: I'm here to ask for advice. You visit an experienced colleague specifically to get guidance about a difficult task.
work-120.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and ben second; hier gives the place and om advies te vragen gives the purpose.
work-120.forms: Om ... te + infinitive expresses purpose. Advies vragen takes advies as a direct object; Dutch does not insert voor in this expression. Advies is uncountable here and needs no een.
work-120.compare: English ask for advice uses for; Dutch advies vragen does not translate that preposition. Both can explain why the speaker is here.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben hier om advies vragen.
mistake.right: Ik ben hier om advies te vragen.
mistake.why: The purpose construction om ... te requires te before vragen.

work-120.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-121.meaning: I'm busy with the planning today. You are arranging several appointments at your desk and explain why you cannot help immediately.
work-121.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and ben second; vandaag gives the time, followed by druk bezig and met de planning.
work-121.forms: Druk bezig zijn met means to be busy with an activity. This expanded wording is natural in Belgium as well as the Netherlands. Planning is a de-word. Met introduces the activity occupying you.
work-121.compare: English busy with and Dutch druk bezig met describe involvement in an activity. Dutch retains the finite form ben of zijn.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben vandaag druk bezig de planning.
mistake.right: Ik ben vandaag druk bezig met de planning.
mistake.why: Met introduces the activity after bezig in this construction.

work-121.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-121.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

work-122.meaning: Listen carefully. You ask a colleague to pay close attention while you explain a tricky assembly step.
work-122.order: The instruction begins with Luister; goed describes how to listen. The understood subject is the person addressed.
work-122.forms: The ordinary imperative is the stem luister, without -t. Goed is an adverb here, so it has no adjective -e ending. Luisteren is paying attention to sounds; horen is perceiving them.
work-122.compare: English listen carefully and Dutch luister goed both use an imperative followed by a manner expression.

mistake.why: Goed describes the action as an adverb and does not receive -e.

work-122.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-123.meaning: We need their input before Friday. Your team asks external collaborators for feedback in time to finish a plan before Friday.
work-123.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. We is first and hebben second; the object and deadline precede nodig.
work-123.forms: Hun is possessive before input, not an object pronoun in this use. Iets nodig hebben means to need something. Vóór emphasizes before rather than for. Dutch weekdays are lowercase.
work-123.compare: English uses need and before; Dutch uses hebben ... nodig and vóór for the deadline.

mistake.wrong: We hebben hen input vóór vrijdag nodig.
mistake.right: We hebben hun input vóór vrijdag nodig.
mistake.why: Use possessive hun before the noun input.

work-123.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-124.meaning: I'm waiting for a phone call. You keep your mobile nearby while waiting for a customer to call you back.
work-124.order: Ik comes first and wacht is second; op een telefoontje completes what you are waiting for.
work-124.forms: Wachten op is a fixed combination. Telefoontje means phone call here, not a miniature telephone. The diminutive has het as its definite article; een does not show noun gender.
work-124.compare: English waits for but Dutch waits op. The preposition belongs to the verb phrase and is not translated word for word.

mistake.why: Use wachten op for waiting for an expected call.

work-124.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-125.meaning: They're practising their skills. Colleagues practise a presentation together, taking turns demonstrating what they have learned.
work-125.order: Ze comes first and oefenen is second; hun vaardigheden is the direct object.
work-125.forms: The plural verb oefenen makes ze mean they. Hun is possessive before the plural vaardigheden. De vaardigheid has the plural vaardigheden; oefenen can take the skill as a direct object.
work-125.compare: English progressive are practising corresponds here to a Dutch present. Their and hun both mark possession.

mistake.why: Hun is the possessive form before a noun.

work-125.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-126.meaning: Can we close this deal? After negotiating the terms, you ask whether both sides can now agree and shake hands.
work-126.order: The yes/no question begins with Kunnen, then we, the object, and the final infinitive sluiten.
work-126.forms: Kunnen agrees with plural we. De deal takes deze. Een deal sluiten means to conclude an agreement here, not to close a physical door. After kunnen use the infinitive without te.
work-126.compare: English keeps can and close close together; Dutch can place the deal between kunnen and sluiten.

mistake.why: Use deze with the singular de-word deal.

work-126.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-127.meaning: Let's start the presentation. The audience is seated and you suggest beginning the prepared presentation with your colleague.
work-127.order: Laten we introduces the shared proposal; the object precedes the final infinitive starten.
work-127.forms: De presentatie uses de. Starten is an infinitive after laten. The plural we includes the speaker and the people addressed in the proposed action.
work-127.compare: English Let’s start the presentation places start before its object; Dutch puts de presentatie before starten after Laten we.

mistake.why: Use an infinitive after Laten we.

work-127.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-128.meaning: This is our shared vision. A team presents one agreed plan for the future, pointing together at a common design.
work-128.order: Independent Dit is the subject, is is second, and onze gedeelde visie identifies what Dit refers to.
work-128.forms: Dit used on its own need not agree with de visie. Before de visie, our is onze. Gedeelde is an attributive participle used like an adjective; it receives -e in this definite possessive noun phrase.
work-128.compare: English this and Dutch independent dit can point to an idea. Dutch marks the adjective ending and chooses onze according to the noun.

mistake.why: The singular de-word visie takes onze.

work-128.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-129.meaning: How's work going? During a break, you ask a colleague how things are going with their work.
work-129.order: Hoe comes first, gaat is second, and het follows as the grammatical subject. Met je werk gives the topic.
work-129.forms: In Hoe gaat het met ...?, het is the subject of gaat. Je is possessive before werk, so it does not trigger the inversion rule that removes -t when subject jij/je follows its verb. Het werk is a het-word.
work-129.compare: English asks how work is going; Dutch uses the expression how it goes with your work.

mistake.wrong: Hoe ga het met je werk?
mistake.right: Hoe gaat het met je werk?
mistake.why: The subject is het, so the verb retains -t.

work-129.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-130.meaning: Give the spare battery to the technician. You ask a colleague to hand a spare battery to the technician repairing a device.
work-130.order: An instruction starts with the verb. The instruction starts with Geef, then names the item and its recipient with aan.
work-130.forms: Geef is the stem and ordinary imperative of geven. Reservebatterij is one compound word and takes de from its head batterij. Aan introduces the receiver. De technicus names the professional receiving the battery.
work-130.compare: English give to and Dutch geef aan express the same transfer. Both can place the item before a recipient phrase.

mistake.wrong: Geef het reservebatterij aan de technicus.
mistake.right: Geef de reservebatterij aan de technicus.
mistake.why: The compound reservebatterij takes de from batterij.

work-130.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-131.meaning: I'm sorry to hear that. A colleague tells you disappointing news and you respond with sympathy.
work-131.order: Het comes first, spijt is second, and me names the person who feels sorry. Dat is the object of horen in the infinitive phrase.
work-131.forms: Het spijt me is an idiomatic sympathy or regret expression. Here dat means that news, not a conjunction introducing a finite clause. Te horen uses an infinitive; me is an object pronoun.
work-131.compare: English makes I the subject; Dutch makes het the grammatical subject and me the experiencer.

mistake.wrong: Het spijt ik dat te horen.
mistake.right: Het spijt me dat te horen.
mistake.why: Use the object pronoun me for the person feeling sorry.

work-131.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-132.meaning: He told us that the train is delayed. A colleague shares a message about a delayed train before your group leaves for the station.
work-132.order: Hij heeft starts the main clause. Ons is the recipient; verteld precedes the full content clause. Inside that dat-clause, the finite verb heeft comes last.
work-132.forms: Vertellen uses hebben in the perfect and the inseparable participle verteld, without ge-. Ons is the recipient pronoun. Vertraging hebben means to be delayed. A full content clause can follow the main clause’s participle.
work-132.compare: English told us that ... corresponds naturally to a Dutch perfect. Dutch places the subordinate finite verb after vertraging.

mistake.wrong: Hij heeft ons verteld dat de trein heeft vertraging.
mistake.right: Hij heeft ons verteld dat de trein vertraging heeft.
mistake.why: In this dat-clause the finite verb follows its object.

work-132.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-132.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-133.meaning: What's the speed? While testing a moving conveyor, you ask a technician how fast it is running.
work-133.order: Wat asks for a value; is is second and de snelheid follows it as the subject.
work-133.forms: Snelheid is a de-word. The suffix -heid forms an abstract noun from snel. The question asks about speed, not the time at which something happens.
work-133.compare: English and Dutch can both use what is the speed; how fast is it is another natural English formulation.

mistake.why: The singular subject de snelheid requires is.

work-133.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-134.meaning: Find the answer in the manual. A colleague directs you to consult the device manual to answer a technical question.
work-134.order: An instruction starts with the verb. The instruction begins with Vind, followed by the object and the location where the answer can be found.
work-134.forms: Vind is the stem of vinden and an ordinary imperative. Antwoord is a het-word; handleiding is a de-word. In introduces the source location.
work-134.compare: English and Dutch both put the imperative before its object; both can add in the manual afterwards.

mistake.wrong: Vind de antwoord in de handleiding.
mistake.right: Vind het antwoord in de handleiding.
mistake.why: Antwoord takes het in the singular.

work-134.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-135.meaning: I'll send my email. You finish composing a message and tell a colleague you will send it now.
work-135.order: Ik comes first and stuur is second; mijn e-mail is the object.
work-135.forms: Sturen has the ik form stuur. Mijn is possessive and replaces an article before e-mail. The present can express an immediate intention; no zal is required. E-mail retains its hyphen.
work-135.compare: English can use will send for an immediate intention that Dutch expresses with the present stuur.

mistake.why: A possessive determiner replaces the article in this noun phrase.

work-135.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-136.meaning: Acting is a demanding profession. An actor practises a difficult scene repeatedly while you discuss the demands of the profession.
work-136.order: The infinitive Acteren functions as the subject; is is second. The profession is described in the predicate.
work-136.forms: An infinitive used as an activity subject normally takes a singular verb. Beroep is a het-word, so after indefinite een the adjective has no -e: veeleisend beroep. With definite het: het veeleisende beroep.
work-136.compare: English often uses an -ing activity as subject; Dutch uses an infinitive. English adjectives do not show the Dutch indefinite-het ending distinction.

mistake.why: An adjective before an indefinite singular het-word normally has no -e.

work-136.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-136.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-137.meaning: I returned the borrowed key to you. You remind a colleague that you already handed their borrowed key back to them.
work-137.order: Ik comes first and heb second. The short recipient pronoun je precedes the full noun object; teruggegeven closes the perfect verb bracket.
work-137.forms: Teruggeven is separable: ik geef terug; in the participle ge- goes between terug and geven. Geven has the irregular participle gegeven. Je is an object pronoun here. Geleende is an attributive participle before de sleutel.
work-137.compare: English returned can correspond to Dutch heb teruggegeven. Dutch can put the short recipient before the full object without aan.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb je de geleende sleutel geteruggeven.
mistake.right: Ik heb je de geleende sleutel teruggegeven.
mistake.why: The participle combines terug with gegeven.

work-137.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-137.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-138.meaning: She knows what she is talking about. An experienced specialist explains a difficult technical subject confidently and accurately.
work-138.order: Ze weet starts the main clause. In the embedded clause, waar comes first, then ze het over, and the finite verb heeft comes last.
work-138.forms: Het ergens over hebben means to talk about something. Waar ... over asks about that topic and can be separated around the other clause words. The singular weet and heeft make ze mean she here.
work-138.compare: English what she is talking about is idiomatic; Dutch uses waar ... over heeft. Both describe knowledge of the topic rather than literal possession.

mistake.wrong: Ze weet waar ze heeft het over.
mistake.right: Ze weet waar ze het over heeft.
mistake.why: In the embedded question the finite verb comes after the other clause material.

work-138.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-139.meaning: Could you explain that in more detail? During a briefing, you politely ask the speaker to explain an unclear point further.
work-139.order: The polite yes/no request starts with Kunt, followed by u, dat, and the final infinitive toelichten.
work-139.forms: Kunt u is a standard polite form; kan u is also standard, especially in Belgium. Toelichten means explain or clarify and is separable in a finite statement: u licht dat toe. After a modal the infinitive stays together.
work-139.compare: English could politely requests clarification; Dutch can use present kunt u without implying a past event.

mistake.why: After kunt use the infinitive toelichten.

work-139.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-140.meaning: What's left? After sorting the available supplies, you ask what remains on the table.
work-140.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Wat asks which thing remains; is follows it. Er supports the presentation of a remainder, while over means left/remaining.
work-140.forms: Over zijn means to be left over. Wat is the grammatical question subject. Er is not replacing a met/op object in this sentence and is not translated literally as there in the natural English question.
work-140.compare: English left expresses the remaining amount; Dutch uses over. The word order is a subject question with wat.

mistake.why: In this ordinary unspecified wat-question use singular is.

work-140.practiceGuide: Existential er introduces something present or available: er is/zijn, er ligt/staat/hangt. The verb agrees with the noun introduced (er is een boek, er zijn boeken). Ligt/staat/hangt is already the finite verb, so do not add another is. Position verbs make the physical arrangement explicit. If a place phrase comes first, normal V2 still applies.

work-141.meaning: His time has come. A colleague finally receives the opportunity to lead after years of preparation.
work-141.order: The whole phrase Zijn tijd is the subject; is is second and gekomen closes the perfect bracket.
work-141.forms: Zijn is possessive before tijd, not an infinitive. In this personal scenario it means his. Komen uses zijn in the perfect: is gekomen. The expression signals that a person’s opportunity has arrived; other contexts can give it a more ominous meaning.
work-141.compare: English has come uses have; Dutch is gekomen uses zijn. Source its is possible for an inanimate antecedent, but his matches this explicit person scenario.

mistake.why: Komen uses zijn as its perfect auxiliary.

work-141.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-141.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-142.meaning: I want to use the new scanner. You choose a new scanner for digitising paper documents.
work-142.order: Ik comes first and wil is second; the object stands before the final infinitive gebruiken.
work-142.forms: Willen expresses desire rather than future will. After wil use an infinitive without te. De scanner takes the attributive adjective nieuwe. Gebruiken is inseparable.
work-142.compare: English want to use contains to; Dutch wil gebruiken uses no te. Wil is not the English future auxiliary will.

mistake.wrong: Ik wil de nieuwe scanner te gebruiken.
mistake.right: Ik wil de nieuwe scanner gebruiken.
mistake.why: Willen takes the infinitive without te.

work-142.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-143.meaning: That's a good point. You acknowledge a useful observation that a colleague has raised during discussion.
work-143.order: Dat comes first and is second; een goed punt identifies the observation as useful.
work-143.forms: Punt in the observation sense is a het-word. After indefinite een the adjective has no -e: goed punt. Dat stands independently and points to the previous remark.
work-143.compare: English good point and Dutch goed punt have the same conversational meaning; Dutch additionally marks noun gender through adjective inflection.

mistake.why: In this sense punt is a het-word and the indefinite adjective has no -e.

work-143.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-144.meaning: Can they teach him how to operate the machine? You ask whether experienced colleagues can train a new worker to operate a machine.

parts.label: subordinate clause
parts.text: hoe hij de machine moet bedienen

work-144.order: Kunnen starts the question. The main infinitive leren precedes the embedded how-clause. Inside that clause, hij de machine comes before the final verb group moet bedienen.
work-144.forms: Ze is plural because of kunnen. Leren means teach when someone is its recipient. Hem is the object form. Moet is finite inside the embedded clause; bedienen is an infinitive without te. The order bedienen moet is also possible in a subordinate verb group.
work-144.compare: English teach him how to operate uses an embedded infinitive; Dutch explicitly names hij and the modal moet in a finite embedded clause.

mistake.wrong: Kunnen ze hij leren hoe hij de machine moet bedienen?
mistake.right: Kunnen ze hem leren hoe hij de machine moet bedienen?
mistake.why: Use hem as the recipient object, not subject hij.

work-144.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-145.meaning: We're planning our budget. Your team allocates a limited budget among several planned purchases.
work-145.order: We comes first and plannen is second; ons budget is the object.
work-145.forms: Ons and onze both mean our. Budget is singular and takes het, so use ons budget. Use onze before a singular de-word (onze auto) and every plural (onze budgetten). The number of owners does not decide the ending. We plannen is the plural present of plannen; Ik plande is simple past and We hebben gepland is perfect.
work-145.compare: English are planning corresponds to the Dutch present plannen without a separate auxiliary.

mistake.why: A singular het-word takes possessive ons.

work-145.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-146.meaning: They taught me how to fasten the safety belt. A colleague has demonstrated fastening a safety belt and you repeat the action they taught you.

parts.label: subordinate clause
parts.text: hoe ik de veiligheidsriem moet vastmaken

work-146.order: Ze hebben begins the main clause. Me precedes geleerd; the embedded how-clause follows the participle. Its verb group moet vastmaken comes after ik and the object.
work-146.forms: Hebben geleerd is a perfect. Me is the recipient, so leren means teach. Vastmaken is separable in a finite simple clause but stays whole as an infinitive after moet. Vastmaken moet is also a possible subordinate verb order.
work-146.compare: English taught can correspond to a Dutch perfect. Dutch explicitly includes ik and moet in the embedded how-clause.

mistake.wrong: Ze hebben me geleerd hoe ik de veiligheidsriem moet vastmaakt.
mistake.right: Ze hebben me geleerd hoe ik de veiligheidsriem moet vastmaken.
mistake.why: After moet use the infinitive vastmaken.

work-146.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-146.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-147.meaning: Help them with the tidying up. You ask a colleague to join two people who are clearing the workroom after an activity.
work-147.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Help begins the instruction. Ze is its object; met het opruimen names the activity requiring help.
work-147.forms: Ze can be an unstressed plural object pronoun as well as a subject pronoun in other clauses. Het opruimen is an infinitive used as an activity noun. Opruimen is separable in a finite clause: zij ruimen op.
work-147.compare: English them is always an object form; Dutch unstressed ze can also serve as an object. English tidying up corresponds to het opruimen.

mistake.why: Zij is a subject form; unstressed ze can be the plural object here.

work-147.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-148.meaning: What's our secret weapon? Your team discusses the distinctive strength that gives its new product an advantage.
work-148.order: Wat asks which advantage the team has; is is second and the subject phrase follows.
work-148.forms: Wapen is a singular het-word, so our is ons. After possessive ons, the attributive adjective takes -e: geheime. Geheime wapen is figurative here, referring to a special strength rather than a physical weapon.
work-148.compare: English secret weapon can share the figurative meaning. Dutch uses ons and an adjective ending according to the possessive noun phrase.

mistake.why: A singular het-word takes ons.

work-148.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-149.meaning: We're late. You and a colleague arrive as the scheduled meeting is already starting.
work-149.order: Wij comes first and plural zijn is second; te laat describes being beyond the expected time.
work-149.forms: Wij is the stressed form of we. Te before laat means too, not the infinitive marker te. Zijn agrees with the plural subject. Laat is predicative and has no adjective ending.
work-149.compare: English late can correspond naturally to Dutch te laat. Dutch te marks exceeding the expected time.

mistake.why: A plural subject requires zijn.

work-149.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-150.meaning: Sell the old printer to him. You ask a colleague to sell a spare old printer to an interested buyer.
work-150.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Verkoop starts the instruction; the object precedes the recipient aan hem.
work-150.forms: Verkopen is inseparable: verkoop, verkocht, heeft verkocht. Verkoop is the imperative stem. Je in Verkoop je auto means your; Verkoop je de auto? instead has subject je and asks are you selling? Aan introduces the buyer; te introduces an infinitive, not a buyer. Naar also occurs in non-movement expressions such as luisteren naar, so it is not simply a movement-only word.
work-150.compare: English sell to and Dutch verkoop aan mark the receiver of the sold item.

mistake.wrong: Verkoop de oude printer aan hij.
mistake.right: Verkoop de oude printer aan hem.
mistake.why: Use an object pronoun after aan.

work-150.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-151.meaning: His training was effective. After a colleague’s training session, the team successfully applies the skills he demonstrated.
work-151.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Zijn training is the first constituent; was is second and effectief describes the training.
work-151.forms: Zijn is possessive. Was is the singular past of zijn. Effectief is predicative after was and receives no attributive -e. The sentence evaluates the training result, not the trainer’s physical fitness.
work-151.compare: English was effective and Dutch was effectief have similar clause order; Dutch distinguishes predicative effectief from de effectieve training.

mistake.why: A predicative adjective after was has no attributive -e.

work-151.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-152.meaning: Running a business is difficult. A small-business owner balances stock, staff and administration while discussing the challenge of managing it all.
work-152.order: The entire infinitive phrase Een bedrijf runnen is the first constituent. Is is second even though several words precede it.
work-152.forms: Runnen is a borrowed Dutch verb meaning manage or operate. The whole activity phrase acts as a singular subject. Bedrijf is a het-word but takes een when indefinite. Moeilijk is predicative and has no -e.
work-152.compare: English uses running as an activity subject; Dutch uses the infinitive runnen with its object before it. V2 means second constituent, not second written word.

mistake.why: The activity phrase is a singular subject.

work-152.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-152.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-153.meaning: Can you write the invitation for me? You ask a colleague to draft an invitation on your behalf.
work-153.order: Kun starts the question, followed by subject je, the object and beneficiary; schrijven is final.
work-153.forms: In this question je is the subject following kun. Kun je is the normal form of kunnen with subject inversion. Me after voor is an object pronoun naming the beneficiary. This is different from possessive je inside a noun phrase.
work-153.compare: English can you write and Dutch kun je ... schrijven differ in where the object and beneficiary sit relative to the main infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Kun je de uitnodiging voor ik schrijven?
mistake.right: Kun je de uitnodiging voor me schrijven?
mistake.why: After voor use the object pronoun me or mij.

work-153.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-154.meaning: The economy is growing. You discuss a positive economic trend while looking at a simple upward graph.
work-154.order: De economie is the first constituent; groeit is the finite second-position verb.
work-154.forms: Groeien has the singular third-person present groeit. Economie is a singular de-word. Groeien is intransitive in this use, so it does not require a direct object.
work-154.compare: English uses is growing; Dutch can describe the ongoing trend with its simple present groeit.

mistake.why: The singular subject requires finite groeit.

work-154.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-155.meaning: The meeting has been cancelled. You tell arriving colleagues that the scheduled meeting will not take place.
work-155.order: De vergadering comes first, is is second, and geannuleerd closes the verb bracket.
