work-155.forms: Annuleren has participle geannuleerd. Is geannuleerd presents the completed passive cancellation or resulting cancelled state. It does not say who cancelled it. Wordt geannuleerd would describe an ongoing or scheduled cancellation.
work-155.compare: English has been cancelled expresses the completed passive naturally; Dutch commonly omits geworden in a perfect passive with zijn.

mistake.why: The meeting receives the cancellation rather than performing it, so use the passive is.

work-155.practiceGuide: In a passive clause the subject receives the action: het formulier wordt ingevuld. Worden forms an ongoing/event passive; zijn plus a participle can describe the completed passive or resulting state. In the simple past use werd/werden. Do not classify every is + participle as an active movement perfect; identify whether the subject performed the action.

work-156.meaning: They're planning to stay late. Two colleagues decide to remain at the office after the usual finishing time.
work-156.order: Ze comes first and zijn is second. Van plan expresses an intention; om laat te blijven explains the intended action.
work-156.forms: Van plan zijn om ... te + infinitive means to intend to do something. The plural zijn makes ze mean they. Laat describes the time until which they remain; blijven is an infinitive.
work-156.compare: English planning to and Dutch van plan zijn om ... te express intention, rather than an action already happening.

mistake.wrong: Ze zijn van plan om laat blijven.
mistake.right: Ze zijn van plan om laat te blijven.
mistake.why: This intention phrase requires te before the infinitive.

work-156.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-157.meaning: Are you available now? You ask a colleague whether they can help with a task at this moment.
work-157.order: Ben begins the yes/no question; je is the subject, followed by nu and beschikbaar.
work-157.forms: Zijn has the inverted informal form ben je, corresponding to statement je bent. Beschikbaar is predicative, without -e, and means available for use or help in this scenario.
work-157.compare: English uses are you available; Dutch uses ben je beschikbaar. Both complete questions explicitly name the person addressed.

mistake.why: With subject je directly after the verb, the ordinary informal form is ben je.

work-157.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-158.meaning: We're thinking about changing the menu. Restaurant colleagues consider replacing some dishes in the current menu.
work-158.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and denken second. Erover anticipates the action explained by om het menu te veranderen.
work-158.forms: Denken over becomes erover when its topic is represented pronominally. The following om ... te phrase states the contemplated action. Menu is a het-word. Veranderen is inseparable.
work-158.compare: English about changing becomes Dutch erover om ... te veranderen, with the action at the end of the infinitive phrase.

mistake.wrong: We denken erover om het menu veranderen.
mistake.right: We denken erover om het menu te veranderen.
mistake.why: Use te in the om ... te infinitive construction.

work-158.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-159.meaning: Tell us about it. A colleague returns from a professional visit and you invite them to describe the experience.
work-159.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Vertel starts the instruction, then ons names the listeners and erover refers to the previously mentioned experience.
work-159.forms: Vertellen has the imperative vertel. Erover combines er and over, referring to a thing or topic. Ons is an object/recipient pronoun, not a subject.
work-159.compare: English about it remains two words; Dutch erover is written together when adjacent.

mistake.why: Use the recipient pronoun ons rather than subject wij.

work-159.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-160.meaning: I appreciate your advice. You thank a colleague for helpful guidance on a difficult decision.
work-160.order: Ik comes first and waardeer is second; je advies is the direct object.
work-160.forms: Waarderen has the ik form waardeer. Je is possessive before advies, not the subject. Advies is uncountable here and needs no plural or indefinite article.
work-160.compare: English appreciate and Dutch waardeer directly take the advice as object.

mistake.why: The ik form has no third-person -t.

work-160.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-161.meaning: Our customers are important. Your team gives careful attention to the needs of customers during a service discussion.
work-161.order: Onze klanten is the first constituent, zijn is second, and belangrijk describes the plural subject.
work-161.forms: Klanten is plural, so our is onze regardless of the noun’s singular article. The plural subject requires zijn. Belangrijk is predicative and has no -e ending.
work-161.compare: English customers are important has parallel structure; Dutch additionally marks onze for the plural noun.

mistake.why: A plural subject takes zijn.

work-161.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-162.meaning: I'd already sent the letter. When a colleague asks whether a letter was still awaiting dispatch, you explain it had gone out earlier.
work-162.order: Ik comes first and had is second. De brief and al stand before the final participle gestuurd.
work-162.forms: Had + past participle forms the past perfect, describing an action completed before another past reference point. Sturen uses hebben, whose singular past is had. Al means already.
work-162.compare: English had already sent and Dutch had al gestuurd both place the sending before a past moment, but Dutch puts the object inside the verb bracket.

mistake.wrong: Ik had de brief al sturen.
mistake.right: Ik had de brief al gestuurd.
mistake.why: The past perfect needs the participle gestuurd.

work-162.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
work-162.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

work-163.meaning: I have three of them. A colleague asks how many spare keys you have, and you show exactly three.
work-163.order: Ik comes first and heb is second; quantitative er stands before the number drie.
work-163.forms: Er refers to a previously named plural item, here spare keys. It is quantitative rather than a place word. When an indefinite countable noun is omitted after a number, er supplies that reference.
work-163.compare: English can say three or three of them. Dutch normally uses quantitative er when the previously mentioned countable noun is omitted.

mistake.why: Use quantitative er to refer back to the counted items; zij is not an object form.

work-163.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-164.meaning: The team met the deadline despite the malfunction. A team finishes its delivery on time even though equipment malfunctioned earlier.
work-164.order: Het team is first and heeft second. The object and concession phrase precede the final participle gehaald.
work-164.forms: Een deadline halen means to meet a deadline. Team is grammatically singular, requiring heeft. Ondanks introduces an obstacle that did not prevent success. Storing is a de-word; halen uses participle gehaald.
work-164.compare: English despite and Dutch ondanks both introduce a concession. English simple past met can correspond to a Dutch completed perfect.

mistake.wrong: Het team hebben de deadline ondanks de storing gehaald.
mistake.right: Het team heeft de deadline ondanks de storing gehaald.
mistake.why: The singular collective noun team requires heeft.

work-164.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-164.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-165.meaning: I'm not sure about that. You question a colleague’s prediction about whether a plan will work.
work-165.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and ben second; daar and van can be separated by niet zeker.
work-165.forms: Zeker zijn van means to be sure of something. Daar ... van refers back to the claim; it is a pronominal adverb, not a literal location. Niet negates the certainty.
work-165.compare: English about that comes after sure; Dutch can split daarvan around niet zeker.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben daar geen zeker van.
mistake.right: Ik ben daar niet zeker van.
mistake.why: Use niet to negate the adjective zeker.

work-165.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
work-165.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

work-166.meaning: He wasn't at the desk. You looked for a colleague at his usual desk but found his chair empty.
work-166.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Hij is first and was second; niet negates presence at the following desk location.
work-166.forms: Was is singular past of zijn. Bureau in the desk sense is a het-word. Aan het bureau locates the person at the desk; it is not the aan het + infinitive progressive construction.
work-166.compare: English at and Dutch aan express desk location here. Neither clause describes a continuing action.

mistake.wrong: Hij was niet aan de bureau.
mistake.right: Hij was niet aan het bureau.
mistake.why: Bureau takes het in the desk sense.

work-166.practiceFocus: Learn the preposition with its expression
work-166.practiceGuide: English at/to/on does not determine a single Dutch preposition. Learn the combination: verkopen aan a buyer; luisteren naar; houden van; wachten op. Op een feest names an event, in de zaal a physical space. Naar often introduces a destination but also belongs to non-motion expressions such as luisteren naar. Te before an infinitive is not a recipient preposition.

work-167.meaning: I'm trying to repair the broken lamp. You examine a broken desk lamp and try to repair it.
work-167.order: Ik comes first and probeer second; the object stands before te repareren.
work-167.forms: Proberen takes a te-infinitive, unlike modal kunnen. Lamp is a de-word; the adjective is kapotte. Repareren is a whole infinitive, with te placed directly before it.
work-167.compare: English trying to repair and Dutch probeer te repareren both mark the attempted action, but Dutch can place its object before the infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ik probeer de kapotte lamp repareren.
mistake.right: Ik probeer de kapotte lamp te repareren.
mistake.why: Proberen requires te in this construction.

work-167.practiceFocus: Proberen: try a thing or try to act
work-167.practiceGuide: Proberen means try. Ik probeer is present; ik probeerde is singular simple past; wij probeerden is plural past; ik heb geprobeerd uses the participle with hebben. The regular participle is ge + probeer + d. A thing can be tried directly; trying to do something uses proberen + te + infinitive. After zal the verb becomes proberen: ik zal proberen te bellen. Trying on clothes usually uses passen; tasting food can use proeven.

work-168.meaning: This program is easy to learn. A colleague quickly learns the basic controls of a new computer program.
work-168.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Dit programma is the first constituent, is is second, and makkelijk te leren describes it.
work-168.forms: Programma is a het-word, so attributive this is dit. Makkelijk is predicative and has no -e. Te leren specifies the action that is easy; the program is what is learned, not the learner.
work-168.compare: English easy to learn and Dutch makkelijk te leren use parallel adjective-plus-infinitive structures.

mistake.wrong: Deze programma is makkelijk te leren.
mistake.right: Dit programma is makkelijk te leren.
mistake.why: The singular het-word programma takes dit.

work-168.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-169.meaning: What's better: repairing or replacing? You compare repairing a worn device with buying a replacement.
work-169.order: Wat is beter forms the main question. After the colon, two infinitives name the alternatives being compared.
work-169.forms: Beter is the irregular comparative of goed. Of joins alternatives. Repareren and vervangen name activities as infinitives; betterer is not a Dutch comparative form.
work-169.compare: English uses repairing/replacing as activities; Dutch can use the infinitives. Both use an irregular better/beter comparative.

mistake.wrong: Wat is goeder: repareren of vervangen?
mistake.right: Wat is beter: repareren of vervangen?
mistake.why: This statement order can be used as an echo or confirmation question, with questioning intonation. For an ordinary neutral yes/no question, put the finite verb before the subject, as in the model.

work-169.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-170.meaning: The discussion is very short. A team has only a brief discussion before returning to its tasks.
work-170.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Het overleg is first and is second; erg modifies the adjective kort.
work-170.forms: Overleg is a het-word. Kort describes duration here, not physical length. Erg means very as a degree adverb; kort is predicative and receives no -e.
work-170.compare: English very short and Dutch erg kort express a high degree of short duration.

mistake.why: A predicative adjective does not receive the attributive -e ending.

work-170.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-171.meaning: We'd already closed the shop. When a late customer arrived, your team had already locked the shop and finished for the day.
work-171.order: We is first and hadden second. The object and al precede the participle gesloten.
work-171.forms: Hadden is the plural past of hebben. Hadden gesloten is a past perfect, locating closure before the customer’s past arrival. Sluiten has irregular participle gesloten. The shop is the object, so the auxiliary is hebben.
work-171.compare: English had already closed and Dutch hadden al gesloten both express an earlier completed action relative to a past event.

mistake.wrong: We had de winkel al gesloten.
mistake.right: We hadden de winkel al gesloten.
mistake.why: The plural subject we requires hadden.

work-171.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
work-171.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

work-172.meaning: Their proposal was accepted. A decision maker approves the proposal submitted by two colleagues.
work-172.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Hun voorstel is the first constituent; werd is second and geaccepteerd closes the passive bracket.
work-172.forms: Voorstel is grammatically singular even though hun names plural possessors, so use werd. Hun is possessive. Accepteren has participle geaccepteerd. This is a past passive, not a completed passive with is.
work-172.compare: English was accepted and Dutch werd geaccepteerd both focus on the proposal receiving the action.

mistake.why: Agreement follows the singular voorstel, not the plural possessors.

work-172.practiceGuide: In a passive clause the subject receives the action: het formulier wordt ingevuld. Worden forms an ongoing/event passive; zijn plus a participle can describe the completed passive or resulting state. In the simple past use werd/werden. Do not classify every is + participle as an active movement perfect; identify whether the subject performed the action.

work-173.meaning: Have you shown me the new design? You ask whether a colleague has already shown you a newly revised design.
work-173.order: Heb begins the perfect question, then je, me and the object; laten zien forms the final verb group.
work-173.forms: Laten zien means show. In the perfect with a following infinitive, laten is a replacing infinitive rather than the participle gelaten. Zien remains an infinitive too. Heb je lacks -t because subject je follows the verb. Ontwerp is a het-word, but definite het gives nieuwe an -e.
work-173.compare: English have shown uses one participle; Dutch heb laten zien uses two infinitives after the perfect auxiliary.

mistake.wrong: Heb je me het nieuwe ontwerp gelaten zien?
mistake.right: Heb je me het nieuwe ontwerp laten zien?
mistake.why: Laten appears as a replacing infinitive before zien in this perfect construction.

work-173.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-173.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-174.meaning: Do this before you leave. You point to a final desk task that a colleague should complete before going home.
work-174.order: Doe begins the main instruction and dit is its object. In the voordat-clause, subject je precedes the final finite verb vertrekt.
work-174.forms: Doe is the imperative of doen. Dit points independently to the indicated task. Voordat introduces a subordinate time clause. Vertrekt retains -t because je precedes the verb inside that clause.
work-174.compare: English before you leave and Dutch voordat je vertrekt describe the same time relationship; Dutch uses subordinate verb-final order.

mistake.why: Subject je before the finite verb requires vertrekt.

work-174.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-175.meaning: We'd already closed the financial year. When a late invoice arrived, the accounts team had already closed the financial year.
work-175.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and hadden second; the object and al stand before afgesloten.
work-175.forms: Afsluiten is separable: sluiten af; its participle is afgesloten, with ge- inserted after af. Boekjaar is a het-word inherited from jaar. Past perfect hadden afgesloten puts closing the accounts before another past event.
work-175.compare: English closed the financial year and Dutch het boekjaar afgesloten refer to completing that accounting period, not physically locking something.

mistake.wrong: We hadden het boekjaar al geafsloten.
mistake.right: We hadden het boekjaar al afgesloten.
mistake.why: In the separable participle, ge comes between af and sloten.

work-175.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
work-175.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

work-176.meaning: I'm thinking carefully about the goal. You pause to consider what a new project should actually achieve before planning its details.
work-176.order: Ik comes first and denk second. The separated particle na appears before the over-phrase describing the topic.
work-176.forms: Nadenken is separable: ik denk na. Nadenken over means reflect on. Doel is a het-word. The present expresses current reflection; na belongs to the verb and is not the time preposition after here.
work-176.compare: English thinking carefully captures reflection rather than simply having a thought. Dutch separates nadenken in this finite main clause.

mistake.right: Ik denk na over het doel.
mistake.why: Separate nadenken into finite denk and particle na in this main clause.

work-176.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-177.meaning: I'll stay standing here. You keep standing beside a collection point while your colleague fetches the needed materials.
work-177.order: Ik is first and blijf second; hier locates the continuing posture, and staan is the final infinitive.
work-177.forms: Blijven + infinitive expresses continuing an activity or posture without te. Staan means stand; hier is a place adverb. Blijf has no -t with ik.
work-177.compare: English stay standing preserves the continuing meaning of blijf; simply stand here would omit that continuation.

mistake.why: Blijven in this continuation construction takes an infinitive without te.

work-177.practiceGuide: Zitten/staan/liggen describe a position: ik zit op de stoel. Gaan zitten expresses moving into sitting: ik ga zitten. Its perfect is ik ben gaan zitten, with gaan as an infinitive in the verb cluster. A posture verb can describe an ongoing action with te: ik sta te wachten. These differ from bare is + infinitive, which is not the progressive.

work-178.meaning: They're talking about the quality, not the colour. Colleagues compare the workmanship of product samples rather than their different colours.
work-178.order: Ze is first and praten second. A second over-phrase contrasts the excluded topic after niet.
work-178.forms: Plural praten makes ze mean they. Over introduces a conversation topic. Niet can negate a whole prepositional phrase for an explicit contrast. Kwaliteit and kleur are de-words.
work-178.compare: English not the colour and Dutch niet over de kleur can contrast two topics; Dutch repeats over to make the negated phrase clear.

mistake.wrong: Ze praten over de kwaliteit, geen over de kleur.
mistake.right: Ze praten over de kwaliteit, niet over de kleur.
mistake.why: Use niet to negate a prepositional phrase.

work-178.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
work-178.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

work-179.meaning: Let me have a quick look. You ask for a brief moment to inspect a colleague’s document before answering a question.
work-179.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Laat begins the request; me is the person who will look, even softens the request, and kijken is final.
work-179.forms: Laten takes an infinitive without te. Me is an object form in the main clause and the understood subject of kijken. Even here means for a brief moment and softens the request, not the English adjective even.
work-179.compare: English let me have a quick look and Dutch laat me even kijken both request a brief opportunity to inspect something.

mistake.why: Laten in this construction takes an infinitive without te.

work-179.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-180.meaning: Our company values diversity. Colleagues with different backgrounds contribute ideas during an inclusive team discussion.
work-180.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ons bedrijf is first and waardeert is second; diversiteit is the object.
work-180.forms: Bedrijf is a singular het-word, so our is ons. The singular company requires waardeert with -t. Diversiteit is an abstract noun used without an article here. Waarderen means value/appreciate.
work-180.compare: English values and Dutch waardeert take diversity as a direct object; Dutch marks the possessive according to bedrijf.

mistake.why: A singular het-word takes ons.

work-180.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-181.meaning: That is his computer. You identify which workstation belongs to a particular colleague.
work-181.order: Dat is the subject, is is second, and zijn computer identifies the object being pointed out.
work-181.forms: Dat stands independently; it does not have to agree with de computer. Zijn is possessive before computer, not the verb zijn. A possessive replaces the article.
work-181.compare: English that is his computer has parallel clause order. Dutch independent dat differs from attributive die computer.

mistake.why: The possessive replaces the article in this noun phrase.

work-181.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-182.meaning: Can you talk for a moment? You ask a colleague whether they have a moment for a private conversation.
work-182.order: Kun starts the yes/no question, subject je follows it, and praten is the final infinitive.
work-182.forms: Kun je is an informal inverted form. Even softens the request and suggests a brief conversation. Praten after kunnen is an infinitive without te. This context asks about availability rather than physical speech ability.
work-182.compare: English can you talk for a moment and Dutch kun je even praten share the practical request meaning.

mistake.why: Kunnen takes an infinitive without te.

work-182.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-183.meaning: She's happy with her new job. A colleague happily describes her new workplace after changing jobs.
work-183.order: Ze comes first and is second; blij is followed by met and the thing she is happy with.
work-183.forms: Blij zijn met is the normal combination for satisfaction with something. Haar is possessive. Baan is a de-word, so the adjective is nieuwe. The singular is makes ze mean she.
work-183.compare: English happy with matches Dutch blij met; do not translate with as over by default.

mistake.wrong: Ze is blij met haar nieuw baan.
mistake.right: Ze is blij met haar nieuwe baan.
mistake.why: Before this possessive de-word the attributive adjective takes -e.

work-183.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-184.meaning: He sent me an email. You tell a colleague that someone contacted you directly by email.
work-184.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Hij is first and stuurde second. Recipient mij comes before the full object een e-mail.
work-184.forms: Stuurde is singular simple past of sturen. Mij is a stressed recipient object form; me is also possible. The indirect object does not require aan when placed before the direct object here.
work-184.compare: English sent me an email and Dutch stuurde mij een e-mail can both place recipient before the sent item.

mistake.why: The recipient requires object mij or me, not subject ik.

work-184.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-185.meaning: They have written you a letter. You tell a colleague that several people have jointly written a letter addressed to them.
work-185.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ze is first and hebben second. Recipient je and the letter stand before final geschreven.
work-185.forms: Hebben geschreven is a perfect. Schrijven has irregular participle geschreven. Je is an object recipient here, not possessive, because it is not a determiner of een brief. Plural hebben makes ze mean they.
work-185.compare: English have written you a letter can also put recipient before object; Dutch moves the participle after both.

mistake.wrong: Ze hebben je een brief geschrijfd.
mistake.right: Ze hebben je een brief geschreven.
mistake.why: Schrijven has irregular participle geschreven.

work-185.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-185.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-186.meaning: Buying clothes is expensive. You compare the cost of replacing a work wardrobe while browsing clothing racks.
work-186.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The whole activity Kleding kopen is the first constituent. Is is second, followed by the predicate duur.
work-186.forms: Kleding is an uncountable collective noun in Dutch. The infinitive phrase is a singular activity subject. Duur is predicative without -e. The object kleding comes before the infinitive kopen inside the subject phrase.
work-186.compare: English uses buying clothes as an -ing subject; Dutch uses the infinitive phrase kleding kopen. English clothes is plural while Dutch kleding is collective singular.

mistake.why: The activity phrase is grammatically singular.

work-186.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-186.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-187.meaning: They'll call you as soon as the order is ready. A shop employee explains that colleagues will telephone the customer when the order can be collected.
work-187.order: Ze zullen starts the main clause; u is the person called and bellen closes its verb group. In the zodra-clause, the finite is follows the subject and klaar.
work-187.forms: Zullen agrees with plural ze, not object u. Zodra means as soon as and introduces a subordinate clause. Klaar is a predicate adjective with no -e. The time clause follows the main infinitive naturally.
work-187.compare: English will call you as soon as ... and Dutch zullen u bellen zodra ... convey a future commitment tied to a condition in time.

mistake.wrong: Ze zullen u bellen zodra de bestelling is klaar.
mistake.right: Ze zullen u bellen zodra de bestelling klaar is.
mistake.why: The subordinate finite verb comes after klaar.

work-187.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-188.meaning: What was his feedback? After a colleague’s review, you ask what the reviewer said about the work.
work-188.order: Wat asks for the content; was is second and zijn feedback follows as the subject phrase.
work-188.forms: Was is singular past of zijn. Zijn is possessive before feedback. Feedback is normally uncountable in this use; the possessive supplies the determiner.
work-188.compare: English and Dutch both use what was his feedback for a past response; neither sentence asks for a future prediction.

mistake.why: Feedback is treated as singular in this use.

work-188.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-189.meaning: Please share your screen. During a video call, you politely ask another participant to show their screen to the group.
work-189.order: Deel starts the imperative, alstublieft makes the request polite, and uw scherm is the object.
work-189.forms: The ordinary imperative is the stem deel. Uw is the polite possessive before scherm; u is a personal pronoun. Het scherm is a het-word, but a possessive replaces the article. Scherm delen has the digital sharing meaning here.
work-189.compare: English please share your screen and Dutch deel alstublieft uw scherm can place please/alstublieft differently without changing the request.

mistake.why: Use possessive uw before the noun.

work-189.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-190.meaning: She returned the deposit to us. After you return rented equipment, the rental worker refunds your deposit.
work-190.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Zij is first and heeft second. The short recipient ons precedes the full object de borg, followed by teruggegeven.
work-190.forms: Teruggeven uses hebben in the perfect and separable participle teruggegeven. Borg here means a refundable deposit, not a person guaranteeing a debt. The singular auxiliary heeft agrees with zij meaning she.
work-190.compare: English returned the deposit to us and Dutch heeft ons de borg teruggegeven describe a refund; Dutch can omit aan before the short indirect object.

mistake.wrong: Zij heeft wij de borg teruggegeven.
mistake.right: Zij heeft ons de borg teruggegeven.
mistake.why: The recipient uses object ons, not subject wij.

work-190.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-190.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-191.meaning: This is my responsibility. You volunteer to take ownership of a task that falls within your role.
work-191.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Dit is first and is second; mijn verantwoordelijkheid identifies the duty being pointed to.
work-191.forms: Verantwoordelijkheid is a de-word, but independent dit does not need to agree with it. Mijn is possessive. The noun refers to responsibility for a duty, rather than blame for a specific mistake in this scenario.
work-191.compare: English this is my responsibility and Dutch dit is mijn verantwoordelijkheid express ownership of a duty with parallel order.

mistake.why: Independent singular dit takes is.

work-191.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-192.meaning: I'll send the report. You commit to sending the finished report after its final review.
work-192.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ik is first and zal second; the object stands before final versturen.
work-192.forms: Versturen is inseparable because of ver-; the infinitive remains whole. Rapport is a het-word. Zal expresses the speaker’s future commitment; its plural counterpart is zullen.
work-192.compare: English will send stays together before the report; Dutch puts the report inside the zal ... versturen bracket.

mistake.why: After zal use the infinitive, not a finite verb.

work-192.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-193.meaning: How reliable is this measurement? You compare repeated measurements and ask how much confidence you can place in the result.
work-193.order: Hoe betrouwbaar is one question constituent, so is is second even though two words precede it. Deze meting is the subject.
work-193.forms: Betrouwbaar is predicative without -e. Meting is a de-word, so use deze. Hoe asks about the degree of reliability. A measurement’s reliability differs from whether a person is honest.
work-193.compare: English how reliable and Dutch hoe betrouwbaar each form a multiword question phrase before the verb.

mistake.why: The predicative adjective has no attributive -e.

work-193.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-194.meaning: Staying positive is important. After a setback, a colleague encourages the team to maintain a hopeful attitude.
work-194.order: Positief blijven is the first constituent and activity subject; is is second and belangrijk describes that activity.
work-194.forms: Blijven with an adjective means remain in a state. Positief remains uninflected as a predicative complement inside the subject phrase. The activity subject takes singular is.
work-194.compare: English staying positive uses an -ing subject; Dutch uses an infinitive phrase. The phrase can contain an adjective before the infinitive.

mistake.why: The infinitive activity phrase is a singular subject.

work-194.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-194.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-195.meaning: Are you busy with the preparation? You check whether a colleague is currently working on preparing an upcoming activity.
work-195.order: Ben starts the yes/no question, followed by subject je, bezig, and the activity with met.
work-195.forms: Ben je is the inverted informal form of zijn. Bezig zijn met names an activity in progress. Voorbereiding is a de-word. Bezig is predicative and takes no -e.
work-195.compare: English busy with and Dutch bezig met describe ongoing involvement; the question asks about the specific preparation.

mistake.right: Ben je bezig met de voorbereiding?
mistake.why: Met introduces the activity after bezig here.

work-195.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-195.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

work-196.meaning: He explained his theory. A colleague explains the reasoning behind a theory using a diagram and model.
work-196.order: Hij is first and legde second. The object stands between legde and the final separable particle uit.
work-196.forms: Uitleggen is separable: legt uit; its singular past is legde uit. The doubled g in leggen reduces to one g before -de. Zijn is possessive before theorie.
work-196.compare: English explained is a single past word; Dutch legde ... uit separates the verb around its object.

mistake.why: Separate the particle uit in this finite main clause.

work-196.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-197.meaning: Please check my work. You ask an experienced colleague to inspect the work you have completed.
work-197.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Controleer begins the instruction/request, followed by alstublieft and the object mijn werk.
work-197.forms: Controleren has stem controleer. Alstublieft adds polite tone; it does not require a subject pronoun in an ordinary imperative. Mijn replaces the article before werk.
work-197.compare: English please check and Dutch controleer alstublieft can place the politeness word differently.

mistake.why: Use the ordinary modern imperative stem without -t.

work-197.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-198.meaning: Talk now, because the meeting starts shortly. A colleague has a brief window to speak before a meeting begins.
work-198.order: Praat nu is an imperative clause. After coordinating want, the second clause keeps main-clause order: straks first, begint second, then de vergadering.
work-198.forms: Want gives a reason without introducing subordinate verb-final order. Beginnen has singular begint. Straks means shortly/later soon, in contrast with nu.
work-198.compare: English because can introduce a reason with ordinary English order; Dutch want is coordinating and preserves V2 in its following clause.

mistake.wrong: Praat nu, want straks de vergadering begint.
mistake.right: Praat nu, want straks begint de vergadering.
mistake.why: After want use main-clause V2, including inversion after straks.

work-198.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-199.meaning: What's his next move? You discuss a colleague’s next strategic action while planning the response to a business proposal.
work-199.order: Wat asks which action is next; is is second and zijn volgende zet follows as the subject.
work-199.forms: Zet means a strategic move in this context, not a seat or the verb put. De zet takes attributive volgende after possessive zijn. Zijn is possessive.
work-199.compare: English next move and Dutch volgende zet share a figurative strategic use derived from games.

mistake.why: The attributive adjective before this de-word takes -e.

work-199.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-200.meaning: What time does he arrive? You coordinate collecting a colleague from the station and ask for his arrival time.
work-200.order: Hoe laat is one question phrase; komt is second, followed by hij and final aan.
work-200.forms: Aankomen is separable: komt aan. The present can refer to a planned arrival. Komt retains -t with subject hij after it; the informal jij inversion exception does not apply to hij.
work-200.compare: English what time is he arriving and Dutch hoe laat komt hij aan ask about the planned time; Dutch splits aankomen.

mistake.why: With subject hij the finite verb retains -t.

work-200.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-201.meaning: We have to stay competitive. Your team discusses maintaining the quality and efficiency needed to compete with similar businesses.
work-201.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and moeten second; competitief describes the state to maintain, and blijven is final.
work-201.forms: Moeten expresses necessity, not a suggestion with should. Blijven plus an adjective means remain in a state. Competitief is predicative and does not receive -e. After moeten use blijven without te.
work-201.compare: English have to stay competitive captures obligation; Dutch moeten competitief blijven puts the adjective before the infinitive.

mistake.why: The adjective is predicative, without attributive -e.

work-201.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-202.meaning: I'll send an invitation to all the neighbours. You organise a neighbourhood gathering and invite everyone living nearby.
work-202.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and stuur second; the object precedes the recipient aan alle buren.
work-202.forms: The present stuur can express an immediate intention. Alle is a plural determiner before buren and does not combine with een. Aan marks the recipients. Uitnodiging is an indefinite singular de-word.
work-202.compare: English will send and Dutch present stuur can convey the same intention. To all the neighbours becomes aan alle buren.

mistake.wrong: Ik stuur een uitnodiging aan alle buur.
mistake.right: Ik stuur een uitnodiging aan alle buren.
mistake.why: Alle requires a plural count noun here.

work-202.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-203.meaning: They're being patient. Several people wait calmly for their turn at a service counter.
work-203.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ze is first and oefenen second; geduld completes the fixed expression.
work-203.forms: Geduld oefenen is an established expression meaning to be patient, often while waiting. Geduld is uncountable and has no article here. Plural oefenen makes ze mean they. It need not mean a deliberate training exercise.
work-203.compare: Literal practising patience is possible English, but being patient better captures the idiomatic waiting context.

mistake.why: For plural they, use oefenen; oefent would make ze singular she.

work-203.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-204.meaning: He'll explain the diversion to him. A colleague will explain a changed road route to someone travelling to the office.
work-204.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Hij is first and zal second; short recipient hem comes before the full object, followed by uitleggen.
work-204.forms: Uitleggen is separable in a finite simple clause but stays whole as an infinitive after zal. Hem names the listener and is an object form. Omleiding means the rerouted road route in this context.
work-204.compare: English explain the diversion to him uses to; Dutch can express the recipient directly before the full object without aan.

mistake.wrong: Hij zal hij de omleiding uitleggen.
mistake.right: Hij zal hem de omleiding uitleggen.
mistake.why: The listener requires object hem rather than subject hij.

work-204.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-205.meaning: Wait for him by the entrance. You ask a colleague to meet a late arrival at the entrance before entering together.
work-205.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Wacht starts the instruction; op hem names the person expected, and bij de ingang locates the waiting.
work-205.forms: Wachten op is a fixed combination. Hem is an object pronoun after op. Bij marks a nearby location. Ingang is a de-word. This imperative uses the stem wacht.
work-205.compare: English wait for him becomes Dutch wacht op hem; for is not translated with voor in this fixed expression.

mistake.wrong: Wacht op hij bij de ingang.
mistake.right: Wacht op hem bij de ingang.
mistake.why: A preposition takes object hem, not subject hij.

work-205.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-206.meaning: I promise you that I'll be on time. You reassure a colleague that you will arrive punctually for an agreed meeting.

parts.label: subordinate clause
parts.text: dat ik op tijd zal zijn

work-206.order: Ik is first and beloof second; recipient je precedes the content clause. Its final verb group is zal zijn.
work-206.forms: Beloven can take a recipient and a dat-clause naming the promise. Je is an object pronoun. Op tijd means on time. In the subordinate future group, zal zijn is standard; zijn zal is also possible.
work-206.compare: English promise that I will be and Dutch beloof dat ik ... zal zijn both specify a future commitment.

mistake.wrong: Ik beloof je dat ik zal op tijd zijn.
mistake.right: Ik beloof je dat ik op tijd zal zijn.
mistake.why: In this dat-clause the verb group comes after op tijd.

work-206.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-207.meaning: I'll see you tomorrow at the stop. You arrange to meet a colleague by the bus stop the following day.
work-207.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and zie second; je is followed by the planned time and meeting place.
work-207.forms: Zien has the irregular ik form zie. Je is an object pronoun here. The future time morgen makes the present express a planned meeting. Halte is a de-word; bij means by/near.
work-207.compare: English will see naturally expresses the plan; Dutch uses present zie with morgen rather than requiring zal.

mistake.wrong: Ik ziet je morgen bij de halte.
mistake.right: Ik zie je morgen bij de halte.
mistake.why: The ik form of zien is zie without -t.

work-207.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-208.meaning: Please carry the folders for me. With your hands occupied, you politely ask a colleague to carry a stack of folders.
work-208.order: Draag starts the imperative; alstublieft softens it. The object precedes the beneficiary voor mij.
work-208.forms: Dragen has stem draag and irregular participle gedragen. Mappen is the plural of de map, with doubled p preserving the short vowel. Mij is the stressed object pronoun after voor.
work-208.compare: English carry for me and Dutch draag voor mij mark the same beneficiary; please/alstublieft can appear in several positions.

mistake.wrong: Draag alstublieft de mappen voor ik.
mistake.right: Draag alstublieft de mappen voor mij.
mistake.why: A preposition requires the object form mij or me.

work-208.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-209.meaning: I'm here to work on the renovation project. You arrive at a renovation site and explain the purpose of your visit.

parts.label: om te phrase
parts.text: om aan het renovatieproject te werken

work-209.order: Ik is first and ben second; the purpose phrase follows hier and ends with te werken.
work-209.forms: Om ... te gives the purpose. Werken aan introduces the project being worked on. Renovatieproject is one compound and takes het from project. The project phrase precedes te werken.
work-209.compare: English to work on the project places the project after work; Dutch places aan het project before te werken.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben hier om aan het renovatieproject werken.
mistake.right: Ik ben hier om aan het renovatieproject te werken.
mistake.why: Om-purpose phrases require te.

work-209.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-210.meaning: Start this program after installation. A colleague asks you to open newly installed software once installation has finished.
work-210.order: Start begins the instruction, followed by its object and a time prepositional phrase.
work-210.forms: Programma is a het-word, so attributive this is dit. Start is the imperative stem. Na here means after, not the separable particle of nadenken. Installatie is a de-word.
work-210.compare: English start this program after installation and Dutch start dit programma na de installatie have parallel imperative order.

mistake.wrong: Start deze programma na de installatie.
mistake.right: Start dit programma na de installatie.
mistake.why: Use dit with the singular het-word programma.

work-210.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-211.meaning: They're focusing on their work. Colleagues put distractions aside and concentrate on their assigned work.
work-211.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ze is first and richten second; reflexive zich comes before op hun werk.
work-211.forms: Zich richten op means focus on. The reflexive matches plural ze; with ik it is me. Hun is possessive before werk. Op belongs to the fixed expression.
work-211.compare: English focus on does not require themselves; Dutch uses the reflexive zich in zich richten op.

mistake.right: Ze richten zich op hun werk.
mistake.why: The focus expression zich richten op requires the reflexive.

work-211.practiceFocus: Reflexive pronouns refer to the subject
work-211.practiceGuide: Match the reflexive to the subject: ik/me, jij/je, hij-zij/zich, wij/ons, jullie/je, zij plural/zich. A question can contain two je forms: Voel je je beter? The first is the subject, the second reflexive. The reflexive belongs to the Dutch expression even if natural English does not say myself. In an embedded clause the verb group normally closes the clause.

work-212.meaning: He left early because the train was cancelled. A colleague leaves earlier than planned to arrange alternative transport after his train is cancelled.
work-212.order: Hij is first and vertrok second. In the omdat-clause, subject de trein precedes final uitviel.
work-212.forms: Vertrok is irregular singular past of vertrekken. Omdat introduces a subordinate reason clause. Uitvallen is separable, but in this verb-final subordinate clause its finite past uitviel stays together. A train uitvallen means not running/cancelled.
work-212.compare: English because and Dutch omdat give a reason; Dutch moves the finite subordinate verb to the end.

mistake.wrong: Hij vertrok vroeg omdat de trein viel uit.
mistake.right: Hij vertrok vroeg omdat de trein uitviel.
mistake.why: In this subordinate clause the separable finite verb stays together at the end.

work-212.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-213.meaning: What's the best approach? Your team compares ways to tackle a newly identified problem.
work-213.order: Wat asks for the chosen method; is is second and the subject follows.
work-213.forms: Aanpak is a de-word. Beste is the irregular superlative of goed and takes the attributive -e ending. De beste aanpak identifies the most suitable method among alternatives.
work-213.compare: English best approach and Dutch beste aanpak share the superlative meaning; Dutch marks the adjective ending.

mistake.why: Goed has irregular superlative best/beste.

work-213.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-214.meaning: I'm going to repair the broken zip. You show a broken coat zip and state your intention to repair it.
work-214.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ik is first and ga second; the object stands before final repareren.
work-214.forms: Gaan + infinitive here states an intention, without requiring physical travel. Repareren takes no te after ga. Rits is a de-word, so the attributive adjective is kapotte.
work-214.compare: English going to repair and Dutch ga repareren both express an intention; Dutch places the object before the final infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ik ga de kapotte rits te repareren.
mistake.right: Ik ga de kapotte rits repareren.
mistake.why: Gaan takes an infinitive without te in this construction.

work-214.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-215.meaning: Let's review our progress. Your team checks how much of a shared project has been completed.
work-215.order: A suggestion with Laten we starts with the verb laten; the other verb (the infinitive) normally occurs toward the end. Laten we introduces a shared suggestion; the object comes before final bekijken.
work-215.forms: Voortgang is a de-word, so our is onze. Bekijken is inseparable because of be- and stays whole. It means examine/review here, rather than simply look casually.
work-215.compare: English review our progress and Dutch onze voortgang bekijken express assessment of completed work; Dutch puts the object before its infinitive.

mistake.why: A singular de-word takes onze.

work-215.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-216.meaning: Is this your decision? You ask a colleague whether they personally made a choice rather than following someone else’s decision.
work-216.order: Is begins the yes/no question; independent dit is the subject and jouw beslissing identifies the choice.
work-216.forms: Jouw is a stressed possessive, appropriate when contrasting whose decision it is. Jou would be an object pronoun. Beslissing is a de-word, but independent dit need not agree with it.
work-216.compare: English stressed your and Dutch jouw can emphasize personal ownership of the decision.

mistake.why: Use possessive jouw before the noun.

work-216.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-217.meaning: He's checking the time. A colleague checks the clock while coordinating the timing of an activity.

parts.label: noun phrase
parts.text: met het controleren van de tijd

work-217.order: Hij is first and is second; bezig met is followed by a nominalised activity phrase.
work-217.forms: Het controleren is an infinitive used as a noun. Van de tijd names what is checked in the nominal construction; ordinary verb form would be de tijd controleren. Bezig met presents current involvement.
work-217.compare: English checking uses an -ing form; Dutch met het controleren uses an article plus infinitive and adds van for its noun complement.

mistake.wrong: Hij is bezig met controleren de tijd.
mistake.right: Hij is bezig met het controleren van de tijd.
mistake.why: This nominal construction uses het and van for the checked thing.

work-217.practiceFocus: Bezig met: a noun or an activity
work-217.practiceGuide: Bezig met introduces what occupies someone: a noun (de was) or an infinitive used as an activity noun (het wassen). Infinitives used as nouns take het, not de: het koken. Met het schoonmaken van de ramen is a noun-like phrase; compare the verbal progressive de ramen aan het schoonmaken. Bezig can also introduce te + infinitive, with different word order.

work-218.meaning: I liked your idea. You recall a creative suggestion from a colleague and tell them you liked it.
work-218.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and vond second; je idee is the object and leuk evaluates it.
work-218.forms: Vinden in this construction means consider/find something nice. Vond is irregular singular past. Je is possessive. Leuk is an object predicate with no -e; it does not stand attributively before idee.
work-218.compare: English liked uses one verb; Dutch vond ... leuk combines a verb with an adjective evaluating its object.

mistake.why: The object-predicate adjective does not take attributive -e.

work-218.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-219.meaning: Please confirm your booking. A receptionist asks a guest to confirm a reservation before arrangements are finalised.
work-219.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Bevestig begins the request, followed by alstublieft and uw boeking.
work-219.forms: Bevestigen has stem bevestig. Uw is polite possessive. Boeking is a de-word meaning a reservation; it is not the noun boek meaning book. The prefix be- is inseparable.
work-219.compare: English confirm your booking and Dutch bevestig uw boeking use a direct object without an additional preposition.

mistake.why: Use possessive uw before the noun.

work-219.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-220.meaning: We're considering the risk of this investment. Your team reviews the uncertainty of an investment proposal before deciding.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: over het risico van deze investering

work-220.order: We is first and denken second; na is separated from the verb, followed by the full topic phrase.
work-220.forms: Nadenken over means reflect on. Risico is a het-word; investering is a de-word and takes deze. Van specifies which risk is considered.
work-220.compare: English considering can naturally express Dutch nadenken over. Dutch separates the particle na in the main clause.

mistake.wrong: We nadenken over het risico van deze investering.
mistake.right: We denken na over het risico van deze investering.
mistake.why: Separate nadenken in a finite main clause.

work-220.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-221.meaning: What's our competitive advantage compared with larger companies? A small team compares its particular strengths with those of larger competitors.
work-221.order: Wat is first and is second; the subject is followed by a comparison phrase naming the competitors.
work-221.forms: Concurrentievoordeel is one compound with het voordeel as its head, so possessive our is ons. Ten opzichte van means relative to/compared with. Grotere is an attributive comparative before plural bedrijven.
work-221.compare: English compared with larger companies and Dutch ten opzichte van grotere bedrijven specify the comparison rather than a generic advantage.

mistake.wrong: Wat is onze concurrentievoordeel ten opzichte van grotere bedrijven?
mistake.right: Wat is ons concurrentievoordeel ten opzichte van grotere bedrijven?
mistake.why: The singular het-word takes ons.

work-221.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-222.meaning: Will this solution work? You ask whether a proposed arrangement will solve an access problem before testing it.
work-222.order: Zal starts the yes/no question, followed by its subject and final infinitive werken.
work-222.forms: Werken here means function or succeed, not perform a job. Oplossing is a de-word and takes deze. The singular subject requires zal. Zullen asks about a predicted result.
work-222.compare: English will this solution work has parallel auxiliary-first order; work/werken both have the function/succeed sense.

mistake.why: Use singular zal with deze oplossing.

work-222.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-223.meaning: We need our manager to resolve this conflict. Your team asks a manager to help resolve a disagreement between colleagues.

parts.label: om te phrase
parts.text: om dit conflict op te lossen

work-223.order: We is first and hebben second. The need expression ends with nodig, followed by the purpose clause.
work-223.forms: Manager is a de-word, so possessive our is onze. Conflict is a het-word and takes dit. Oplossen is separable; te goes between op and lossen in the purpose infinitive.
work-223.compare: English resolve and Dutch op te lossen convey the intended help. Dutch splits a separable infinitive around te.

mistake.wrong: We hebben onze manager nodig om dit conflict te oplossen.
mistake.right: We hebben onze manager nodig om dit conflict op te lossen.
mistake.why: Place te between the separable particle op and infinitive lossen.

work-223.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-224.meaning: Let's celebrate our success. After reaching a shared goal, you invite the team to a small celebration.
work-224.order: A suggestion with Laten we starts with the verb laten; the other verb (the infinitive) normally occurs toward the end. Laten we introduces the shared proposal; ons succes precedes final vieren.
work-224.forms: Succes is a singular het-word, so our is ons. Vieren is an infinitive after Laten we. The proposal includes the speaker and colleagues in celebrating a completed success.
work-224.compare: English Let’s celebrate our success and Dutch Laten we ons succes vieren convey the same joint proposal, with different infinitive/object order.

mistake.why: The singular het-word succes takes ons.

work-224.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-225.meaning: This is very important for our cooperation. You stress the importance of an agreed way to share information during a joint project.
work-225.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Dit is first and is second. Erg modifies belangrijk; voor introduces what the importance concerns.
work-225.forms: Dit stands independently. Erg is a degree adverb, not an attributive adjective here. Samenwerking is a de-word and takes onze. Belangrijk is predicative without -e.
work-225.compare: English important for and Dutch belangrijk voor can specify the activity that depends on the point being discussed.
