mistake.wrong: Dit is erg belangrijke voor onze samenwerking.
mistake.right: Dit is erg belangrijk voor onze samenwerking.
mistake.why: The predicative adjective has no -e ending.

work-225.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-226.meaning: Explain the difference between these materials to us. You ask a specialist to explain how two material samples differ.
work-226.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Leg starts the instruction and uit ends it; recipient ons and the full object stand inside that bracket.
work-226.forms: Uitleggen is separable, with imperative leg ... uit. Verschil is a het-word; tussen names the compared items. Deze agrees with plural materialen. A short recipient naturally precedes a full noun object.
work-226.compare: English explain the difference to us uses one verb; Dutch separates leg and uit around its recipient and object.

mistake.wrong: Uitleg ons het verschil tussen deze materialen.
mistake.right: Leg ons het verschil tussen deze materialen uit.
mistake.why: The imperative of uitleggen separates into leg and uit.

work-226.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-227.meaning: Have you repaired my bicycle for me? You collect your bicycle and ask whether a colleague has completed the repair for you.
work-227.order: Heb starts the perfect question, then je, the object and beneficiary, followed by gerepareerd.
work-227.forms: Heb je is inverted and lacks -t with subject je. Repareren uses hebben and participle gerepareerd. Mijn is possessive; me after voor is an object beneficiary pronoun.
work-227.compare: English have you repaired and Dutch heb je ... gerepareerd express a completed repair; Dutch places its participle after the object and beneficiary.

mistake.wrong: Heb je mijn fiets voor ik gerepareerd?
mistake.right: Heb je mijn fiets voor me gerepareerd?
mistake.why: Use an object pronoun after voor.

work-227.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-227.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-228.meaning: Will the repair take a long time? You ask how much time a repair is likely to require before deciding whether to wait.
work-228.order: Zal starts the question, followed by its subject, lang, and final infinitive duren.
work-228.forms: Duren concerns how long an event takes or lasts. Lang makes the intended duration question explicit; it does not assess whether a repaired object is durable. Reparatie is a singular de-word.
work-228.compare: English take a long time expresses event duration accurately. Going to last could misleadingly suggest durability for an unspecified object.

mistake.why: Lang describes duration adverbially and has no attributive -e.

work-228.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-229.meaning: The customer has approved the final design. A customer signs off the final version of a design before production begins.
work-229.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. De klant is first and heeft second; the object precedes final goedgekeurd.
work-229.forms: Goedkeuren is separable: keurt goed; its participle is goedgekeurd. Ontwerp is a het-word, but after definite het the adjective receives -e: definitieve. The perfect presents completed approval.
work-229.compare: English has approved and Dutch heeft goedgekeurd both describe completed acceptance. Removing the unexplained possessive avoids guessing whose design it was.

mistake.wrong: De klant heeft het definitieve ontwerp gegoedkeurd.
mistake.right: De klant heeft het definitieve ontwerp goedgekeurd.
mistake.why: Ge is inserted after the separable particle goed.

work-229.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-229.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-230.meaning: He finished the work. A colleague completes the remaining work on a task and clears away his tools.
work-230.order: Hij is first and maakte second; the object stands before final particle af.
work-230.forms: Afmaken is separable. Its singular past is maakte af; the participle is afgemaakt. Werk is a het-word and is the object of finishing. This simple past differs from heeft afgemaakt.
work-230.compare: English finished is one verb; Dutch maakte ... af separates the particle around its object.

mistake.why: Separate afmaken in this finite main clause.

work-230.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-231.meaning: You haven't made a mistake. You reassure a colleague after checking that their work is correct.
work-231.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Je is first and hebt second; geen fout precedes final gemaakt.
work-231.forms: Geen negates indefinite een fout: no mistake/not a mistake. Hebt gemaakt is a perfect; maken uses hebben. Je before the verb requires hebt with -t.
work-231.compare: English not a mistake corresponds to Dutch geen fout, not a word-for-word niet een.

mistake.why: Negate this indefinite count-noun object with geen.

work-231.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-231.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-232.meaning: Call her after lunch. You ask a colleague to telephone a contact after the lunch break.
work-232.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Bel begins the instruction; haar is the person called and na de lunch gives the time.
work-232.forms: Bellen directly takes a person as object. Haar is an object pronoun here, not possessive. Bel is the imperative stem, with one l; na means after.
work-232.compare: English call her and Dutch bel haar need no to/aan before the person.

mistake.why: The person called is an object, so use haar.

work-232.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-233.meaning: His meeting starts soon. You warn a colleague that the meeting he is due to attend is about to begin.
work-233.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Zijn vergadering is first and begint second; spoedig gives the approaching time.
work-233.forms: Zijn is possessive, not a verb. Vergadering is singular, requiring begint. Spoedig means soon and has a relatively formal tone; binnenkort or straks can fit different time frames.
work-233.compare: English starts soon and Dutch begint spoedig both use the present for an approaching scheduled event.

mistake.why: The singular meeting requires finite begint.

work-233.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-234.meaning: Who's calling? You hear an incoming call and ask which person is calling.
work-234.order: Wie is the question subject, followed by belt and presentative er; no additional subject pronoun is needed.
work-234.forms: Wie normally takes singular agreement in this unspecified question. Er is common in presentative subject questions and need not be translated as a literal place. Belt can mean telephones here.
work-234.compare: English who is calling and Dutch wie belt er ask for the caller without a do auxiliary.

mistake.why: Use the ordinary singular verb in this unspecified who-question.

work-234.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-235.meaning: What are the key insights? After a workshop, you ask the group to identify the most important things they learned.
work-235.order: Wat asks for the content, zijn is second, and the plural subject follows.
work-235.forms: Inzichten is plural, so the verb is zijn. Belangrijkste is the attributive superlative of belangrijk. Inzicht means understanding or insight, not a physical view in this context.
work-235.compare: English key insights gives a clear meaning without requiring the informal workshop term takeaways.

mistake.why: Agreement follows the plural noun phrase inzichten.

work-235.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-236.meaning: What's the date of registration? You ask when registration for a course takes place.
work-236.order: Wat is first and is second; the full date phrase is the subject.
work-236.forms: Datum is a de-word. Van de inschrijving specifies which date is requested, rather than asking for today’s date. Inschrijving means registration in this context.
work-236.compare: English date of registration and Dutch datum van de inschrijving identify the same administrative event.

mistake.wrong: Wat zijn de datum van de inschrijving?
mistake.right: Wat is de datum van de inschrijving?
mistake.why: The head noun datum is singular.

work-236.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-237.meaning: Have you sent me the invoice? You ask whether the invoice needed for payment has already been sent to you.
work-237.order: Heb starts the perfect question; subject je, recipient me and the full object come before gestuurd.
work-237.forms: Sturen uses hebben and participle gestuurd. Heb je loses -t with the following informal subject. Factuur is a de-word. A short indirect object naturally precedes a full direct object.
work-237.compare: English have you sent me the invoice and Dutch heb je me de factuur gestuurd share recipient-first object order, but Dutch puts the participle last.

mistake.wrong: Heb je ik de factuur gestuurd?
mistake.right: Heb je me de factuur gestuurd?
mistake.why: Use the object recipient me, not subject ik.

work-237.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-237.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-238.meaning: I want to repair the damaged chair. You want to repair a damaged chair rather than discard it.
work-238.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ik is first and wil second; the damaged chair stands before final repareren.
work-238.forms: Willen means want, not the English future will. Repareren takes no te after wil. Beschadigde is an attributive participle/adjective before de stoel.
work-238.compare: English want to repair needs to; Dutch wil repareren does not use te.

mistake.wrong: Ik wil de beschadigde stoel te repareren.
mistake.right: Ik wil de beschadigde stoel repareren.
mistake.why: Willen takes an infinitive without te.

work-238.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-239.meaning: They share their ideas. Team members contribute different ideas and discuss them openly.
work-239.order: Zij is the subject in first position and the finite verb delen is second; hun ideeën is the object and follows the verb.
work-239.forms: Plural delen makes zij mean they. Hun is possessive before ideeën. Idee has plural ideeën with a diaeresis to show the vowel begins a new syllable.
work-239.compare: English their ideas and Dutch hun ideeën mark possession; Dutch plural spelling requires the diaeresis.

mistake.why: Use possessive hun before a noun.

work-239.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-240.meaning: Could you guide me through it? You politely ask a colleague to guide you step by step through an unfamiliar procedure.
work-240.order: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, so no constituent comes before it. Kunt starts the request, followed by u and me; erdoorheen specifies the process and leiden is final.
work-240.forms: Leiden means guide/lead, not lijden meaning suffer. Erdoorheen refers back to the procedure: through it. Kunt u is standard; kan u is also standard. The infinitive follows the modal without te.
work-240.compare: English guide me through it and Dutch me erdoorheen leiden express guided progress through a process rather than literal walking.

mistake.why: Leiden means guide; lijden means suffer.

work-240.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-241.meaning: Have you assessed his work? You politely ask a supervisor whether they have evaluated a colleague’s finished work.
work-241.order: Heeft starts the perfect question, followed by polite subject u, object and final beoordeeld.
work-241.forms: Heeft u and hebt u are both standard. Beoordelen is inseparable with participle beoordeeld, without added ge-. Zijn is possessive; werk is the object rather than the subject.
work-241.compare: English assessed emphasizes evaluation, matching beoordeeld rather than a casual glance.

mistake.why: The inseparable be- verb uses participle beoordeeld without added ge-.

work-241.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-241.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-242.meaning: Thank you for your patience while waiting. After a delay at a reception desk, you thank a guest for waiting patiently.
work-242.order: Bedankt begins a conventional thanks expression without a finite verb; the following phrases name the reason and time.
work-242.forms: Bedankt voor is a standard polite expression. Uw is possessive. Geduld is uncountable; het wachten is a nominalised infinitive after tijdens. It is natural standalone thanks, not a finite full clause.
work-242.compare: English while waiting and Dutch tijdens het wachten name the waiting period; Dutch uses an activity noun after a preposition.

mistake.wrong: Bedankt voor u geduld tijdens het wachten.
mistake.right: Bedankt voor uw geduld tijdens het wachten.
mistake.why: Use polite possessive uw before geduld.

work-242.practiceFocus: Short expressions and their intended meaning
work-242.practiceGuide: Some useful expressions are fragments rather than full subject-plus-verb clauses: Hartelijk dank, Graag gedaan. Do not invent V2 inversion for a phrase with no finite verb. Learn what the expression does in the conversation, and compare related full sentences. A polite formula can have several natural English equivalents.

work-243.meaning: Buy the train ticket for him. You ask a colleague to buy a train ticket on behalf of someone who cannot do it themselves.
work-243.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Koop starts the instruction; the object comes before beneficiary voor hem.
work-243.forms: Kopen has stem koop. Voor names the person benefiting from the purchase. Hem is an object form after the preposition. Treinkaart is a compound with de kaart as its head.
work-243.compare: English buy for him and Dutch koop voor hem identify the same beneficiary.

mistake.why: Use an object pronoun after voor.

work-243.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-244.meaning: She has stolen my idea. You object when another person presents your original concept as her own.
work-244.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ze is first and heeft second; mijn idee stands before final gestolen.
work-244.forms: Stelen has irregular participle gestolen and uses hebben. Singular heeft makes ze mean she. Mijn is possessive. Een idee stelen is figurative taking credit for someone else’s idea.
work-244.compare: English has stolen my idea preserves the completed perfect and figurative ownership complaint.

mistake.why: Stelen has irregular participle gestolen.

work-244.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-244.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-245.meaning: He worked very hard. You recall the sustained effort a colleague put into a demanding task.
work-245.order: Hij is first and werkte second; heel modifies manner adverb hard.
work-245.forms: Werken has singular past werkte with -te. Hard describes effort rather than the physical hardness of an object. Heel means very and modifies hard; both are adverbial here.
work-245.compare: English worked very hard and Dutch werkte heel hard have parallel manner structure.

mistake.why: Hard describes the action as an adverb and has no adjective -e.

work-245.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-246.meaning: You looked very tired. You notice that a colleague looked exhausted after a long workday.
work-246.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Je is first and zag second; er and uit surround the appearance description.
work-246.forms: Er ... uitzien describes appearance. Zag is irregular past of zien; uit separates in a main clause. Er belongs to the appearance construction and is not a literal place. Vermoeid is predicative without -e.
work-246.compare: English looked tired describes appearance; Dutch uses zag er ... uit, rather than a literal visual-perception object.

mistake.wrong: Je zag er erg vermoeide uit.
mistake.right: Je zag er erg vermoeid uit.
mistake.why: The appearance adjective is predicative and has no attributive -e.

work-246.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-247.meaning: Take the samples to the laboratory. You ask a colleague to deliver test samples to a laboratory.
work-247.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Breng starts the instruction; the object precedes the destination naar het laboratorium.
work-247.forms: Brengen has stem breng and irregular participle gebracht. Monsters means test samples here, not mythical creatures. Laboratorium is a het-word. Naar marks the destination.
work-247.compare: English take the samples to and Dutch breng de monsters naar specify transport to a destination, avoiding the unexplained to yourself in the source.

mistake.wrong: Breng de monsters naar de laboratorium.
mistake.right: Breng de monsters naar het laboratorium.
mistake.why: Laboratorium takes het.

work-247.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-248.meaning: What's the overall aim of this training course? At the start of a training course, you ask what the course as a whole is intended to achieve.

parts.label: subject
parts.text: het algemene doel van deze opleiding

work-248.order: Wat asks for the aim; is is second and the complete subject phrase follows.
work-248.forms: Doel is a het-word, but definite het requires attributive algemene with -e. Opleiding is a de-word and takes deze. Van specifies the course whose aim is asked about.
work-248.compare: English overall aim and Dutch algemene doel ask about the broader purpose rather than an individual exercise.

mistake.wrong: Wat is de algemene doel van deze opleiding?
mistake.right: Wat is het algemene doel van deze opleiding?
mistake.why: Doel is a singular het-word.

work-248.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-249.meaning: How much time do we have? You ask how much time remains to finish an activity before the next appointment.
work-249.order: Hoeveel tijd is the first question constituent and object; hebben is second and subject we follows.
work-249.forms: Tijd is uncountable in this quantity use. Hoeveel asks for an amount; many countable hours would be hoeveel uur. Plural subject we requires hebben.
work-249.compare: English how much time and Dutch hoeveel tijd form multiword question phrases; Dutch does not use do-support.

mistake.why: Plural we requires hebben.

work-249.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-250.meaning: May I use my laptop? You ask permission to use your laptop during a training session.
work-250.order: Mag starts the permission question; ik and the object follow, and gebruiken is final.
work-250.forms: Mogen expresses permission, whereas kunnen primarily expresses ability or possibility. Mijn is possessive. Gebruiken after mag takes no te. Mag is singular present of mogen.
work-250.compare: English may makes the permission meaning explicit; can is also conversational English, but should not obscure the Dutch modal distinction.

mistake.wrong: Mag ik mijn laptop te gebruiken?
mistake.why: Mogen takes an infinitive without te.

work-250.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-251.meaning: Her computer is offline. A colleague’s computer is disconnected from the network during a work session.
work-251.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Haar computer is the first constituent; is is second and offline describes its connection state.
work-251.forms: Haar is possessive, not an object pronoun here. Computer is singular, requiring is. Offline means not connected to the network; it does not necessarily mean the machine is broken.
work-251.compare: English and Dutch both use offline for the connection state and put it after the copula.

mistake.why: The singular computer requires is.

work-251.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-252.meaning: This worktop is easy to clean. You show a smooth work surface that can be wiped clean with little effort.
work-252.order: Dit werkblad is first and is second; gemakkelijk is followed by the final infinitive phrase schoon te maken.
work-252.forms: Werkblad is a het-word, so use dit. Schoonmaken is separable, with te between schoon and maken. Gemakkelijk is predicative without -e. The worktop is what gets cleaned.
work-252.compare: English easy to clean and Dutch gemakkelijk schoon te maken have similar meaning, but Dutch splits the separable infinitive around te.

mistake.wrong: Dit werkblad is gemakkelijk te schoonmaken.
mistake.right: Dit werkblad is gemakkelijk schoon te maken.
mistake.why: Put te between schoon and maken.

work-252.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-253.meaning: This is our agenda for the training day. You show the planned list of sessions and discussion items for a shared training day.
work-253.order: Independent Dit is first and is second; the following noun phrase identifies the schedule of activities.
work-253.forms: Agenda here means the planned list of items/sessions, not a personal appointment diary. It is a de-word and takes onze. Dit stands independently and need not agree with agenda. Studiedag is a compound ending in de dag.
work-253.compare: English agenda for the training day and Dutch agenda voor de studiedag specify an organised set of sessions.

mistake.wrong: Dit is ons agenda voor de studiedag.
mistake.right: Dit is onze agenda voor de studiedag.
mistake.why: The singular de-word agenda takes onze.

work-253.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-254.meaning: We worked at the office. You recall working together at the office rather than remotely.
work-254.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. We is first and werkten second; op kantoor gives the workplace.
work-254.forms: Werkten is plural simple past of werken, with -ten. Op kantoor is a conventional workplace expression without an article. It does not mean physically standing on top of an office.
work-254.compare: English at the office and Dutch op kantoor use different prepositions/articles in this conventional location phrase.

mistake.why: The plural subject requires werkten.

work-254.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-255.meaning: I understand why you are unsure. You listen to a colleague’s concerns and acknowledge why they hesitate.
work-255.order: Ik is first and begrijp second; the embedded why-clause is its object, with twijfelt final.
work-255.forms: Begrijpen is inseparable because of be-. Waarom introduces an embedded question, not a direct question with inversion. Je before its finite verb requires twijfelt with -t. Twijfelen means doubt or hesitate.
work-255.compare: English understand why and Dutch begrijp waarom introduce the reason understood; Dutch uses verb-final subordinate order.

mistake.why: An embedded question uses subordinate order, not direct-question inversion.

work-255.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-256.meaning: This cycle path is very safe. You describe a protected cycle path separated from road traffic.
work-256.order: Dit fietspad is one phrase in first position and the finite verb is second; erg modifies the predicate adjective veilig, which stays at the end.
work-256.forms: Fietspad is a het-word, so this is dit before the noun. Veilig is predicative without -e. Erg means very as a degree adverb.
work-256.compare: English very safe and Dutch erg veilig describe degree; Dutch chooses dit by noun gender.

mistake.why: The singular het-word fietspad takes dit.

work-256.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-257.meaning: Is this your report of the accident? A receptionist checks which guest wrote a submitted accident report.
work-257.order: Is starts the question; independent dit is subject and the report phrase follows it.
work-257.forms: Uw is polite possessive; u is a personal pronoun. Verslag and ongeval are het-words. Van specifies the event described. Independent dit is not an attributive demonstrative of verslag.
work-257.compare: English your report of the accident and Dutch uw verslag van het ongeval both identify document authorship in context.

mistake.wrong: Is dit u verslag van het ongeval?
mistake.right: Is dit uw verslag van het ongeval?
mistake.why: Use possessive uw before the noun.

work-257.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-258.meaning: He sells his bicycle to them. A colleague sells his bicycle to two interested neighbours.
work-258.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Hij is first and verkoopt second; the sold item precedes recipient aan hen.
work-258.forms: Verkopen is inseparable and takes third-person verkoopt. Hen is the standard stressed plural object form after a preposition; unstressed ze is also possible. Zijn is possessive before fiets.
work-258.compare: English to them and Dutch aan hen identify the buyers; Dutch does not use possessive hun here.

mistake.wrong: Hij verkoopt zijn fiets aan zij.
mistake.right: Hij verkoopt zijn fiets aan hen.
mistake.why: Use a plural object form after the preposition.

work-258.practiceFocus: Learn the preposition with its expression
work-258.practiceGuide: English at/to/on does not determine a single Dutch preposition. Learn the combination: verkopen aan a buyer; luisteren naar; houden van; wachten op. Op een feest names an event, in de zaal a physical space. Naar often introduces a destination but also belongs to non-motion expressions such as luisteren naar. Te before an infinitive is not a recipient preposition.

work-259.meaning: What's your plan for the move? You ask how a colleague intends to organise moving to a new home.
work-259.order: Wat is the question word in first position and the finite verb is second; the phrase after it is the subject, so a question word does not change the verb-second rule.
work-259.forms: Je is possessive before plan, not the subject of is. Plan is a het-word. Voor specifies the move the plan concerns. Verhuizing is a de-word.
work-259.compare: English plan for the move and Dutch plan voor de verhuizing have parallel noun-complement meaning.

mistake.wrong: Wat zijn je plan voor de verhuizing?
mistake.right: Wat is je plan voor de verhuizing?
mistake.why: The head noun plan is singular.

work-259.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-260.meaning: Could you send me the report? You politely ask a colleague to send you a finished report for review.
work-260.order: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, so no constituent comes before it. Kunt starts the request; u, recipient mij and the object come before final sturen.
work-260.forms: Kunt u and kan u are both standard. Mij is a stressed recipient object, with me possible unstressed. Sturen after a modal is an infinitive without te. Rapport is a het-word.
work-260.compare: English could politely requests action; Dutch present kunt u can convey that politeness. Both can put recipient before the direct object.

mistake.wrong: Kunt u ik het rapport sturen?
mistake.right: Kunt u mij het rapport sturen?
mistake.why: The recipient requires object mij or me.

work-260.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-261.meaning: What's their biggest obstacle to finding accommodation? You discuss why a group is having difficulty finding suitable accommodation.

parts.label: subject
parts.text: hun grootste obstakel bij het vinden van huisvesting

work-261.order: Wat is first and is second; the whole obstacle phrase is subject.
work-261.forms: Hun is possessive. Grootste is an attributive superlative. Het vinden is a nominalised infinitive after bij; van huisvesting names what is being found. Huisvesting is uncountable accommodation.
work-261.compare: English obstacle to finding and Dutch obstakel bij het vinden express difficulty associated with the search; Dutch uses a nominalised infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Wat zijn hun grootste obstakel bij het vinden van huisvesting?
mistake.right: Wat is hun grootste obstakel bij het vinden van huisvesting?
mistake.why: Agreement follows singular obstakel.

work-261.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-262.meaning: May I borrow your pen to sign this form? At a reception desk, you ask to borrow a pen so you can sign a form.
work-262.order: Mag starts the permission question, then ik, je pen and lenen. The following purpose phrase ends with te ondertekenen.
work-262.forms: Mogen expresses permission. Je is possessive before pen. Lenen means borrow from the owner in this context. Ondertekenen is inseparable, so te goes before the whole infinitive. Formulier is a het-word and takes dit.
work-262.compare: English may I borrow to sign and Dutch mag ik lenen om ... te ondertekenen express permission with a purpose.

mistake.wrong: Mag ik je pen te lenen om dit formulier te ondertekenen?
mistake.right: Mag ik je pen lenen om dit formulier te ondertekenen?
mistake.why: Lenen after mag has no te; the separate purpose phrase does use te.

work-262.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-263.meaning: I'm too late for the last tram. You reach a tram stop after the last tram has already left.
work-263.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and ben second; te laat is followed by the missed event with voor.
work-263.forms: Te before laat is a degree word, not an infinitive marker. Tram is a de-word; laatste is attributive with -e. Ben is the ik form of zijn.
work-263.compare: English too late for the last tram and Dutch te laat voor de laatste tram express missing the available departure.

mistake.wrong: Ik is te laat voor de laatste tram.
mistake.right: Ik ben te laat voor de laatste tram.
mistake.why: The first-person singular form of zijn is ben.

work-263.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-264.meaning: We have to encourage innovation. Your team discusses supporting new ideas and experiments in its work.
work-264.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and moeten second; innovatie precedes final stimuleren.
work-264.forms: Moeten expresses necessity. Innovatie is an abstract uncountable noun without an article here. Stimuleren is an infinitive without te after moeten.
work-264.compare: English have to encourage preserves necessity; should encourage would weaken the modal meaning.

mistake.why: Moeten takes an infinitive without te.

work-264.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-265.meaning: What's their secret weapon for baking bread? You ask skilled bakers what special technique gives their bread its distinctive quality.

parts.label: subject
parts.text: hun geheime wapen bij het bakken van brood

work-265.order: Wat is first and is second; the full figurative weapon phrase is subject.
work-265.forms: Geheime wapen is figurative for a special strength or technique. Hun is possessive. Het bakken is a nominalised infinitive after bij; van brood names what is baked. No physical weapon is meant.
work-265.compare: English secret weapon can also be figurative; baking bread is rendered with Dutch het bakken van brood.

mistake.wrong: Wat is hun geheime wapens bij het bakken van brood?
mistake.right: Wat is hun geheime wapen bij het bakken van brood?
mistake.why: The singular question uses singular wapen; plural would require Wat zijn hun geheime wapens.

work-265.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-266.meaning: I'm sorry, the coffee machine is broken. You apologise to a visitor because the coffee machine is unavailable due to a fault.
work-266.order: Two short main clauses are linked by a comma in this spoken-style apology. Each has its own subject and finite verb.
work-266.forms: Het spijt me is an idiomatic apology; me is the experiencer object. Koffieautomaat is a de-word. Kapot is predicative without -e. The machine being broken does not itself say who caused the damage.
work-266.compare: English sorry followed by a problem statement and Dutch het spijt me followed by a second clause express the same apology.

mistake.wrong: Het spijt ik, de koffieautomaat is kapot.
mistake.right: Het spijt me, de koffieautomaat is kapot.
mistake.why: The regret expression requires object me.

work-266.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-267.meaning: What's the next number in this sequence? During an exercise, you ask a learner to identify the next number in a sequence.

parts.label: subject
parts.text: het volgende getal in deze reeks

work-267.order: Wat is first and is second; the next-number phrase follows as subject.
work-267.forms: Getal is a het-word; definite het takes attributive volgende. Reeks is a de-word and takes deze. The noun makes the omitted next thing explicit in a number-pattern situation.
work-267.compare: English next number in the sequence and Dutch volgende getal in deze reeks have parallel ordering inside the noun phrase.

mistake.wrong: Wat is de volgende getal in deze reeks?
mistake.right: Wat is het volgende getal in deze reeks?
mistake.why: Getal is a singular het-word.

work-267.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-268.meaning: I'll handle the logistics. You volunteer to organise transport, delivery and materials for a shared activity.
work-268.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and regel second; de logistiek is the direct object.
work-268.forms: Regelen has the ik form regel. Logistiek names practical organisation of movement and supplies and takes de. The present expresses a commitment in context, not necessarily an action already complete.
work-268.compare: English will handle corresponds naturally to the Dutch present commitment ik regel.

mistake.why: The ik form has no third-person -t.

work-268.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-269.meaning: What's the next step in applying for a permit? At an administrative desk, you ask what to do next in the permit application process.

parts.label: subject
parts.text: de volgende stap bij het aanvragen van een vergunning

work-269.order: Wat is first and is second; the full next-step phrase is subject.
work-269.forms: Stap is a de-word. Het aanvragen is a nominalised infinitive after bij; van een vergunning specifies what is requested. Aanvragen is separable in a finite clause, but stays whole in this activity noun.
work-269.compare: English applying for a permit uses for; Dutch noun construction uses het aanvragen van een vergunning.

mistake.wrong: Wat zijn de volgende stap bij het aanvragen van een vergunning?
mistake.right: Wat is de volgende stap bij het aanvragen van een vergunning?
mistake.why: The head noun stap is singular.

work-269.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-270.meaning: We're looking forward to the start of the language course. You and fellow learners eagerly await a language course that has not begun yet.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: naar de start van de taalcursus

work-270.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. We is first and kijken second; uit is separated and the anticipated event follows naar.
work-270.forms: Uitkijken naar means look forward to. This noun reference uses naar de start, unlike pronominal ernaar uitkijken. Taalcursus is a de-compound; van specifies what starts. The event is still in the future.
work-270.compare: English looking forward to and Dutch kijken uit naar express anticipation, not watching an event in progress.

mistake.wrong: We uitkijken naar de start van de taalcursus.
mistake.right: We kijken uit naar de start van de taalcursus.
mistake.why: Separate uitkijken in this finite main clause.

work-270.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-271.meaning: I'm here to repair the lift. A technician arrives at a building and explains the reason for the visit.
work-271.order: Ik is first and ben second; the purpose phrase follows hier and ends with te repareren.
work-271.forms: Om ... te expresses purpose. Lift is a de-word; it is the object within the infinitive phrase. Repareren is not separable, so te stands before the whole verb.
work-271.compare: English here to repair and Dutch hier om ... te repareren explain the visit, not a promise that the repair is already complete.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben hier om de lift repareren.
mistake.right: Ik ben hier om de lift te repareren.
mistake.why: The om-purpose construction requires te.

work-271.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-272.meaning: This form can be filled in quickly. You show a short form that requires only a few entries to complete.
work-272.order: Dit formulier is first and is second. Snel describes completing speed; in te vullen is the final infinitive phrase.
work-272.forms: Formulier is a het-word and takes dit. Invullen is separable, with te between in and vullen. The construction presents the form as something that can be completed quickly; snel is adverbial here.
work-272.compare: English can be filled in quickly captures the passive-like interpretation of the Dutch adjective/adverb plus te-infinitive construction.

mistake.wrong: Dit formulier is snel te invullen.
mistake.right: Dit formulier is snel in te vullen.
mistake.why: Put te between the separable particle in and vullen.

work-272.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-273.meaning: They'll be too late for registration. You expect two applicants to arrive after registration has finished.
work-273.order: Ze is first and zullen second; te laat precedes infinitive zijn, followed by the registration phrase.
work-273.forms: Zullen agrees with plural ze. Zijn after the auxiliary is an infinitive. Te is a degree word before laat, not an infinitive marker. The sentence predicts future lateness.
work-273.compare: English will be too late and Dutch zullen te laat zijn use future prediction, distinct from a present statement of already being late.

mistake.wrong: Ze zullen te laat is voor de inschrijving.
mistake.right: Ze zullen te laat zijn voor de inschrijving.
mistake.why: After zullen use infinitive zijn.

work-273.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-274.meaning: I wasn't at the office when the delivery arrived. You explain why you did not receive a delivery personally at the office.
work-274.order: Ik is first and was second. The toen-clause follows the location and ends with its finite verb aankwam.
work-274.forms: Toen refers to a particular past moment. Aankomen is separable, but finite aankwam stays whole in this subordinate clause. Op kantoor is a conventional article-free location expression.
work-274.compare: English when the delivery arrived and Dutch toen de levering aankwam specify the past occasion; Dutch puts the subordinate verb at the end.

mistake.wrong: Ik was niet op kantoor toen de levering kwam aan.
mistake.right: Ik was niet op kantoor toen de levering aankwam.
mistake.why: The separable finite verb stays together at the subordinate clause end.

work-274.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.

work-275.meaning: It's better to wait for confirmation. You compare acting immediately with waiting until an arrangement has been confirmed.

parts.label: infinitive (te phrase)
parts.text: om op de bevestiging te wachten

work-275.order: Het is first and is second; beter evaluates the action named by the following infinitive phrase.
work-275.forms: Beter is comparative better, not superlative best. Het anticipates the action clause. Wachten op is fixed; om ... te names the evaluated action here rather than the purpose of a visit. Bevestiging is a de-word.
work-275.compare: Dutch beter means English better; English best would express a superlative instead of this comparative.

mistake.wrong: Het is betert om op de bevestiging te wachten.
mistake.right: Het is beter om op de bevestiging te wachten.
mistake.why: Beter is the irregular comparative adjective, without a verb -t ending.

work-275.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-276.meaning: Please explain the content of this letter to me. You ask a colleague to explain a letter whose content you do not understand.
work-276.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Leg begins the instruction and uit ends it; recipient, politeness word and object stand between them.
work-276.forms: Uitleggen is separable. Inhoud is a de-word; deze agrees with de brief. Me is a recipient object. Alsjeblieft is the informal politeness word, compared with formal alstublieft.
work-276.compare: English explain the content to me and Dutch leg me de inhoud uit use different recipient construction and a separated verb.

mistake.wrong: Leg me alsjeblieft de inhoud van deze brief uitleg.
mistake.right: Leg me alsjeblieft de inhoud van deze brief uit.
mistake.why: The imperative uses leg with final particle uit, not a second verb form.

work-276.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-277.meaning: I'm planning to continue living in Belgium. You explain that you intend to keep living in Belgium rather than move abroad.
work-277.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ik is first and ben second. The intended activity follows van plan and ends with te blijven wonen.
work-277.forms: Van plan zijn takes a te-infinitive, optionally introduced by om. Blijven wonen expresses continued residence; wonen follows blijven without another te. België uses a diaeresis. This is intention, not seeking an opportunity.
work-277.compare: English planning to continue living preserves van plan and blijven; source looking to stay could obscure the intention.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben van plan in België te blijven te wonen.
mistake.right: Ik ben van plan in België te blijven wonen.
mistake.why: The continuation verb blijven takes wonen without a second te.

work-277.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-278.meaning: Let's brainstorm ideas for a neighbourhood party. Neighbours propose generating ideas together for a community gathering.
work-278.order: A suggestion with Laten we starts with the verb laten; the other verb (the infinitive) normally occurs toward the end. Laten we introduces the shared proposal; the topic over ideas stands before final brainstormen.
work-278.forms: Brainstormen is commonly used with over for the topic. Ideeën is plural with a diaeresis. Buurtfeest is a compound ending in het feest, indefinite een here. The proposal infinitive has no te.
work-278.compare: English brainstorm ideas can take a direct object; this Dutch version uses an over-topic phrase instead of copying English transitivity.

mistake.wrong: Laten we over ideeën voor een buurtfeest brainstormt.
mistake.right: Laten we over ideeën voor een buurtfeest brainstormen.
mistake.why: After Laten we use the infinitive.

work-278.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-279.meaning: It's important to stay calm during a conflict. A colleague stresses remaining calm when discussing a disagreement.

parts.label: infinitive (te phrase)
parts.text: om kalm te blijven tijdens een conflict

work-279.order: Het is first and is second; belangrijk evaluates the following action/state infinitive phrase.
work-279.forms: Het anticipates the clause describing what is important. Kalm is predicative after blijven and has no -e. Om ... te names the evaluated action; tijdens introduces the time circumstance.
work-279.compare: English stay calm and Dutch kalm blijven express continuing a state, rather than remaining at a location.

mistake.wrong: Het is belangrijk om kalme te blijven tijdens een conflict.
mistake.right: Het is belangrijk om kalm te blijven tijdens een conflict.
mistake.why: Kalm is predicative and does not take attributive -e.

work-279.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-280.meaning: This parking meter is easy to use. You show a visitor how straightforward the parking payment machine is to operate.
work-280.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Deze parkeerautomaat is first and is second; gemakkelijk is followed by te gebruiken.
work-280.forms: Parkeerautomaat is a de-word and takes deze. Gemakkelijk is predicative without -e. The machine is the thing used in the te-infinitive construction, not the person doing the using.
work-280.compare: English easy to use and Dutch gemakkelijk te gebruiken describe usability; no added subject for the user is required.

mistake.wrong: Dit parkeerautomaat is gemakkelijk te gebruiken.
mistake.right: Deze parkeerautomaat is gemakkelijk te gebruiken.
mistake.why: The singular de-word parkeerautomaat takes deze.

work-280.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-281.meaning: We have to align our goals with each other. Two colleagues lay their separate plans side by side and agree on shared goals.
work-281.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and moeten second; the object and op elkaar come before final afstemmen.
work-281.forms: Afstemmen op means to coordinate with. Elkaar is reciprocal: the goals are aligned with each other. Onze agrees with plural doelen. After moeten the separable infinitive stays whole, without te.
work-281.compare: English align with and Dutch afstemmen op use different prepositions for the same coordination.

mistake.wrong: We moeten onze doelen op elkaar af te stemmen.
mistake.right: We moeten onze doelen op elkaar afstemmen.
mistake.why: Moeten takes an infinitive without te.

work-281.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-282.meaning: He completed his training without financial support. A colleague proudly holds his training certificate after paying for the course himself.
work-282.order: Hij is first and past-tense voltooide second; the object is followed by the without phrase.
work-282.forms: Voltooien has regular past voltooide. Zijn is possessive, not a finite verb. Financiële has -e before the de-word steun. Steun is uncountable here. Zonder introduces what was absent.
work-282.compare: English completed and Dutch voltooide describe a finished past achievement. Training is opleiding here.

mistake.wrong: Hij voltooid zijn opleiding zonder financiële steun.
mistake.right: Hij voltooide zijn opleiding zonder financiële steun.
mistake.why: A past main clause needs finite voltooide, not the participle voltooid.

work-282.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-283.meaning: I'm afraid of failure. Before attempting an important new project, you admit your fear to a supportive colleague.
work-283.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and ben second; bang takes its fear object with voor.
work-283.forms: Bang voor is a fixed adjective-preposition combination. Bang is predicative without -e. Abstract mislukking can refer to failure generally without an article. A particular failed attempt would be een mislukking.
work-283.compare: English afraid of uses of; Dutch bang voor uses voor, not van.

mistake.why: The first-person singular of zijn is ben.

work-283.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-284.meaning: This is my greatest challenge during the internship. An intern looks at a demanding assembly task while explaining why it is the hardest part of the placement.
work-284.order: Dit is first and is second; the challenge phrase is followed by the internship period.
work-284.forms: Grootste is the superlative of groot, used with -e before uitdaging. Mijn is possessive. Stage means internship or work placement, not an English performance stage. Tijdens takes a noun phrase.
work-284.compare: English greatest challenge and Dutch grootste uitdaging both compare this challenge with the others in the internship.

mistake.wrong: Dit is mijn grootst uitdaging tijdens de stage.
mistake.right: Dit is mijn grootste uitdaging tijdens de stage.
mistake.why: The attributive superlative before uitdaging takes -e.

work-284.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-285.meaning: We have to turn on the heating. Two people in coats stand beside a cold radiator and reach for its control.
work-285.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and moeten second; the object comes before final aanzetten.
work-285.forms: Aanzetten is separable: We zetten de verwarming aan. After moeten it remains one infinitive without te. Verwarming is a de-word and here means the heating system.
work-285.compare: Dutch names the required action turn on, rather than only the desired state of the heating.

mistake.wrong: We moeten de verwarming aan te zetten.
mistake.why: No te follows modal moeten.

work-285.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-286.meaning: I'm here to stay. A new team member settles personal belongings on a desk and reassures a welcoming colleague of a lasting commitment.
work-286.order: Ik is first and ben second; hier is followed by the om te phrase.
work-286.forms: Om te blijven expresses intention. Blijven is an infinitive after te. The idiom signals a lasting presence or commitment, rather than only remaining for a few minutes. Hier points to the current workplace.
work-286.compare: English here to stay has the same idiomatic permanent-commitment meaning.

mistake.right: Ik ben hier om te blijven.
mistake.why: This om construction needs te before blijven.

work-286.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-287.meaning: We're looking forward to the reply to our job application. Two job applicants wait hopefully for a reply while looking at their submitted application materials.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: naar het antwoord op onze sollicitatie

work-287.order: We is first and kijken second. The particle uit precedes the naar phrase naming the anticipated reply.
work-287.forms: Uitkijken naar means to look forward to. Antwoord op introduces what the reply concerns. Onze agrees with the de-word sollicitatie. This present sentence expresses anticipation, not receipt of the answer.
work-287.compare: English reply to a job application and Dutch antwoord op een sollicitatie use different prepositions.

mistake.wrong: We kijken naar uit het antwoord.
mistake.right: We kijken uit naar het antwoord.
mistake.why: In this construction uit comes before naar plus its noun phrase.

work-287.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-288.meaning: We'll try to repair the leak in the roof. Two people examine a leaking roof above a bucket and prepare tools to attempt the repair.
work-288.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Zullen is finite in second position, followed by proberen and its complement containing object plus te repareren.
work-288.forms: Zullen takes proberen without te; proberen takes te repareren. Lek and dak are het-words. The promise concerns an attempt; success is not guaranteed. In het dak specifies the location of the leak.
work-288.compare: English will try to repair and Dutch zullen proberen te repareren both contain a future auxiliary and two action verbs.

mistake.wrong: We zullen te proberen het lek te repareren.
mistake.right: We zullen proberen het lek te repareren.
mistake.why: Te belongs before repareren, not directly after zullen.

work-288.practiceFocus: Proberen: try a thing or try to act
work-288.practiceGuide: Proberen means try. Ik probeer is present; ik probeerde is singular simple past; wij probeerden is plural past; ik heb geprobeerd uses the participle with hebben. The regular participle is ge + probeer + d. A thing can be tried directly; trying to do something uses proberen + te + infinitive. After zal the verb becomes proberen: ik zal proberen te bellen. Trying on clothes usually uses passen; tasting food can use proeven.

work-289.meaning: Please update your status. An administrator politely asks a colleague at a shared project desk to update a task-status indicator.
work-289.order: The formal request begins with fixed Gelieve; uw status precedes the separable te-infinitive bij te werken.
work-289.forms: Gelieve in this fixed request formula is an old subjunctive form, with understood subject u; it is not the ordinary imperative stem. Uw is formal possessive. Bijwerken is separable, so te goes between bij and werken. This wording is formal and mainly written.
work-289.compare: English please plus an imperative is often rendered by ordinary Dutch requests; this Dutch formula has a different grammatical origin.

mistake.right: Gelieve uw status bij te werken.
mistake.why: Te goes inside the separable infinitive.

work-289.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-290.meaning: Ask him for directions to the station. You direct a visitor with a travel bag to ask a nearby local person for the way to the station.
work-290.order: The imperative Vraag starts the instruction. The short recipient hem comes before the full object phrase.
work-290.forms: Iemand de weg vragen means to ask someone for directions. Hem is an object pronoun. Weg is a de-word; station is a het-word. Naar introduces the destination.
work-290.compare: English ask him for directions uses for; Dutch asks iemand de weg without an equivalent voor.

mistake.wrong: Vraag hij de weg naar het station.
mistake.right: Vraag hem de weg naar het station.
mistake.why: The recipient needs object hem, not subject hij.

work-290.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-291.meaning: What are your expectations? A trainer invites a new participant to explain what they hope to gain from a course.
work-291.order: Wat is first and zijn second; plural uw verwachtingen is the subject.
work-291.forms: Verwachtingen is plural, requiring zijn. Uw is formal possessive, not subject u. Wat asks for the content of the expectations. A singular question would be Wat is uw verwachting?
work-291.compare: English expectations and Dutch verwachtingen are plural in this question; formal uw does not change the noun agreement.

mistake.why: Plural verwachtingen requires zijn.

work-291.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-292.meaning: She's ready to explain her proposal. A prepared presenter waits beside her proposal materials, ready to explain them to a small group.

parts.label: infinitive (te phrase)
parts.text: om haar voorstel toe te lichten

work-292.order: Zij is first and is second; klaar is followed by an om phrase with object and final toe te lichten.
work-292.forms: Klaar om expresses readiness for an action. Toelichten is separable, so its te-infinitive is toe te lichten. Haar is possessive with voorstel. Ready does not mean that the explanation has already begun.
work-292.compare: English ready to explain and Dutch klaar om toe te lichten describe readiness rather than completion.

mistake.wrong: Zij is klaar om haar voorstel te toelichten.
mistake.right: Zij is klaar om haar voorstel toe te lichten.
mistake.why: Te separates toe and lichten.

work-292.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-293.meaning: This requires immediate attention. A colleague points urgently to water leaking beside office equipment and asks the team to address it at once.
work-293.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Dit is first and vereist second; the required attention is the object.
work-293.forms: Vereisen means to require. Vereist is the third-person present. Aandacht is an abstract de-word; attributive onmiddellijke takes -e even without an article in this phrase.
work-293.compare: English requires immediate attention corresponds to Dutch vereist onmiddellijke aandacht.

mistake.why: Singular dit takes finite vereist.

work-293.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-294.meaning: Keep your promises. A colleague reminds you of an agreed commitment while pointing to a task you promised to finish.
work-294.order: The imperative Kom begins the instruction and na closes the separable verb around its object.
work-294.forms: Nakomen means to fulfil or honour a promise. Je before beloften is possessive, not the subject of a question. Both beloften and beloftes are accepted plurals. The participle is nagekomen.
work-294.compare: English keep promises and Dutch beloften nakomen use different literal verbs for the same commitment.

mistake.why: The separable particle of nakomen is na.

work-294.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-295.meaning: You haven't made a change. You compare the latest draft with the previous version and point out that no alteration has been made.
work-295.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Je is first and hebt second; geen verandering stands inside the perfect-tense bracket before aangebracht.
