work-295.forms: Een verandering aanbrengen means to make a change. Geen negates an indefinite noun phrase. Aanbrengen has participle aangebracht: separable aan plus ge plus irregular bracht. Hebben forms the perfect here.
work-295.compare: English have not made a change and Dutch hebt geen verandering aangebracht report an unchanged result.

mistake.why: An indefinite noun phrase is negated with geen.

work-295.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-295.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-296.meaning: What's my next step after this job interview? After a job interview, you ask the interviewer what action you should take next.
work-296.order: Wat is first and is second; the subject is followed by the after-interview phrase.
work-296.forms: Volgende takes -e before de stap. Sollicitatiegesprek is a het-word and takes dit. Mijn is possessive. Stap is figurative for an action in a process.
work-296.compare: English next step and Dutch volgende stap share the figurative action meaning.

mistake.why: The adjective before de-word stap takes -e.

work-296.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-297.meaning: I'm doing my best. You concentrate on a difficult practical task and reassure a colleague that you are making your strongest effort.
work-297.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and doe second; mijn best completes the fixed expression.
work-297.forms: Je best doen means to make your best effort. Doe is the ik form of doen. Best stays without -e in this expression. The present can describe current effort or a commitment, depending on context.
work-297.compare: English do my best uses the same idiomatic pattern; this scenario chooses current effort rather than a future promise.

mistake.why: The fixed expression is mijn best doen.

work-297.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-298.meaning: They weren't in the room during the conversation. You explain that two colleagues could not have heard a private conversation because their seats in the room were empty.
work-298.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Plural Ze is first and waren second; niet negates their being in the room during the conversation.
work-298.forms: Waren is plural past of zijn. Kamer is a de-word and gesprek a het-word. Tijdens takes a noun phrase. Niet negates the location claim rather than an indefinite object.
work-298.compare: English were not in the room and Dutch waren niet in de kamer describe past absence.

mistake.wrong: Ze was niet in de kamer.
mistake.right: Ze waren niet in de kamer.
mistake.why: They requires plural waren.

work-298.practiceFocus: Niet and geen with the right scope
work-298.practiceGuide: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen tijd, geen koffie. Niet can negate a predicate, action or more specific constituent: niet moe, de vraag niet begrijpen. Its location depends on what is negated, not on an absolute rule 'always at the end'. With a second verb the final verb bracket stays after niet. Dutch niet hoeven te means not having to; niet mogen means not being allowed to.

work-299.meaning: He was happy with the result. A colleague smiles proudly at the finished piece of furniture he has made.
work-299.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Hij is first and was second; blij takes the reason for satisfaction with met.
work-299.forms: Was is singular past of zijn. Blij met expresses satisfaction with a result; blij is predicative without -e. Resultaat is a het-word.
work-299.compare: English happy with and Dutch blij met describe the same past satisfaction.

mistake.wrong: Hij waren blij met het resultaat.
mistake.right: Hij was blij met het resultaat.
mistake.why: Singular hij takes was.

work-299.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-300.meaning: Bring the borrowed tools back to me. A person who lent tools asks a colleague to return the tool case after the repair.
work-300.order: Breng starts the instruction; short recipient me precedes the full object, and terug closes the verb.
work-300.forms: Terugbrengen is separable. Me is an unstressed object pronoun. Gereedschap is an uncountable het-word for tools collectively. Geleende is an attributive participle with -e after definite het.
work-300.compare: English bring back and Dutch terugbrengen both express returning an item to its lender.

mistake.wrong: Breng ik het geleende gereedschap terug.
mistake.right: Breng me het geleende gereedschap terug.
mistake.why: The receiver needs object me in this instruction.

work-300.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-301.meaning: What's the trick to untying this knot? You hold a knotted cord and ask a skilled colleague how to loosen it.

parts.label: subject
parts.text: de truc om deze knoop los te maken

work-301.order: Wat is first and is second; the subject phrase includes an om te explanation of the trick.
work-301.forms: Truc means a clever method here, not a hidden disadvantage. Knoop is a de-word and takes deze; it means knot in this context. Losmaken is separable: los te maken. The object precedes that infinitive.
work-301.compare: English untie this knot is expressed by Dutch deze knoop losmaken; trick means a useful technique.

mistake.wrong: Wat is de truc om deze knoop te losmaken?
mistake.right: Wat is de truc om deze knoop los te maken?
mistake.why: Te belongs between los and maken.

work-301.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-302.meaning: It's time to call the customers back. You set aside other work and reach for the phone to return waiting customers’ calls.

parts.label: infinitive (te phrase)
parts.text: om de klanten terug te bellen

work-302.order: Het is first and is second; tijd is followed by an om phrase with the customers before terug te bellen.
work-302.forms: Het is tijd om introduces an action that should now begin. Terugbellen is separable and takes te between terug and bellen. Klanten is plural of klant. Het is a dummy subject, not a particular object.
work-302.compare: English it is time to call back and Dutch het is tijd om terug te bellen have corresponding dummy subjects.

mistake.wrong: Het is tijd om de klanten te terugbellen.
mistake.right: Het is tijd om de klanten terug te bellen.
mistake.why: Te goes inside the separable infinitive.

work-302.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-303.meaning: He's used to heavy lifting. An experienced warehouse worker lifts a bulky crate with a practised stance while a colleague watches.
work-303.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Hij is first and is second; gewend takes the activity with aan.
work-303.forms: Gewend aan describes familiarity. Tillen is an infinitive used to name an activity after aan. Zwaar modifies the lifting as an adverb, not an adjective before a noun. This is a present state, not a past habit.
work-303.compare: English is used to heavy lifting differs from used to lift: only the first expresses current familiarity.

mistake.wrong: Hij is gewend voor zwaar tillen.
mistake.right: Hij is gewend aan zwaar tillen.
mistake.why: Gewend uses fixed preposition aan.

work-303.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-303.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-304.meaning: They're here for the guided tour. A small group of visitors has arrived at a museum reception to meet their guide.
work-304.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ze is first and plural zijn second; hier gives location and voor names the reason for being there.
work-304.forms: Plural zijn makes ze mean they. Rondleiding is a de-word and means a guided tour. Voor introduces a noun purpose phrase; it is not the om te construction used before an infinitive.
work-304.compare: English here for the guided tour and Dutch hier voor de rondleiding both describe arrived visitors and their purpose.

mistake.wrong: Ze is hier voor de rondleiding.
mistake.right: Ze zijn hier voor de rondleiding.
mistake.why: They requires zijn.

work-304.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-305.meaning: I'm thinking about starting a business. You sketch a possible small-business idea at home while discussing whether to start it.
work-305.order: Ik is first and denk second; erover anticipates the om te phrase explaining what is being considered.
work-305.forms: Erover refers to the contemplated action, not a place. Denken over is followed here by om plus object and te starten. Bedrijf is a het-word, but indefinite een does not reveal gender. Thinking about it is not a firm decision.
work-305.compare: English thinking about starting uses an -ing form; Dutch can use erover om ... te starten.

mistake.wrong: Ik denk erover om een bedrijf starten.
mistake.right: Ik denk erover om een bedrijf te starten.
mistake.why: The om construction needs te.

work-305.practiceGuide: Some verbs/expressions introduce te + infinitive: proberen te slapen, klaar zijn om te gaan. Om ... te often introduces purpose or an infinitive clause, not a recipient. With a separable verb, te occurs between prefix and verb: af te maken, deel te nemen. A preceding modal does not erase the te required by proberen: Ik zal proberen te bellen.

work-306.meaning: I bought a dictionary for you. You present a newly purchased dictionary to a friend who is learning Dutch.
work-306.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ik is first and heb second; the object and beneficiary are inside the perfect bracket before gekocht.
work-306.forms: Kopen has irregular participle gekocht and takes hebben in this perfect. Voor je names the person benefiting. Woordenboek is a compound ending in het boek. Je is an object pronoun after voor.
work-306.compare: English bought can correspond to Dutch heb gekocht when reporting a completed purchase with a present result.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb een woordenboek voor jij gekocht.
mistake.right: Ik heb een woordenboek voor je gekocht.
mistake.why: A preposition takes an object pronoun, not subject jij.

work-306.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-306.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-307.meaning: We're over our budget. Two event organisers compare their spending with the funds available and discover they have exceeded their budget.
work-307.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. We is first and zitten second; boven ons budget expresses the financial position.
work-307.forms: Zitten describes being in a situation here, not necessarily physical sitting. Boven means above or beyond the permitted amount. Budget is a het-word, so the possessive is ons, not onze.
work-307.compare: English over budget and Dutch boven ons budget express spending beyond the available amount.

mistake.why: Singular het-word budget takes ons.

work-307.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-308.meaning: The water level is rising. You watch water rise against a riverbank and point out the increasing level to a companion.
work-308.order: The full subject Het waterpeil is one phrase in first position, so the finite verb stijgt is second; there is nothing after it.
work-308.forms: Waterpeil is a compound het-word for water level. Stijgt is the third-person singular present of stijgen. The present can describe a change happening now; Dutch does not require a progressive auxiliary.
work-308.compare: English is rising uses the progressive; Dutch stijgt alone can describe the same ongoing change.

mistake.why: The singular subject needs finite stijgt.

work-308.practiceGuide: The finite verb changes with the subject: ik werk, hij werkt, wij werken. In an ordinary statement it follows the subject; a complete time/place phrase can occupy first position instead. Dutch simple present can also describe what is happening now; English often uses an -ing form. Do not put is before an unrelated infinitive.

work-309.meaning: That's enough paint for this wall. While painting a room, you show that the remaining paint in the tin will cover the wall.
work-309.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Dat is first and is second; genoeg precedes the uncountable material and voor names its use.
work-309.forms: Genoeg is a quantity word before verf. Verf is uncountable here, with no indefinite article. Muur is a de-word and takes deze. Dat can refer to the amount of paint just shown.
work-309.compare: English enough paint for this wall and Dutch genoeg verf voor deze muur describe sufficient material.

mistake.wrong: Dat is genoeg verf voor dit muur.
mistake.right: Dat is genoeg verf voor deze muur.
mistake.why: Muur is a de-word and takes deze.

work-309.practiceGuide: Zijn describes a state; worden describes becoming/changing: het is koud versus het wordt koud. Use one finite verb for the main clause, not is wordt. The predicate adjective normally stays uninflected: het huis is mooi. A noun complement keeps its own article/possessive, and the finite verb agrees with its subject (de kamers zijn).

work-310.meaning: We stayed at the hotel during the conference. Two conference participants recall their stay beside hotel luggage and conference folders.
work-310.order: We is first and plural past verbleven second; the conference period precedes the hotel location here.
work-310.forms: Verblijven has past singular verbleef and plural verbleven. It means to stay temporarily, not to live permanently. Hotel is a het-word. Tijdens is a preposition before a noun, not a conjunction before a clause.
work-310.compare: English stay at a hotel commonly corresponds to Dutch verblijven in een hotel.

mistake.why: Plural we requires verbleven.

work-310.practiceGuide: The simple past places an action/state in a past situation. Regular verbs use -de/-te in the singular and -den/-ten in the plural; irregular forms must be learned. Compare ik probeerde and wij probeerden. The finite past verb still follows main-clause V2, or comes first in a yes/no question. A past-time expression does not require one particular past tense in every context.

work-311.meaning: You didn't leave a message on my voicemail. After a missed call, you explain to the caller that there was no voicemail message to tell you what they needed.
work-311.order: Je is first and hebt second; the negated message and voicemail phrase precede final achtergelaten.
work-311.forms: Achterlaten is separable; its participle is achtergelaten with ge between achter and laten. Geen negates an indefinite message. Mijn is possessive. Op mijn voicemail specifies where the message would have been left.
work-311.compare: English did not leave a message can correspond to Dutch hebt geen bericht achtergelaten in a completed-call context.

mistake.why: The perfect needs a participle, not an infinitive.

work-311.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-311.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-312.meaning: Show them the new design. You ask a designer to show a small group the newly finished design drawing.
work-312.order: An instruction starts with the verb. Laat starts the instruction; short recipient ze comes before the full design object, with zien at the end.
work-312.forms: Laten zien means to show. Zien is a bare infinitive, without te. Ze is an unstressed object pronoun meaning them here. Ontwerp is a het-word; definite het takes attributive nieuwe with -e.
work-312.compare: English show is one verb; Dutch often uses the two-verb expression laten zien.

mistake.wrong: Laat ze het nieuwe ontwerp te zien.
mistake.right: Laat ze het nieuwe ontwerp zien.
mistake.why: Laten takes zien without te.

work-312.practiceGuide: A normal imperative uses the verb's stem without a spoken subject: Verkoop de printer. Je in Verkoop je auto means YOUR, not YOU. A separable prefix normally goes later: Ruim je kamer op. Pronouns naming recipients occur early (Geef het me); aan can explicitly identify the recipient/buyer. A command is not an ordinary subject-first statement.

work-313.meaning: I'm going to work in the library. You prepare your laptop and books at a quiet library table before beginning a work session.
work-313.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. Ik is first and ga second; the library location stands before final werken.
work-313.forms: Gaan plus an infinitive can express an intention or upcoming action. Werken stays without te. In de bibliotheek says where the work will happen; it does not say that the speaker works as a librarian.
work-313.compare: English going to work can be ambiguous between travel and intention; this sentence expresses the planned activity in the library.

mistake.wrong: Ik ga in de bibliotheek te werken.
mistake.right: Ik ga in de bibliotheek werken.
mistake.why: Gaan takes a bare infinitive here.

work-313.practiceGuide: A modal such as kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen or zullen is the finite verb. The action verb stays an infinitive, normally at the end of the main clause: Ik wil de soep proberen. No te directly after these modals. If the infinitive itself requires te, that separate relationship remains: Ik zal proberen te slapen. English to has no single Dutch translation.

work-314.meaning: Our cooking lesson starts now. At a teaching kitchen, the instructor calls the gathered learners to begin preparing ingredients.
work-314.order: The full subject Onze kookles is first and begint second; nu gives the start time.
work-314.forms: Kookles is a de-word and takes possessive onze. Begint is third-person singular because lesson is singular, even though onze refers to several people. Nu means now.
work-314.compare: English our lesson starts and Dutch onze les begint agree with the singular lesson rather than its plural participants.

mistake.why: The singular de-word kookles takes onze.

work-314.practiceGuide: Ons/onze both mean our. Use ons before a singular het-word (ons huis, ons budget); onze before singular de-words and all plurals (onze auto, onze huizen). The number of owners does not choose ons/onze. Other possessives such as mijn/je/jouw/zijn/haar do not change that way. Je can mean you or your depending on its grammatical role.

work-315.meaning: She bought the paint for us. A friend brings the paint she bought for your home-decorating project and gives it to your group.
work-315.order: Zij is first and heeft second; paint and beneficiary are before the final participle.
work-315.forms: Heeft makes zij singular she. Ons is the object pronoun us after voor, not a possessive before verf. Kopen has participle gekocht. Verf is a de-word for paint.
work-315.compare: English bought for us and Dutch heeft voor ons gekocht express a completed purchase for a group’s benefit.

mistake.wrong: Zij hebben de verf voor ons gekocht.
mistake.right: Zij heeft de verf voor ons gekocht.
mistake.why: She requires singular heeft; hebben would mean they.

work-315.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-315.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-316.meaning: Let's make a decision about the holiday dates. Two friends compare possible holiday periods and agree that it is time to choose the dates.
work-316.order: Laten we introduces a joint proposal; the full decision phrase comes before final nemen.
work-316.forms: Een beslissing nemen means to make a decision. Over introduces its topic. Vakantiedata is plural of vakantiedatum, with data meaning dates here, not computer information. Nemen is bare after laten.
work-316.compare: English make a decision corresponds to Dutch een beslissing nemen, literally take a decision.

mistake.wrong: Laten we een beslissing over de vakantiedata te nemen.
mistake.right: Laten we een beslissing over de vakantiedata nemen.
mistake.why: Laten takes a bare infinitive.

work-316.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-317.meaning: I need a pen with blue ink. You need a blue-ink pen to complete a paper form and ask a nearby colleague for one.
work-317.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. Ik is first and heb second; the full requested item stands before nodig.
work-317.forms: Iets nodig hebben expresses need and is present tense here, not perfect. Met blauwe inkt specifies the pen; blauwe has -e before the de-word inkt. Inkt is uncountable. Nodig is an adjective.
work-317.compare: English need a pen is one verb; Dutch places the item between heb and nodig.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb een pen met blauwe inkt nodigen.
mistake.right: Ik heb een pen met blauwe inkt nodig.
mistake.why: Nodig is not an infinitive.

work-317.practiceGuide: In iets nodig hebben, hebben is the finite verb and nodig is a predicative word, not a participle. Ik heb een pen nodig is present, not perfect just because it contains heb. Contrast ik had een pen nodig (past) and ik zal een pen nodig hebben (future/modal). Geen negates an indefinite needed item: ik heb geen pen nodig.

work-318.meaning: Will you be free next week to move house? You ask a friend whether their schedule allows them to move house next week, beside packed boxes.
work-318.order: The yes/no question starts with Zal, followed by je; zijn closes the future bracket before the purpose phrase.
work-318.forms: Both zal je and zul je are standard. Vrij means available here. Zijn is bare after zal; verhuizen takes te in the separate om phrase. Volgende week needs no preposition.
work-318.compare: English will you be free to move uses a future auxiliary and purpose; Dutch distinguishes bare zijn from om te verhuizen.

mistake.wrong: Zal je volgende week vrij te zijn?
mistake.right: Zal je volgende week vrij zijn?
mistake.why: The future auxiliary takes zijn without te.

work-318.practiceGuide: In a yes/no question the finite modal comes before the subject, and the other verb remains an infinitive: Kun je het raam openen? With subject je/jij AFTER the finite verb, the usual second-person -t drops (kun je); u retains its form. With u, both kunt u and kan u are possible; both hebt u and heeft u are standard. A bare noun request can leave an understood action unspoken: Mag ik de bon?

work-319.meaning: The recipe for this soup is simple. You show a friend the few basic ingredients needed for an uncomplicated soup recipe.
work-319.order: The full recipe phrase is first and is second; simpel is the predicate adjective.
work-319.forms: Recept is a het-word. Soep is a de-word and takes deze. Simpel after is has no attributive -e. Voor deze soep identifies which recipe is meant.
work-319.compare: English the recipe is simple and Dutch het recept is simpel have matching copular patterns.

mistake.wrong: Het recept voor deze soep is simpele.
mistake.right: Het recept voor deze soep is simpel.
mistake.why: A predicate adjective has no -e here.

work-319.practiceGuide: Before a noun an adjective usually has -e: de rode tas, het rode boek. The main beginner exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een rood boek, een nieuw gerecht. Possessives/demonstratives make that het-noun definite: ons nieuwe huis. A predicate adjective after zijn normally has no agreement -e: het huis is mooi. Comparative forms have their own spelling; do not form every ending by simply appending e.

work-320.meaning: Let's identify opportunities for volunteer work. A group compares local community projects to find where they could volunteer.
work-320.order: Laten we introduces the joint proposal; the opportunities phrase precedes final identificeren.
work-320.forms: Identificeren means to identify or establish which options are available, not yet to choose one. Kansen is plural of kans. Vrijwilligerswerk is an uncountable het-word for volunteer work. No te follows laten.
work-320.compare: English identify opportunities and Dutch kansen identificeren are both fairly formal planning language.

mistake.wrong: Laten we kansen voor vrijwilligerswerk te identificeren.
mistake.right: Laten we kansen voor vrijwilligerswerk identificeren.
mistake.why: Laten takes a bare infinitive.

work-320.practiceGuide: Laten we + infinitive means let's do something together. Laten introduces the suggestion; we names the people included, and the action verb remains an infinitive. With two action verbs, both can be infinitives: Laten we koffie gaan drinken. This is a suggestion, not the normal declarative wij laten pattern.

work-321.meaning: I'd already done the preparatory work when the technician arrived. You show a technician a workspace that you had already cleared and prepared before their arrival.
work-321.order: Had is second in the main clause and gedaan closes its bracket. Toen introduces a past-event clause with final aankwam.
work-321.forms: Had plus gedaan is past perfect: completion before another past event. Al means already. Voorbereidende takes -e after definite het werk. Aankomen is separable, but its finite verb stays joined at the end of this subordinate clause.
work-321.compare: English had already done when he arrived corresponds to Dutch had al gedaan toen hij aankwam.

mistake.wrong: Ik had het werk al doen.
mistake.right: Ik had het werk al gedaan.
mistake.why: A perfect construction needs participle gedaan.

work-321.practiceFocus: An action before another past moment
work-321.practiceGuide: Had/hadden or was/waren plus a participle expresses something already completed before a past reference point. Compare Ik heb gegeten (a completed event) with Ik had al gegeten toen hij kwam (completed before he came). Keep the auxiliary finite and the participle in its verb bracket; a toen-clause has its own final verb.

work-322.meaning: Are you working on the report about the excursion now? You ask a student at a desk whether they are currently writing the report on their class excursion.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: aan het verslag van de excursie

work-322.order: The yes/no question starts with Werk before subject je; nu and the task phrase follow.
work-322.forms: When subject je or jij follows the finite present verb, werk has no -t. Werken aan names the task being worked on. Verslag is a het-word; van de excursie specifies the report’s topic.
work-322.compare: English are you working uses a progressive question; Dutch Werk je can express the same current activity.

mistake.wrong: Werkt je nu aan het verslag?
mistake.right: Werk je nu aan het verslag?
mistake.why: Before subject je, the present werk loses -t.

work-322.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-323.meaning: Is that your final answer to the invitation? You check whether a friend’s decision about an invitation is settled before replying to the organiser.

parts.label: predicate adjective
parts.text: je definitieve antwoord op de uitnodiging

work-323.order: The yes/no question begins with Is; dat is subject and the answer phrase follows.
work-323.forms: Je is possessive before definitieve antwoord. Definitieve takes -e after a possessive, including with het-word antwoord. Antwoord op names what is answered. Definitief means final rather than provisional.
work-323.compare: English final answer to and Dutch definitieve antwoord op use different prepositions.

mistake.why: A possessive noun phrase takes the attributive -e here.

work-323.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-324.meaning: Where is his office in this building? At an office-building reception, you ask where a colleague’s office is located.
work-324.order: Waar is first and is second; zijn kantoor is subject, with the building phrase specifying the search area.
work-324.forms: Zijn before kantoor is possessive his, not an infinitive. Kantoor and gebouw are het-words; gebouw takes dit. Waar asks for location, not direction.
work-324.compare: English where is his office and Dutch waar is zijn kantoor both put the location question first.

mistake.wrong: Waar is zijn kantoor in deze gebouw?
mistake.right: Waar is zijn kantoor in dit gebouw?
mistake.why: Singular het-word gebouw takes dit.

work-324.practiceGuide: A question word or complete question phrase comes first, then the finite verb and usually the subject: Hoe laat komt de trein? Hoe laat is ONE constituent despite being two words. Subject questions are different: Wie komt? already has wie as its subject. Other infinitives/participles usually close the clause's verb bracket.

work-325.meaning: The maintenance of this machine is important. You explain the importance of regular maintenance while inspecting a workshop machine with a colleague.
work-325.order: The full maintenance phrase is first and is second; belangrijk gives the judgement.
work-325.forms: Onderhoud is an uncountable het-word. Van deze machine names what is maintained; machine is a de-word. Belangrijk is predicative without -e. This statement evaluates maintenance, rather than issuing a specific obligation.
work-325.compare: English maintenance of this machine and Dutch onderhoud van deze machine are noun phrases serving as subject.

mistake.wrong: Het onderhoud van deze machine is belangrijke.
mistake.right: Het onderhoud van deze machine is belangrijk.
mistake.why: Predicate belangrijk has no -e.

work-325.practiceFocus: An infinitive used to name an activity
work-325.practiceGuide: An infinitive can name an activity and function like a noun: het lezen, het schoonmaken. A whole activity phrase can be the subject: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak. Its finite verb still follows that entire first constituent. Infinitives used as nouns normally take het; de was is a separate noun meaning laundry. Do not confuse the activity noun with a conjugated verb.

work-326.meaning: I'll call the dentist back after work. You check a missed call from the dental practice while leaving work and plan to return it afterward.
work-326.order: Ik is first and bel second; the recipient and time phrase come before final terug.
work-326.forms: Terugbellen is separable. Bel is the ik form. Na mijn werk means after my work period. The present can express a firm near-future intention in this context. Tandarts is a de-word.
work-326.compare: English call the dentist back and Dutch bel de tandarts terug split the callback idea around its object.

mistake.wrong: Ik terugbel de tandarts na mijn werk.
mistake.right: Ik bel de tandarts na mijn werk terug.
mistake.why: In this main clause the separable particle goes at the end.

work-326.practiceGuide: In a main clause a separable verb's finite part and particle separate: ik ruim ... op. With a modal, the infinitive stays together: ik moet opruimen. A participle normally puts ge between prefix and stem (opgeruimd), but stems beginning with unstressed be-/ver-/ont-/her- may not add ge. With te, split around te: op te ruimen. Learn the whole expression and its meaning.

work-327.meaning: We have found a solution to the storage problem. A team shows newly fitted shelves that solve the shortage of storage space in their room.
work-327.order: In a main clause the finite verb is in second position, after one first constituent. The other verb normally occurs toward the end. We is first and hebben second; the full solution object precedes final gevonden.
work-327.forms: Vinden has irregular participle gevonden and takes hebben here. Oplossing voor names the problem solved. Opslagprobleem is a compound het-word. The perfect reports a completed discovery, not only the need to find a solution.
work-327.compare: English solution to and Dutch oplossing voor use different prepositions.

mistake.why: The perfect needs participle gevonden.

work-327.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-327.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-328.meaning: Is the bicycle shop open on Mondays? Outside a bicycle shop with a bicycle to repair, you ask a companion whether it opens on Mondays.
work-328.order: Is starts the yes/no question; the shop subject is followed by the Monday phrase and open.
work-328.forms: Fietsenwinkel is a compound de-word. Open is predicative, with no -e. Op maandag can express a recurring Monday schedule in this opening-hours context; it can also mean a specific Monday in other contexts.
work-328.compare: English open on Mondays can correspond to Dutch op maandag open in a regular-schedule question.

mistake.wrong: Zijn de fietsenwinkel op maandag open?
mistake.right: Is de fietsenwinkel op maandag open?
mistake.why: Singular winkel takes is.

work-328.practiceGuide: A yes/no question begins with the finite verb: Je hebt tijd → Heb je tijd? Put the subject after that verb. If je/jij is the subject following the verb, a present-tense -t usually disappears: jij werkt → werk jij. This does not mean that every written je removes -t: possessive je inside je broer is not the subject pronoun.

work-329.meaning: The company has updated its policy. An administrator replaces an old company-policy folder with the newly updated version and informs a colleague.
work-329.order: The company subject is first and heeft second; zijn beleid is inside the perfect bracket before bijgewerkt.
work-329.forms: Bijwerken is separable and has participle bijgewerkt. Bedrijf and beleid are het-words. Zijn refers possessively to the company, meaning its here; grammatical gender does not make the company a person. Beleid is generally uncountable.
work-329.compare: English its policy corresponds to Dutch zijn beleid for this singular company reference.

mistake.wrong: Het bedrijf heeft zijn beleid gebijwerkt.
mistake.right: Het bedrijf heeft zijn beleid bijgewerkt.
mistake.why: Ge goes after separable bij.

work-329.practiceFocus: Perfect tense and the verb bracket
work-329.practiceGuide: Use a finite auxiliary (heb/heeft/hebben or ben/is/zijn) and a past participle. The auxiliary occupies the main clause's finite-verb position; the participle usually closes its verb bracket. Unstressed object pronouns normally occur early: Ik heb het gisteren gedaan. Auxiliary choice depends on the verb and meaning: an activity such as cycling uses hebben, directed movement can use zijn. Perfect and simple past overlap; neither is selected only by 'today' versus 'yesterday'.

work-330.meaning: Be smart and compare the prices before you book. Before booking accommodation, you compare several options and encourage a friend to check their prices.
work-330.order: Two imperatives are joined by en; voordat introduces a clause ending in finite boekt.
work-330.forms: Wees is the irregular imperative of zijn. Slim is predicative without -e. Vergelijk is the imperative stem of vergelijken. In voordat je boekt, subject je precedes boekt, so its -t stays. Prijzen means monetary prices here.
work-330.compare: English be smart and compare before you book has parallel instructions and a time clause, like Dutch.

mistake.wrong: Wees slim en vergelijk de prijzen voordat boekt je.
mistake.right: Wees slim en vergelijk de prijzen voordat je boekt.
mistake.why: The subordinate clause places the verb after its subject.

work-330.practiceGuide: Omdat means because and is written as one word. Subordinators such as omdat, dat, als, terwijl and toen introduce a clause whose verb or verb group normally comes at the end. Dutch allows more than one order inside some final verb clusters; do not call every alternative wrong. If the whole embedded clause comes first, the main clause's finite verb follows it before the subject.
